Kim Yo Jong, a top Democratic People's Republic of Korea official and the sister of leader Kim Jong Un , said on Tuesday that the accusations are another "sinister attempt" by the US to damage Pyongyang's public image. The US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), the Secret Service and cyber analysts have said North Korea orchestrated the hack, which has been described as the largest in history. This is the latest hack to be linked to North Korea, which has been accused of relying on cyber-crime to help finance its sanctioned economy. Blockchain analysts and the FBI have said the attack was led by state-backed hacking group TraderTraitor. The FBI has called on industry partners to help block transactions involving cryptocurrency accounts linked to the group. "The US has made a trite provocation of linking it with the Democratic People's Republic of Korea again," Kim Yo-jong, the director of North Korea's General Affairs Department, said in a statement. Pyongyang has systematically built its cyber operations, recruiting promising students from universities and sending them to hacker units overseen by North Korea's intelligence agency, research groups like the S Rajaratnam School of International Studies think tank have said. Since the incident, the crypto giant has largely focused its public statements on the technical nature of the breach and its response to protect users. That figure reflects the impact of the hack, subsequent withdrawals and market price changes. "Withdrawal levels are stabilising to what we would consider normal and expected on-chain activity," she added. The company said last week that initial checks indicated that an engineer's laptop had been compromised, enabling an attacker to make unauthorised withdrawals. Chainalysis, a crypto analytics firm, said it had "high confidence" that a North Korean is linked to the hack.

North Korea is an impoverished country with very little industry and heavy international sanctions and experts say the regime uses cyber crime as a way to bring money in.

Binance, which was founded in China in 2017, allows users to trade digital assets and is estimated to have more than 300 million registered users worldwide.
A lot of the fear right now from Binance users - and the crypto industry at large - is whether or not Binance will actually be capable of covering this enormous financial loss.

Binance told its users "your money is safe, and we're covering every loss".

Daniel Tunkel, of the London-based Edwin Coe law firm, said that would "come down to what [customers] have been promised in their contracts", and "where Binance can be sued for non-performance, if it comes to it".

extraction.body: Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, says it has frozen around half of the funds stolen in a "complex" hack, after $6.3bn (£4.7bn) was accessed in what is believed to be a record heist . The firm said $3bn of its stolen digital assets had been secured - but many were still in the hands of unidentified hackers. It initially thought an engineer's laptop had been compromised, allowing unauthorised withdrawals, but later said the attack was wider. Several analytics firms have linked the hack, which eclipses a $1.5bn (£1.12bn) heist on the Bybit exchange in 2025, to a North Korean hacking unit. The US Secret Service said it was "working around the clock" "to identify, freeze, trace, and recover" stolen funds. America's lead federal agency for investigating financial crimes added that it would "identify the cyber criminals responsible and bring them to justice", while Binance also said it was working with the FBI. While Binance said its US-facing exchange was unaffected, the US would still have jurisdiction to investigate the hack and help track down stolen funds - an effort which generally involves a global law enforcement effort. The hack also involved some US-linked assets, such as stablecoins Tether and Circle – cryptocurrencies pegged to the dollar. Binance told its users "your money is safe, and we're covering every loss". It had initially suspended all deposits and withdrawals - but then said in an update that "deposits remain unaffected". Who could be behind the Binance hack and what we know so far Binance's co-CEO Richard Teng said: "This was not carried out by one person. Our initial investigation suggested that the security incident may have involved a compromised laptop, however our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach." Teng also describes how the hackers used "a self-destruct mechanism that destroyed tooling and traces as they went, making it more difficult for us to trace and investigate". Initially, the company had indicated the breach "may have started with a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop" but later statements have pointed to a broader breach. In a later update, the firm said it had "set aside" more than $6.34B in company funds to cover the stolen assets and was "actively buying" a range of crypto tokens. The Binance hack spooked cryptocurrency markets on Friday. The price of Bitcoin was down 5% to $76,800 in Friday afternoon trading in New York. Cryptocurrency exchange Coinbase was down 12% as investors also reacted to earnings results in which the firm reported revenue slightly below expectations. Robinhood, a financial services company that trades in cryptocurrency, was down 7.8%. Binance, which was founded in China in 2017, allows users to trade digital assets and is estimated to have more than 300 million registered users worldwide. The company said in 2024 that it had more than $160bn in assets under its custody. A lot of the fear right now from Binance users - and the crypto industry at large - is whether or not Binance will actually be capable of covering this enormous financial loss. The company has said repeatedly that customer funds will be covered and that the firm is strong enough to weather the storm. But crypto history watchers have been pointing out online that this is exactly the kind of message that FTX CEO Sam Bankman-Fried gave before his crypto exchange collapsed in 2022, leading to huge losses for customers and the industry. Several experts have warned customers not to regard Binance's promise to cover losses as legally binding and said they may need to pursue litigation to recover them. Daniel Tunkel, of the London-based Edwin Coe law firm, said that would "come down to what [customers] have been promised in their contracts", and "where Binance can be sued for non-performance, if it comes to it". Binance has been subject of regulatory scrutiny around the world. Meanwhile, AI-powered investigations company TRM Labs said that several elements of the attack resembled earlier North Korean-linked incidents, including the Bybit hack. In the last five years the crypto industry has been beset by enormous losses from hackers. In nearly all cases investigators have blamed hackers from North Korea, pointing to the infamous Lazarus Group - also know as TraderTraitor. The names refer to clusters of cyber criminals accused of working directly for the regime. The FBI has called on industry partners to help block transactions involving cryptocurrency accounts linked to the group.
"The US has made a trite provocation of linking it with the Democratic People's Republic of Korea again," Kim Yo-jong, the director of North Korea's General Affairs Department, said in a statement.

That figure reflects the impact of the hack, subsequent withdrawals and market price changes.
"Withdrawal levels are stabilising to what we would consider normal and expected on-chain activity," she added.
The company said last week that initial checks indicated that an engineer's laptop had been compromised, enabling an attacker to make unauthorised withdrawals.
Trading in major cryptocurrencies on Binance has since resumed after the exchange worked with issuers to freeze assets impacted by the hack.

The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) says North Korea was responsible for the hack.
If the accusations are true, the record-making heist shows how powerful suspected North Korean hackers have become.
The cyber-attack, which the company describes as complex, is believed to be the largest ever of its kind.

It initially thought an engineer's laptop had been compromised, allowing unauthorised withdrawals, but later said the attack was wider. Several analytics firms have linked the hack, which eclipses a $1.5bn (£1.12bn) heist on the Bybit exchange in 2025, to a North Korean hacking unit. The US Secret Service said it was "working around the clock" "to identify, freeze, trace, and recover" stolen funds. America's lead federal agency for investigating financial crimes added that it would "identify the cyber criminals responsible and bring them to justice", while Binance also said it was working with the FBI. While Binance said its US-facing exchange was unaffected, the US would still have jurisdiction to investigate the hack and help track down stolen funds - an effort which generally involves a global law enforcement effort. The hack also involved some US-linked assets, such as stablecoins Tether and Circle – cryptocurrencies pegged to the dollar. Binance told its users "your money is safe, and we're covering every loss". It had initially suspended all deposits and withdrawals - but then said in an update that "deposits remain unaffected". Our initial investigation suggested that the security incident may have involved a compromised laptop, however our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach." Teng also describes how the hackers used "a self-destruct mechanism that destroyed tooling and traces as they went, making it more difficult for us to trace and investigate". Initially, the company had indicated the breach "may have started with a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop" but later statements have pointed to a broader breach. sources.title: Musk is throttling Grok because its cost is 'unsustainably high' - Yahoo Finance
passages: "The cost of serving Grok Bot was unsustainably high relative to revenue," Musk wrote on his social media platform, X.
The sudden throttling highlights one of the biggest questions swirling around the AI revolution: whether demand from users will be enough to sustain a business.
It turns out, at least in Musk's case, that demand isn't the problem.
The tenor of the comments on Musk's own platform, filled with Grok users, turned noticeably sharp : "Yet another Elon rug-pull."
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
Elon Musk said on Sunday that Grok ( SPCX ) users would run up against usage limits more quickly than normal because servicing Grok Bot has become too expensive.
Musk suddenly changing Grok subscriptions so that the AI-usage meter runs faster has struck users and tech observers as unfair and worrisome for SpaceX's business.
Musk was responding to an X user complaining that their Grok Bot usage jumped to 100% before their reset date, when typically they never reached their cap while using the AI agent.
Now it's unsustainable and loses money (???)", wrote former xAI worker Benjamin De Kraker in a post on X .
Other commenters pointed to a bold and now ironic post Musk sent out a few days ago , saying, "Saving money for the distant future is pointless with the advent of super intelligent abundance."
That's why the revenue question is increasingly critical and why Musk's admission is so significant.
The AI business is running into real-world limitations.
Another way to think through the change is that Musk was simply offering an introductory rate to hook users.

Elon Musk said on Sunday that Grok ( SPCX ) users would run up against usage limits more quickly than normal because servicing Grok Bot has become too expensive. "The cost of serving Grok Bot was unsustainably high relative to revenue," Musk wrote on his social media platform, X. The sudden throttling highlights one of the biggest questions swirling around the AI revolution: whether demand from users will be enough to sustain a business. It turns out, at least in Musk's case, that demand isn't the problem. The cost is. Musk was responding to an X user complaining that their Grok Bot usage jumped to 100% before their reset date, when typically they never reached their cap while using the AI agent. User demand is just one side of the AI market equation, and the businesses churning out sophisticated and expensive models have to — or will have to, eventually — generate revenue to cover their heightened costs. The economics of the still-new and messy AI industry suggest that even healthy demand can't always sustain the AI tools they're selling. Not at these prices — for the users (cheap) and for the corporate compute (expensive; just look at the computing bills ). That's why the revenue question is increasingly critical and why Musk's admission is so significant. The AI business is running into real-world limitations. Musk suddenly changing Grok subscriptions so that the AI-usage meter runs faster has struck users and tech observers as unfair and worrisome for SpaceX's business. "Two weeks ago Grok Bot was an incredible success story powering SpaceXai's revenue growth. Now it's unsustainable and loses money (???)", wrote former xAI worker Benjamin De Kraker in a post on X . Other commenters pointed to a bold and now ironic post Musk sent out a few days ago , saying, "Saving money for the distant future is pointless with the advent of super intelligent abundance." The tenor of the comments on Musk's own platform, filled with Grok users, turned noticeably sharp : "Yet another Elon rug-pull." "Just being sensible," he wrote on X , in response to a comment suggesting that investors would punish SpaceX for the decision. In fact, shares are up 5% on Monday. And why shouldn't they be? Wall Street has always loved fiscal responsibility and capitalizing on demand. Another way to think through the change is that Musk was simply offering an introductory rate to hook users. Perhaps AI subscriptions are going through their own version of the "VC subsidy," popularized when Uber, Lyft, and other venture-backed apps offered discounts and super-low rates to boost adoption and engagement, only for the apps to sharply increase prices once users became reliant on the services. The classic introductory rate strategy. Read the latest financial and business news from Yahoo Finance

sources.title: Elon Musk says Grok Bot was throttled because costs were ‘unsustainably high’ — as users call the move a ‘rug pull’ - TechRadar
passages: If you noticed that you burned through your Grok Bot usage much faster than usual in recent days, there’s a reason for that: Elon Musk intentionally limited users’ AI agent allowances in the face of “unsustainably high costs.” And as you’d expect, a lot of people are unhappy with that.
This changing landscape hasn’t gone down well with many users, of course.
Users claimed their usage had suddenly gone from 50% to 100%, 35% to 78%, and 70% to 100%, all supposedly without using Grok Bot at all.
The revelation came about after an X user pinged platform owner Musk , asking for a Grok Bot reset after they surprisingly hit their 100% usage limit, four days before it was due to reset.
They additionally commented that “Normally I don’t even reach 100%.”
But it’s unlikely that AI producers will be able to subsidize their products’ costs to users forever.

If you noticed that you burned through your Grok Bot usage much faster than usual in recent days, there’s a reason for that: Elon Musk intentionally limited users’ AI agent allowances in the face of “unsustainably high costs.” And as you’d expect, a lot of people are unhappy with that. The revelation came about after an X user pinged platform owner Musk , asking for a Grok Bot reset after they surprisingly hit their 100% usage limit, four days before it was due to reset. They additionally commented that “Normally I don’t even reach 100%.” Musk then replied to the post , stating: “The cost of serving Grok Bot was unsustainably high relative to revenue.” Many X users seemed irked by the situation, with several saying that their Grok Bot usage had hit the 100% limit while they were sleeping and not using any AI agents. Users claimed their usage had suddenly gone from 50% to 100%, 35% to 78%, and 70% to 100%, all supposedly without using Grok Bot at all. Elon Musk’s comments come amid broader scrutiny of the financial sustainability of many AI products. Tech stocks — including those of many leading AI firms — fell sharply last week as investors grew concerned over the profitability of the industry , with Google revealing that its own AI summaries have hurt its search advertising revenue. Concerns have also been raised in recent months over the finances involved in many AI companies’ offerings. For instance, users of AI tools like ChatGPT and Claude Code can often spend many times more in tokens than they’re actually paying in monthly subscriptions, leading to questions over how sustainable many AI business models really are and whether things will need to be adjusted in the near future. This changing landscape hasn’t gone down well with many users, of course. One thread on Reddit dubbed Musk’s about-face an “indirect rug pull” of Grok Bot, with features and usage limited in a bid to cut costs. But it’s unlikely that AI producers will be able to subsidize their products’ costs to users forever. Usage limits will necessarily need to tighten (as OpenAI quietly announced recently, much to the frustration of users ) and prices will need to increase for these business models to make sense. So don’t be surprised if Grok Bot’s lower cap is just the first of many big changes looming on the horizon. sources.title: Elon Musk throttles Grok Bot limits due to ‘unsustainably high’ costs
passages: Grok Bot has been positioned as a success story for the newly public SpaceX, which said in a filing last month that AI now makes up 52% of company income.
Its renamed “Super Intelligence” division actually turned a profit of $431 million, which is a rarity in the AI industry.
Its profit would’ve been higher if not for $1.2 billion of one-time costs related to its acquisition of Cursor .
Musk recently referred to Grok Bot as having “the fastest growth of a product that I’ve ever seen in my life.”
Over Halloween weekend, some Grok Bot users awoke to something especially spooky: Their weekly usage limits were unexpectedly maxed out, even if they hadn’t been using SpaceX’s agentic AI overnight.
Some users reported on X that their usage jumped from as low as 50% to 100% .
He has not addressed the issue on his main feed but has continued boasting that Grok Bot can help you buy gifts for your family.
The cost of serving Grok Bot was unsustainably high relative to revenue
Musk has not yet shared how subscribers’ usage limits will be impacted moving forward.
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk confirmed in an X post on Sunday that this was not a glitch.

Start your Independent Membership today. Users of Grok Bot, the personal assistant made by Elon Musk ’s artificial intelligence firm, are finding themselves cut off from their AI agents. SpaceXSI, which includes both Elon Musk’s rocket firm as well as its AI work and the social network X , introduced Grok Bot in August. It described the tool as “AI teammates you can give real work to”. It came amid a flurry of such personal AI assistants launched by many of the world’s biggest artificial intelligence firms. The most prominent among them is Meta ’s Muse , though OpenAI has also pushed its own system, called Dots. Now, however, Mr Musk has been hit by complaints from users of the service who say that they are rapidly running out of usage and so finding themselves unable to access the tool. As with many AI systems, each Grok Bot user is allocated a certain amount of work and any questions will run that down. In response to a complaint from a user who complained that they had hit their weekly maximum usage with four days until it was reset, Mr Musk said that the system was expensive and was not making enough money. “The cost of serving Grok Bot was unsustainably high relative to revenue,” he wrote in a reply on X. Such personal assistants are particularly resource intensive, because they can be asked to undertake complicated tasks and operate as a team of co-ordinated AI systems. But companies are nonetheless pushing them as the future of both our work and personal lives. Many of those companies – including SpaceXSI, Meta and OpenAI – are losing vast sums of money across their AI work. But they appear to be betting that the cost of running the systems will serve as an investment for the future, by allowing them to acquire users and build more complex systems. But it remains unclear how those companies will be able to keep running the tools and making money, given the vast expense required to actually offer them. While all of the companies have some kind of payment system – Grok Bot is only available to those who pay for SpaceXSI’s AI tools, and OpenAI has restricted Dots to users with its more expensive accounts – some, including Meta’s Muse, come with a free tier. At the moment, that is the primary way that companies make back some of the cost of offering those personal agents. But Meta may have offered a hint at how it could make money from its Muse service in other ways: in its latest results, the first since it released its agentic assistant, it noted that shopping was one of the top ways that users were interacting with it, which could presumably be used for advertising in the future. SpaceX’s AI system is intended as a competitor to other personal agent such as Meta’s Muse and OpenAI’s Dots – but the company is finding it expensive to run
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Users of Grok Bot, the personal assistant made by Elon Musk ’s artificial intelligence firm, are finding themselves cut off from their AI agents.

SpaceXSI, which includes both Elon Musk’s rocket firm as well as its AI work and the social network X , introduced Grok Bot in August. It described the tool as “AI teammates you can give real work to”.

It came amid a flurry of such personal AI assistants launched by many of the world’s biggest artificial intelligence firms. The most prominent among them is Meta ’s Muse , though OpenAI has also pushed its own system, called Dots.

Now, however, Mr Musk has been hit by complaints from users of the service who say that they are rapidly running out of usage and so finding themselves unable to access the tool. As with many AI systems, each Grok Bot user is allocated a certain amount of work and any questions will run that down.

In response to a complaint from a user who complained that they had hit their weekly maximum usage with four days until it was reset, Mr Musk said that the system was expensive and was not making enough money. “The cost of serving Grok Bot was unsustainably high relative to revenue,” he wrote in a reply on X.

Such personal assistants are particularly resource intensive, because they can be asked to undertake complicated tasks and operate as a team of co-ordinated AI systems. But companies are nonetheless pushing them as the future of both our work and personal lives.

Many of those companies – including SpaceXSI, Meta and OpenAI – are losing vast sums of money across their AI work. But they appear to be betting that the cost of running the systems will serve as an investment for the future, by allowing them to acquire users and build more complex systems.

But it remains unclear how those companies will be able to keep running the tools and making money, given the vast expense required to actually offer them. While all of the companies have some kind of payment system – Grok Bot is only available to those who pay for SpaceXSI’s AI tools, and OpenAI has restricted Dots to users with its more expensive accounts – some, including Meta’s Muse, come with a free tier.

At the moment, that is the primary way that companies make back some of the cost of offering those personal agents. But Meta may have offered a hint at how it could make money from its Muse service in other ways: in its latest results, the first since it released its agentic assistant, it noted that shopping was one of the top ways that users were interacting with it, which could presumably be used for advertising in the future.

Elon Musk said on Sunday that Grok ( SPCX ) users would run up against usage limits more quickly than normal because servicing Grok Bot has become too expensive. "The cost of serving Grok Bot was unsustainably high relative to revenue," Musk wrote on his social media platform, X. The sudden throttling highlights one of the biggest questions swirling around the AI revolution: whether demand from users will be enough to sustain a business. It turns out, at least in Musk's case, that demand isn't the problem. The cost is. Musk was responding to an X user complaining that their Grok Bot usage jumped to 100% before their reset date, when typically they never reached their cap while using the AI agent. User demand is just one side of the AI market equation, and the businesses churning out sophisticated and expensive models have to — or will have to, eventually — generate revenue to cover their heightened costs. The economics of the still-new and messy AI industry suggest that even healthy demand can't always sustain the AI tools they're selling. Not at these prices — for the users (cheap) and for the corporate compute (expensive; just look at the computing bills ). That's why the revenue question is increasingly critical and why Musk's admission is so significant. The AI business is running into real-world limitations. Musk suddenly changing Grok subscriptions so that the AI-usage meter runs faster has struck users and tech observers as unfair and worrisome for SpaceX's business. "Two weeks ago Grok Bot was an incredible success story powering SpaceXai's revenue growth. Now it's unsustainable and loses money (???)", wrote former xAI worker Benjamin De Kraker in a post on X . Other commenters pointed to a bold and now ironic post Musk sent out a few days ago , saying, "Saving money for the distant future is pointless with the advent of super intelligent abundance." The tenor of the comments on Musk's own platform, filled with Grok users, turned noticeably sharp : "Yet another Elon rug-pull." "Just being sensible," he wrote on X , in response to a comment suggesting that investors would punish SpaceX for the decision. In fact, shares are up 5% on Monday. And why shouldn't they be? Wall Street has always loved fiscal responsibility and capitalizing on demand. Another way to think through the change is that Musk was simply offering an introductory rate to hook users. Perhaps AI subscriptions are going through their own version of the "VC subsidy," popularized when Uber, Lyft, and other venture-backed apps offered discounts and super-low rates to boost adoption and engagement, only for the apps to sharply increase prices once users became reliant on the services. The classic introductory rate strategy. Read the latest financial and business news from Yahoo Finance

passages: Grok Bot has been positioned as a success story for the newly public SpaceX, which said in a filing last month that AI now makes up 52% of company income.

Its profit would’ve been higher if not for $1.2 billion of one-time costs related to its acquisition of Cursor .
Musk recently referred to Grok Bot as having “the fastest growth of a product that I’ve ever seen in my life.”
Over Halloween weekend, some Grok Bot users awoke to something especially spooky: Their weekly usage limits were unexpectedly maxed out, even if they hadn’t been using SpaceX’s agentic AI overnight.
Some users reported on X that their usage jumped from as low as 50% to 100% .
He has not addressed the issue on his main feed but has continued boasting that Grok Bot can help you buy gifts for your family.
The cost of serving Grok Bot was unsustainably high relative to revenue
Musk has not yet shared how subscribers’ usage limits will be impacted moving forward.
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk confirmed in an X post on Sunday that this was not a glitch.

Start your Independent Membership today. Users of Grok Bot, the personal assistant made by Elon Musk ’s artificial intelligence firm, are finding themselves cut off from their AI agents. SpaceXSI, which includes both Elon Musk’s rocket firm as well as its AI work and the social network X , introduced Grok Bot in August. It described the tool as “AI teammates you can give real work to”. It came amid a flurry of such personal AI assistants launched by many of the world’s biggest artificial intelligence firms. The most prominent among them is Meta ’s Muse , though OpenAI has also pushed its own system, called Dots. Now, however, Mr Musk has been hit by complaints from users of the service who say that they are rapidly running out of usage and so finding themselves unable to access the tool. As with many AI systems, each Grok Bot user is allocated a certain amount of work and any questions will run that down. In response to a complaint from a user who complained that they had hit their weekly maximum usage with four days until it was reset, Mr Musk said that the system was expensive and was not making enough money. “The cost of serving Grok Bot was unsustainably high relative to revenue,” he wrote in a reply on X. Such personal assistants are particularly resource intensive, because they can be asked to undertake complicated tasks and operate as a team of co-ordinated AI systems. But companies are nonetheless pushing them as the future of both our work and personal lives. Many of those companies – including SpaceXSI, Meta and OpenAI – are losing vast sums of money across their AI work. But they appear to be betting that the cost of running the systems will serve as an investment for the future, by allowing them to acquire users and build more complex systems. But it remains unclear how those companies will be able to keep running the tools and making money, given the vast expense required to actually offer them. While all of the companies have some kind of payment system – Grok Bot is only available to those who pay for SpaceXSI’s AI tools, and OpenAI has restricted Dots to users with its more expensive accounts – some, including Meta’s Muse, come with a free tier. At the moment, that is the primary way that companies make back some of the cost of offering those personal agents. But Meta may have offered a hint at how it could make money from its Muse service in other ways: in its latest results, the first since it released its agentic assistant, it noted that shopping was one of the top ways that users were interacting with it, which could presumably be used for advertising in the future. sources.title: Crypto firm Binance covers 90% of losses after $6.3bn hack - BBC
passages: Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, says it has covered 90% of the $6.3bn (£4.7bn) assets stolen in a hack on Thursday.

Richard Teng, Binance's co-chief executive officer, said the hack was carried out by more than one person, and the hackers used sophisticated methods to hide their tracks, such as a "self-destruct mechanism".
In an update on Sunday, Binance said withdrawals had been restored on several of its networks, after they were suspended following the hack.
"Binance will absorb the financial impact of these stolen funds, not our users," the company said in a statement on Saturday.

Binance's initial investigation suggested an engineer's laptop was compromised, which allowed access to unauthorised withdrawals, but a later update said they had uncovered "additional points of breach".
The US Secret Service said on Friday it is "working around the clock" with private sector partners "to identify, freeze, trace, and recover funds" stolen from Binance.

Two analytics firms previously told the BBC they had robust intelligence pointing to North Korean state-backed hacking unit the Lazarus Group, also known as TraderTraitor - which was specifically named by the FBI - as the likely culprits.
Binance said it had replenished the stolen assets using various funds and its own corporate treasury.
Binance, founded in China in 2017, lets users buy, sell and trade digital assets - it is estimated to have hundreds of millions of users worldwide.
The hack is believed to be the largest in history, eclipsing the record of a $1.5bn heist on the Bybit exchange in 2025 - for which the FBI also said North Korea was responsible.
Crypto is a digital asset, which doesn't exist physically and is instead accessed via digital wallets or computers.

sources.title: Binance’s $6.3 billion hack raises questions about crypto wallet safety - CNBC
passages: A security incident at digital asset exchange Binance on Thursday affected some $6.3 billion in client assets, making it the largest crypto theft on record.
Experts whom CNBC interviewed said the security incidents on the crypto exchanges aren't surprising, especially in light of recent artificial intelligence hacking incidents .
That's because the hack may have involved a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, Binance said in a post on X .
Two high-profile security breaches this week – including the biggest cryptocurrency theft in history – are raising questions on the safety of storing funds in a wallet on a crypto exchange .
Binance and Polymarket reassured users that they would make affected investors whole.
That's a sign that users should feel confident in crypto exchanges, according to Ido Ben-Natan , CEO of blockchain security company Blockaid.
"I actually think no users will lose any money," he said.
"Binance has said they're going to cover everything… I actually don't think it's a bad idea for users to put money in these exchanges.
As a result, a crypto wallet could ultimately become a safer place to hold funds compared to other options, since the industry will have the experience of how to handle these attacks, Ben-Natan said.
However, crypto may be a unique target for hackers in a changing cybersecurity landscape, these experts told CNBC.

Earlier that day, prediction market platform Polymarket temporarily halted trading on its international exchange after a third-party data provider was hacked, resulting in at least $2.7 million being drained from users' wallets.
The same was true of Polymarket's domestic exchange.
U.S. regulated platforms Coinbase and Robinhood were also unaffected by the security breach on Binance, though shares of both fell on Friday in the aftermath.
In another social media post, BInance later said its investigation uncovered additional points of breach , though the company didn't specify what they were.

extraction.body: Two high-profile security breaches this week – including the biggest cryptocurrency theft in history – are raising questions on the safety of storing funds in a wallet on a crypto exchange . A security incident at digital asset exchange Binance on Thursday affected some $6.3 billion in client assets, making it the largest crypto theft on record. Earlier that day, prediction market platform Polymarket temporarily halted trading on its international exchange after a third-party data provider was hacked, resulting in at least $2.7 million being drained from users' wallets. The company's international platform operates on the Polygon blockchain. Experts whom CNBC interviewed said the security incidents on the crypto exchanges aren't surprising, especially in light of recent artificial intelligence hacking incidents . Most of these experts even said that observers should expect more security incidents, at least in the near term, as that problem worsens. "I think it's extremely dangerous," said Tyler Moore, a cybersecurity professor at the University of Tulsa who has followed the asset class for more than a decade. "I think you should be very wary of leaving any significant amount of funds in an exchange… there are no built-in protections for when these inevitable hacks take place." For instance, banking customers can rely on the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation to insure deposits up to $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, in the event of an institution's failure. There is no similar form of coverage available for funds lost from a cryptocurrency exchange, noted Moore. Binance and Polymarket reassured users that they would make affected investors whole. That's a sign that users should feel confident in crypto exchanges, according to Ido Ben-Natan , CEO of blockchain security company Blockaid. "I actually think no users will lose any money," he said. "Binance has said they're going to cover everything… I actually don't think it's a bad idea for users to put money in these exchanges. These exchanges need to work really hard to make sure they don't take another hit like this." Ben-Natan noted that while he thinks more hacks are likely as the cybersecurity landscape changes due to AI, he said it will only make the crypto industry stronger. As a result, a crypto wallet could ultimately become a safer place to hold funds compared to other options, since the industry will have the experience of how to handle these attacks, Ben-Natan said. A key point is that while Binance experienced a security incident on its offshore platform, its regulated, centralized U.S. exchange did not have a similar issue. The same was true of Polymarket's domestic exchange. U.S. regulated platforms Coinbase and Robinhood were also unaffected by the security breach on Binance, though shares of both fell on Friday in the aftermath. In a Friday appearance on CNBC's " Squawk on the Street ," the Commodity Futures Trading Commission — the federal regulator of derivatives — Chairman Michael Selig said that the offshore nature of these incidents was critical to note. "They don't have the same sorts of safeguards that we have in our financial markets," he said. "We want to offer a federal option to these exchanges to come and register with the CFTC, and they would be subject to the same sorts of cybersecurity safeguards that we have in our markets today." Brett Falk, a professor and director of the Crypto and Society Lab at the University of Pennsylvania, said that U.S. regulations likely wouldn't have stopped an incident like that of Binance on Thursday. That's because the hack may have involved a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, Binance said in a post on X . "Most of the regulation doesn't touch the specific software stack you have to use to authenticate people," Falk said. In another social media post, BInance later said its investigation uncovered additional points of breach , though the company didn't specify what they were. Falk echoed the argument by Ben-Natan that individuals likely won't face losses, and that it's better for traders to leave funds with an exchange where they have the financial backing of a company rather than in a self-custody wallet where no one can refund their losses in the event of a hack. Ben-Natan added that traders should feel secure based on how many incidents companies like his catch that don't become news. That's because the security technology often works and stops them before they become major incidents. However, crypto may be a unique target for hackers in a changing cybersecurity landscape, these experts told CNBC. That's because of how much liquidity individuals can quickly access in the event of a successful breach. It's why Ryan Kirkley, CEO of blockchain infrastructure company Global Settlement Network, thinks traders should be cautious leaving their funds in any wallet that's not backed by insurance until financial companies upgrade their security infrastructure. "I do not think there's anything right now that is a common solution in the marketplace where your assets are truly safe," Kirkley said. "Unless you are dealing with a reputable and firm broker-dealer that provides an asset insurance, you are risking your assets putting them into any ecosystem today just simply because there's so much unknown," he added. sources.title: Binance sees more than $4.6 billion in withdrawals after largest crypto hack in history - Yahoo Finance
passages: Binance has seen $3.64 billion in net outflows since it gradually restored user withdrawals following the largest crypto hack in history, which the FBI linked to North Korea.
The world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange said that it processed $4.649 billion in withdrawals and approximately $1.01 billion in deposits.

"The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) is releasing information advising the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (North Korea) was responsible for the theft of more than $6 billion USD in virtual assets from cryptocurrency exchange Binance, on or about October 29, 2026," a press release said.
Binance was hit late Thursday by a hack that investigators said impacted roughly $6.3 billion in funds, with roughly half of those assets frozen.
Other major crypto assets also tumbled after the hack, with ether ( ETH-USD ) dropping to roughly $2,200.
Binance's native token, BNB ( BND-USD ), also fell.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
"We continue working with industry partners to complete the remaining acquisitions," Binance said in an update on X.
Meanwhile, the total crypto market has lost roughly 3% in value, or $80 billion, over the last seven days, according to CoinMarketCap data.

sources.title: Binance clients pull US$4.7B after hack as crypto world studies fallout
passages: SINGAPORE/PARIS/NEW YORK — Binance’s customers have withdrawn a net $4.72 billion from the world’s biggest cryptocurrency exchange since it reopened, after hackers stole around $6.3 billion of crypto from the platform in what could be the largest-ever financial heist.

Binance, which says it has more than 335 million users worldwide and average daily trading volumes of $95 billion across digital assets and derivatives, said it had also seen $2.7 billion in customer inflows since Sunday and that withdrawal volumes were stabilizing after an “initial spike.” Data from data analytics provider DeFiLlama showed several crypto exchanges received notable inflows to their platforms since Binance opened withdrawals, although it was unclear what share came from users moving funds off Binance.
Binance itself processed net outflows of about $6 billion over 72 hours in 2022 after the collapse of FTX.
Binance said the net outflows amounted to around 3 per cent of the assets on its platform, a relatively modest figure that analysts said suggested customer confidence had largely held up.
“Binance will absorb the financial impact of the stolen funds, not our users,” the company said in a statement on X.
“A hack at a crypto exchange is bank robbery at the speed of the internet, which creates an unstable risk profile for anyone responsible for other people’s capital,” he said.

Analysts and crypto experts said the fallout appeared limited so far, and there was little sign of an impact on broader financial markets despite deepening ties between crypto and mainstream finance in recent years.
NO RUSH TO WITHDRAW Some traders told Reuters they were keeping their accounts on Binance.

extraction.body: SINGAPORE/PARIS/NEW YORK — Binance’s customers have withdrawn a net $4.72 billion from the world’s biggest cryptocurrency exchange since it reopened, after hackers stole around $6.3 billion of crypto from the platform in what could be the largest-ever financial heist. The exchange froze withdrawals for more than two days after the hack, which the FBI said was carried out by North Korea, then started allowing customers to withdraw again on Sunday morning. The theft has underlined the vulnerability of digital assets to attacks and raised questions about the impact of the hack on Binance, which has vowed to repay customers in full. Binance said the net outflows amounted to around 3 per cent of the assets on its platform, a relatively modest figure that analysts said suggested customer confidence had largely held up. Most withdrawals from the platform were in the form of Tether’s USDT stablecoin, Binance added. The outflow compares with about $7 billion withdrawn from Circle’s USDC stablecoin over a week after the collapse of Silicon Valley Bank in 2023. Binance itself processed net outflows of about $6 billion over 72 hours in 2022 after the collapse of FTX. The attack marks a step-up in North Korea’s crypto thefts. Blockchain analytics firm TRM Labs said North Korea-linked hackers have stolen $7.4 billion so far in 2026. Analysts and crypto experts said the fallout appeared limited so far, and there was little sign of an impact on broader financial markets despite deepening ties between crypto and mainstream finance in recent years. “Binance will absorb the financial impact of the stolen funds, not our users,” the company said in a statement on X. Binance said it was covering the losses with company funds and had already raised $6 billion from its corporate treasury, an insurance fund and reserves set aside for security breaches. “It has not yet triggered widespread panic or a massive, concentrated withdrawal,” said Tim Sun, a senior researcher at HashKey Group 3887.HK, a digital asset financial service company in Hong Kong. Binance, which says it has more than 335 million users worldwide and average daily trading volumes of $95 billion across digital assets and derivatives, said it had also seen $2.7 billion in customer inflows since Sunday and that withdrawal volumes were stabilizing after an “initial spike.” Data from data analytics provider DeFiLlama showed several crypto exchanges received notable inflows to their platforms since Binance opened withdrawals, although it was unclear what share came from users moving funds off Binance. OKX recorded $284.87 million in inflows in the last 24 hours, followed by Gate with $93.22 million in inflows and Bybit, which saw $29.25 million in inflows. NO RUSH TO WITHDRAW Some traders told Reuters they were keeping their accounts on Binance. Ryan Tan, a Binance user, said he was in no hurry to withdraw his funds from the platform, as he had already kept his account fairly light since the collapse of FTX four years ago. “After the FTX collapse, I decided to hold everything on my wallet instead of leaving them on exchanges,” said the 39-year-old. After hitting a six-week low on Friday, bitcoin BTC= prices recovered through the weekend to trade above $77,000 on Monday, while ether ETH= also rebounded from a two-month low. Stablecoin market capitalizations, often viewed as a gauge of money moving into and out of crypto markets, have fallen since Friday, suggesting some investors have shifted funds into cash or traditional assets. Binance started allowing US dollar cash withdrawals again on Monday. “HIGHLY COMPLEX” MONEY LAUNDERING The FBI said on Saturday that the North Korean state-sponsored group TraderTraitor was responsible for the attack. Analysts said the attack’s scale could curb institutional appetite for cryptocurrencies. Spot bitcoin ETFs recorded outflows of $643 million on Friday, the largest daily withdrawal in October, while more than $1.3 billion in leveraged positions were liquidated, according to Ari Redbord, global head of policy at TRM Labs. “A hack at a crypto exchange is bank robbery at the speed of the internet, which creates an unstable risk profile for anyone responsible for other people’s capital,” he said. About half of the stolen funds were held in stablecoins and have been frozen by issuers including Circle, which said on Monday it had frozen more than $1.1 billion in USDC USDC=. According to blockchain analytics firm Elliptic, the hackers still control around $3.28 billion, mostly in bitcoin and ether, and only a negligible amount has been cashed out of crypto and into fiat currency. Elliptic described the laundering process as “highly complex and clearly automated.” Jonathan Benton, founder and chief executive at crypto asset recovery firm iSanctuary, said blockchain technology exists to trace stolen funds, but the challenge is turning that intelligence into rapid, coordinated action before those assets disappear. “The future of crypto won’t be decided by how much money enters the market, but by how safe that money is once it’s there,” said Benton, former head of the international corruption unit of the UK’s National Crime Agency. (Reporting by Rae Wee and Ankur Banerjee in Singapore, Elizabeth Howcroft in Paris and Hannah Lang in New York; Writing by Scott Murdoch and Tom Westbrook; Editing by Sonali Paul, Xevi Fontdegloria, Mark Potter, Rod Nickel)

coreStoryFacts.text: Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, says it has covered 90% of the $6.3bn (£4.7bn) assets stolen in a hack on Thursday.

Richard Teng, Binance's co-chief executive officer, said the hack was carried out by more than one person, and the hackers used sophisticated methods to hide their tracks, such as a "self-destruct mechanism".
In an update on Sunday, Binance said withdrawals had been restored on several of its networks, after they were suspended following the hack.
"Binance will absorb the financial impact of these stolen funds, not our users," the company said in a statement on Saturday.

Binance's initial investigation suggested an engineer's laptop was compromised, which allowed access to unauthorised withdrawals, but a later update said they had uncovered "additional points of breach".
The US Secret Service said on Friday it is "working around the clock" with private sector partners "to identify, freeze, trace, and recover funds" stolen from Binance.

Two analytics firms previously told the BBC they had robust intelligence pointing to North Korean state-backed hacking unit the Lazarus Group, also known as TraderTraitor - which was specifically named by the FBI - as the likely culprits.
Binance said it had replenished the stolen assets using various funds and its own corporate treasury.
Binance, founded in China in 2017, lets users buy, sell and trade digital assets - it is estimated to have hundreds of millions of users worldwide.
The hack is believed to be the largest in history, eclipsing the record of a $1.5bn heist on the Bybit exchange in 2025 - for which the FBI also said North Korea was responsible.
Crypto is a digital asset, which doesn't exist physically and is instead accessed via digital wallets or computers.
A security incident at digital asset exchange Binance on Thursday affected some $6.3 billion in client assets, making it the largest crypto theft on record.
Experts whom CNBC interviewed said the security incidents on the crypto exchanges aren't surprising, especially in light of recent artificial intelligence hacking incidents .
That's because the hack may have involved a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, Binance said in a post on X .
Two high-profile security breaches this week – including the biggest cryptocurrency theft in history – are raising questions on the safety of storing funds in a wallet on a crypto exchange .
Binance and Polymarket reassured users that they would make affected investors whole.
That's a sign that users should feel confident in crypto exchanges, according to Ido Ben-Natan , CEO of blockchain security company Blockaid.
"I actually think no users will lose any money," he said.
"Binance has said they're going to cover everything… I actually don't think it's a bad idea for users to put money in these exchanges.
As a result, a crypto wallet could ultimately become a safer place to hold funds compared to other options, since the industry will have the experience of how to handle these attacks, Ben-Natan said.
However, crypto may be a unique target for hackers in a changing cybersecurity landscape, these experts told CNBC.

Earlier that day, prediction market platform Polymarket temporarily halted trading on its international exchange after a third-party data provider was hacked, resulting in at least $2.7 million being drained from users' wallets.
The same was true of Polymarket's domestic exchange.
U.S. regulated platforms Coinbase and Robinhood were also unaffected by the security breach on Binance, though shares of both fell on Friday in the aftermath.

The remaining 10% may take longer to source in the required amounts, the company added. Binance has consistently pledged to cover 100% of the losses from what is suspected to be crypto's biggest hack on record and said it has set aside more than $6.34bn in company funds to do so. "Binance will absorb the financial impact of these stolen funds, not our users," the company said in a statement on Saturday. In an update on Sunday, Binance said withdrawals had been restored on several of its networks, after they were suspended following the hack. It previously said withdrawals would be resumed in phases. The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) said on Saturday that North Korea was responsible for the attack. The FBI said it had observed hackers converting stolen assets into a type of cryptocurrency called Ethereum and that it is expected that the assets will then be converted again using decentralised finance and instant swap services. Two analytics firms previously told the BBC they had robust intelligence pointing to North Korean state-backed hacking unit the Lazarus Group, also known as TraderTraitor - which was specifically named by the FBI - as the likely culprits. Speaking to reporters on Saturday night, US President Donald Trump said the US is still unsure who the culprits are. "We're learning about it. We don't know if it's North Korea - but if it is, we'll talk to North Korea about it," he said. Binance said it had replenished the stolen assets using various funds and its own corporate treasury. All holdings of the cryptocurrencies bitcoin, Ethereum and Tether are covered, along with seven other widely-traded crypto assets, the company said. The hack is believed to be the largest in history, eclipsing the record of a $1.5bn heist on the Bybit exchange in 2025 - for which the FBI also said North Korea was responsible. extraction.body: Two high-profile security breaches this week – including the biggest cryptocurrency theft in history – are raising questions on the safety of storing funds in a wallet on a crypto exchange . A security incident at digital asset exchange Binance on Thursday affected some $6.3 billion in client assets, making it the largest crypto theft on record. Earlier that day, prediction market platform Polymarket temporarily halted trading on its international exchange after a third-party data provider was hacked, resulting in at least $2.7 million being drained from users' wallets. The company's international platform operates on the Polygon blockchain. Experts whom CNBC interviewed said the security incidents on the crypto exchanges aren't surprising, especially in light of recent artificial intelligence hacking incidents . Most of these experts even said that observers should expect more security incidents, at least in the near term, as that problem worsens. "I think it's extremely dangerous," said Tyler Moore, a cybersecurity professor at the University of Tulsa who has followed the asset class for more than a decade. "I think you should be very wary of leaving any significant amount of funds in an exchange… there are no built-in protections for when these inevitable hacks take place." For instance, banking customers can rely on the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation to insure deposits up to $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, in the event of an institution's failure. There is no similar form of coverage available for funds lost from a cryptocurrency exchange, noted Moore. Binance and Polymarket reassured users that they would make affected investors whole. That's a sign that users should feel confident in crypto exchanges, according to Ido Ben-Natan , CEO of blockchain security company Blockaid. "I actually think no users will lose any money," he said. "Binance has said they're going to cover everything… I actually don't think it's a bad idea for users to put money in these exchanges. These exchanges need to work really hard to make sure they don't take another hit like this." Ben-Natan noted that while he thinks more hacks are likely as the cybersecurity landscape changes due to AI, he said it will only make the crypto industry stronger. As a result, a crypto wallet could ultimately become a safer place to hold funds compared to other options, since the industry will have the experience of how to handle these attacks, Ben-Natan said. A key point is that while Binance experienced a security incident on its offshore platform, its regulated, centralized U.S. exchange did not have a similar issue. The same was true of Polymarket's domestic exchange. U.S. regulated platforms Coinbase and Robinhood were also unaffected by the security breach on Binance, though shares of both fell on Friday in the aftermath. In a Friday appearance on CNBC's " Squawk on the Street ," the Commodity Futures Trading Commission — the federal regulator of derivatives — Chairman Michael Selig said that the offshore nature of these incidents was critical to note. "They don't have the same sorts of safeguards that we have in our financial markets," he said. "We want to offer a federal option to these exchanges to come and register with the CFTC, and they would be subject to the same sorts of cybersecurity safeguards that we have in our markets today." Brett Falk, a professor and director of the Crypto and Society Lab at the University of Pennsylvania, said that U.S. regulations likely wouldn't have stopped an incident like that of Binance on Thursday. That's because the hack may have involved a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, Binance said in a post on X . "Most of the regulation doesn't touch the specific software stack you have to use to authenticate people," Falk said. In another social media post, BInance later said its investigation uncovered additional points of breach , though the company didn't specify what they were. Falk echoed the argument by Ben-Natan that individuals likely won't face losses, and that it's better for traders to leave funds with an exchange where they have the financial backing of a company rather than in a self-custody wallet where no one can refund their losses in the event of a hack. Ben-Natan added that traders should feel secure based on how many incidents companies like his catch that don't become news. That's because the security technology often works and stops them before they become major incidents. However, crypto may be a unique target for hackers in a changing cybersecurity landscape, these experts told CNBC. That's because of how much liquidity individuals can quickly access in the event of a successful breach. It's why Ryan Kirkley, CEO of blockchain infrastructure company Global Settlement Network, thinks traders should be cautious leaving their funds in any wallet that's not backed by insurance until financial companies upgrade their security infrastructure. "I do not think there's anything right now that is a common solution in the marketplace where your assets are truly safe," Kirkley said. "Unless you are dealing with a reputable and firm broker-dealer that provides an asset insurance, you are risking your assets putting them into any ecosystem today just simply because there's so much unknown," he added. relevantPassages.text: A security incident at digital asset exchange Binance on Thursday affected some $6.3 billion in client assets, making it the largest crypto theft on record.
Experts whom CNBC interviewed said the security incidents on the crypto exchanges aren't surprising, especially in light of recent artificial intelligence hacking incidents .
That's because the hack may have involved a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, Binance said in a post on X .
Two high-profile security breaches this week – including the biggest cryptocurrency theft in history – are raising questions on the safety of storing funds in a wallet on a crypto exchange .
Binance and Polymarket reassured users that they would make affected investors whole.
That's a sign that users should feel confident in crypto exchanges, according to Ido Ben-Natan , CEO of blockchain security company Blockaid.
"I actually think no users will lose any money," he said.
"Binance has said they're going to cover everything… I actually don't think it's a bad idea for users to put money in these exchanges.
As a result, a crypto wallet could ultimately become a safer place to hold funds compared to other options, since the industry will have the experience of how to handle these attacks, Ben-Natan said.
However, crypto may be a unique target for hackers in a changing cybersecurity landscape, these experts told CNBC.

Earlier that day, prediction market platform Polymarket temporarily halted trading on its international exchange after a third-party data provider was hacked, resulting in at least $2.7 million being drained from users' wallets.
The same was true of Polymarket's domestic exchange.
U.S. regulated platforms Coinbase and Robinhood were also unaffected by the security breach on Binance, though shares of both fell on Friday in the aftermath.
In another social media post, BInance later said its investigation uncovered additional points of breach , though the company didn't specify what they were.

Initial findings pointed to a compromised laptop, but further review revealed broader security breaches. "This was a complex attack," Teng said. "The attacker also used a self-destruct mechanism that destroyed tooling and tracers." Around $3.24 billion remains in addresses linked to the theft, according to Tom Robinson, chief scientist and co-founder at blockchain analytics company Elliptic. The attack has rattled crypto markets, and bitcoin ( BTC-USD ) traded at around $77,700 on Monday. Meanwhile, the total crypto market has lost roughly 3% in value, or $80 billion, over the last seven days, according to CoinMarketCap data. Other major crypto assets also tumbled after the hack, with ether ( ETH-USD ) dropping to roughly $2,200. Binance's native token, BNB ( BND-USD ), also fell.

sources.title: Binance clients pull US$4.7B after hack as crypto world studies fallout
passages: SINGAPORE/PARIS/NEW YORK — Binance’s customers have withdrawn a net $4.72 billion from the world’s biggest cryptocurrency exchange since it reopened, after hackers stole around $6.3 billion of crypto from the platform in what could be the largest-ever financial heist.

Binance, which says it has more than 335 million users worldwide and average daily trading volumes of $95 billion across digital assets and derivatives, said it had also seen $2.7 billion in customer inflows since Sunday and that withdrawal volumes were stabilizing after an “initial spike.” Data from data analytics provider DeFiLlama showed several crypto exchanges received notable inflows to their platforms since Binance opened withdrawals, although it was unclear what share came from users moving funds off Binance.
Binance itself processed net outflows of about $6 billion over 72 hours in 2022 after the collapse of FTX.
Binance said the net outflows amounted to around 3 per cent of the assets on its platform, a relatively modest figure that analysts said suggested customer confidence had largely held up.
“Binance will absorb the financial impact of the stolen funds, not our users,” the company said in a statement on X.
“A hack at a crypto exchange is bank robbery at the speed of the internet, which creates an unstable risk profile for anyone responsible for other people’s capital,” he said.

Analysts and crypto experts said the fallout appeared limited so far, and there was little sign of an impact on broader financial markets despite deepening ties between crypto and mainstream finance in recent years.
NO RUSH TO WITHDRAW Some traders told Reuters they were keeping their accounts on Binance.
Binance started allowing US dollar cash withdrawals again on Monday.

extraction.body: SINGAPORE/PARIS/NEW YORK — Binance’s customers have withdrawn a net $4.72 billion from the world’s biggest cryptocurrency exchange since it reopened, after hackers stole around $6.3 billion of crypto from the platform in what could be the largest-ever financial heist. The exchange froze withdrawals for more than two days after the hack, which the FBI said was carried out by North Korea, then started allowing customers to withdraw again on Sunday morning. The theft has underlined the vulnerability of digital assets to attacks and raised questions about the impact of the hack on Binance, which has vowed to repay customers in full. Binance said the net outflows amounted to around 3 per cent of the assets on its platform, a relatively modest figure that analysts said suggested customer confidence had largely held up. Most withdrawals from the platform were in the form of Tether’s USDT stablecoin, Binance added. The outflow compares with about $7 billion withdrawn from Circle’s USDC stablecoin over a week after the collapse of Silicon Valley Bank in 2023. Binance itself processed net outflows of about $6 billion over 72 hours in 2022 after the collapse of FTX. The attack marks a step-up in North Korea’s crypto thefts. Blockchain analytics firm TRM Labs said North Korea-linked hackers have stolen $7.4 billion so far in 2026. Analysts and crypto experts said the fallout appeared limited so far, and there was little sign of an impact on broader financial markets despite deepening ties between crypto and mainstream finance in recent years. “Binance will absorb the financial impact of the stolen funds, not our users,” the company said in a statement on X. Binance said it was covering the losses with company funds and had already raised $6 billion from its corporate treasury, an insurance fund and reserves set aside for security breaches. “It has not yet triggered widespread panic or a massive, concentrated withdrawal,” said Tim Sun, a senior researcher at HashKey Group 3887.HK, a digital asset financial service company in Hong Kong. Binance, which says it has more than 335 million users worldwide and average daily trading volumes of $95 billion across digital assets and derivatives, said it had also seen $2.7 billion in customer inflows since Sunday and that withdrawal volumes were stabilizing after an “initial spike.” Data from data analytics provider DeFiLlama showed several crypto exchanges received notable inflows to their platforms since Binance opened withdrawals, although it was unclear what share came from users moving funds off Binance. OKX recorded $284.87 million in inflows in the last 24 hours, followed by Gate with $93.22 million in inflows and Bybit, which saw $29.25 million in inflows. NO RUSH TO WITHDRAW Some traders told Reuters they were keeping their accounts on Binance. Ryan Tan, a Binance user, said he was in no hurry to withdraw his funds from the platform, as he had already kept his account fairly light since the collapse of FTX four years ago. “After the FTX collapse, I decided to hold everything on my wallet instead of leaving them on exchanges,” said the 39-year-old. After hitting a six-week low on Friday, bitcoin BTC= prices recovered through the weekend to trade above $77,000 on Monday, while ether ETH= also rebounded from a two-month low. Stablecoin market capitalizations, often viewed as a gauge of money moving into and out of crypto markets, have fallen since Friday, suggesting some investors have shifted funds into cash or traditional assets. Binance started allowing US dollar cash withdrawals again on Monday. “HIGHLY COMPLEX” MONEY LAUNDERING The FBI said on Saturday that the North Korean state-sponsored group TraderTraitor was responsible for the attack. Analysts said the attack’s scale could curb institutional appetite for cryptocurrencies. Spot bitcoin ETFs recorded outflows of $643 million on Friday, the largest daily withdrawal in October, while more than $1.3 billion in leveraged positions were liquidated, according to Ari Redbord, global head of policy at TRM Labs. “A hack at a crypto exchange is bank robbery at the speed of the internet, which creates an unstable risk profile for anyone responsible for other people’s capital,” he said. About half of the stolen funds were held in stablecoins and have been frozen by issuers including Circle, which said on Monday it had frozen more than $1.1 billion in USDC USDC=. According to blockchain analytics firm Elliptic, the hackers still control around $3.28 billion, mostly in bitcoin and ether, and only a negligible amount has been cashed out of crypto and into fiat currency. Elliptic described the laundering process as “highly complex and clearly automated.” Jonathan Benton, founder and chief executive at crypto asset recovery firm iSanctuary, said blockchain technology exists to trace stolen funds, but the challenge is turning that intelligence into rapid, coordinated action before those assets disappear. “The future of crypto won’t be decided by how much money enters the market, but by how safe that money is once it’s there,” said Benton, former head of the international corruption unit of the UK’s National Crime Agency. (Reporting by Rae Wee and Ankur Banerjee in Singapore, Elizabeth Howcroft in Paris and Hannah Lang in New York; Writing by Scott Murdoch and Tom Westbrook; Editing by Sonali Paul, Xevi Fontdegloria, Mark Potter, Rod Nickel)

sources.title: Ford promises not to sell your driving habits to data brokers
passages: “Protecting your personal information is one way we intend to earn it every day.” "“We know that trust is earned.”" - Kristin Jones, Ford’s chief privacy officer The promise comes in the wake of General Motors agreeing to pay $220 million to settle claims that it illegally sold driver and location information to data brokers.

Ford vowed to never sell customer driving data to third-party data brokers as part of a new privacy promise aimed at setting the automaker apart from competitors that have faced legal and regulatory blowback for sharing telematics with data brokers without authorization.

Over half contacted domains that specialize in advertising, tracking, or analytics (ATA), like Adobe, LexisNexis, and Amplitude, which gather details about your vehicle or driving behavior to sell to insurance companies or target you with ads.

Ford said it surveyed over 1,000 US customers, both Ford and non-Ford owners, who agreed that privacy is a top concern while over half of the respondents said they understand that some data sharing is okay.

It will also “provide clear and easy-to-understand information about how we use your personal information.” And while Ford says it will still use data to improve safety, it will allow customers to adjust how much or how little data they would prefer to share.
They can sue Ford, force the company to sign legally binding agreements to correct the issue, and impose substantial financial fines.
Those legal agreements contain standard exceptions that allow Ford to share your data, such as complying with police requests or working with outside service providers.

extraction.body: Ford vowed to never sell customer driving data to third-party data brokers as part of a new privacy promise aimed at setting the automaker apart from competitors that have faced legal and regulatory blowback for sharing telematics with data brokers without authorization. As part of its new promise, Ford says it will strive to protect customer data by using aggregating and anonymizing techniques. It will also “provide clear and easy-to-understand information about how we use your personal information.” And while Ford says it will still use data to improve safety, it will allow customers to adjust how much or how little data they would prefer to share. In making an explicit pledge not to sell customer data to outside firms, Ford is trying to position itself as one of the better actors in an industry rife with shady practices. “We know that trust is earned,” Kristin Jones, chief privacy officer at Ford, writes in a blog post. “Protecting your personal information is one way we intend to earn it every day.” "“We know that trust is earned.”" - Kristin Jones, Ford’s chief privacy officer The promise comes in the wake of General Motors agreeing to pay $220 million to settle claims that it illegally sold driver and location information to data brokers. The agreement requires GM to limit the driving data it collects and obtain “express consent” from drivers before collecting their information. Other automakers have been caught with their hands in the customer data cookie jar. A recent examination of 21 vehicle brands found that every single one transmitted data to at least one third-party domain over Wi-Fi. Over half contacted domains that specialize in advertising, tracking, or analytics (ATA), like Adobe, LexisNexis, and Amplitude, which gather details about your vehicle or driving behavior to sell to insurance companies or target you with ads. In a recent report, Mozilla crowned modern connected cars “the worst category of products for privacy” ever reviewed. The global nonprofit found that 92 percent of the reviewed automakers provide drivers with little (if any) control over their personal data, with 84 percent sharing user data with outside parties. Ford said it surveyed over 1,000 US customers, both Ford and non-Ford owners, who agreed that privacy is a top concern while over half of the respondents said they understand that some data sharing is okay. If Ford publicly promises something like, “We never sell your driving data to brokers” but breaks that promise, the FTC and state attorneys general can step in. They can sue Ford, force the company to sign legally binding agreements to correct the issue, and impose substantial financial fines. It should be noted that a company’s blog post or public promise is not a legal contract. Those legal agreements contain standard exceptions that allow Ford to share your data, such as complying with police requests or working with outside service providers. Also, opting out of data sharing does come with tradeoffs. While Ford states that data collection depends on the features you want to use, turning off vehicle tracking or location sharing often disables key features like built-in navigation, remote start, and wireless software updates.

extraction.body: Just days after General Motors agreed to settle a lawsuit over selling customers' data without their consent, Ford announced a new "Privacy Promise" policy . In a statement shared on a new website from the manufacturer, Ford promised owners that they are in the driver's seat when it comes to their data. The site offers guidance on data sharing and collection and how to deactivate and opt out of sharing various types of data, whether on the automaker's webpages, in its app or within the car itself. "We design and build our products with privacy in mind — from collection of data to its use and storage and even disposal. This can include privacy-enhancing technologies like anonymizing or aggregating data to further protect your privacy," the statement began. "We strive to provide clear and easy-to-understand information about how we use your personal information. This empowers you to navigate your privacy choices with confidence. Once you make those choices, we respect your decision," the statement continued. Calling the move the "right thing to do," Ford shared that its updated vehicle privacy settings will allow users "to control what data you want to share, subject to the features and services you wish to enjoy." "We also never sell data about how you drive your vehicle to data brokers," Ford maintained, a sticking point following General Motors' lawsuit , which saw the Ford rival agree to pay $200 million in a settlement with 36 states following the incident, after it illegally sold drivers' personal information to third parties without their consent, per a Washington State release regarding the suit. As much as Ford said it acknowledged user privacy, it noted that after surveying just over 1,000 Ford customers, it found customers also "understand the value of data sharing" and want to be the ones making the ultimate decision when it comes to what they want to share. "A value our survey respondents kept returning to was control: the ability to adjust their settings on demand and in detail," Ford added. But, as automotive outlet The Drive notes, there is no one place to turn everything off, forcing Ford owners to do lots of reading and searching to fully opt out of data sharing and customize their Ford experience. While some found the timing of Ford's new website launch uncoincidental amid its longtime feud with GM, in a statement to TechCrunch , Ford's chief privacy officer Kristin Jones said she wouldn't be commenting "on what our competitors are doing, or anything that's sort of been in the news." She did say, however, that as more and more consumers grow wary of whether companies will "take care with their data," Ford wants to make sure it's "building that trust relationship with them."
