extraction.body: Ford vowed to never sell customer driving data to third-party data brokers as part of a new privacy promise aimed at setting the automaker apart from competitors that have faced legal and regulatory blowback for sharing telematics with data brokers without authorization. As part of its new promise, Ford says it will strive to protect customer data by using aggregating and anonymizing techniques. It will also “provide clear and easy-to-understand information about how we use your personal information.” And while Ford says it will still use data to improve safety, it will allow customers to adjust how much or how little data they would prefer to share. In making an explicit pledge not to sell customer data to outside firms, Ford is trying to position itself as one of the better actors in an industry rife with shady practices. “We know that trust is earned,” Kristin Jones, chief privacy officer at Ford, writes in a blog post. “Protecting your personal information is one way we intend to earn it every day.” "“We know that trust is earned.”" - Kristin Jones, Ford’s chief privacy officer The promise comes in the wake of General Motors agreeing to pay $220 million to settle claims that it illegally sold driver and location information to data brokers. The agreement requires GM to limit the driving data it collects and obtain “express consent” from drivers before collecting their information. Other automakers have been caught with their hands in the customer data cookie jar. A recent examination of 21 vehicle brands found that every single one transmitted data to at least one third-party domain over Wi-Fi. Over half contacted domains that specialize in advertising, tracking, or analytics (ATA), like Adobe, LexisNexis, and Amplitude, which gather details about your vehicle or driving behavior to sell to insurance companies or target you with ads. In a recent report, Mozilla crowned modern connected cars “the worst category of products for privacy” ever reviewed. The global nonprofit found that 92 percent of the reviewed automakers provide drivers with little (if any) control over their personal data, with 84 percent sharing user data with outside parties. Ford said it surveyed over 1,000 US customers, both Ford and non-Ford owners, who agreed that privacy is a top concern while over half of the respondents said they understand that some data sharing is okay. If Ford publicly promises something like, “We never sell your driving data to brokers” but breaks that promise, the FTC and state attorneys general can step in. They can sue Ford, force the company to sign legally binding agreements to correct the issue, and impose substantial financial fines. It should be noted that a company’s blog post or public promise is not a legal contract. Those legal agreements contain standard exceptions that allow Ford to share your data, such as complying with police requests or working with outside service providers. Also, opting out of data sharing does come with tradeoffs. While Ford states that data collection depends on the features you want to use, turning off vehicle tracking or location sharing often disables key features like built-in navigation, remote start, and wireless software updates.

extraction.body: Your connected car knows more about your daily driving habits than you realize. This is why Ford unveiled its new Privacy Promise to keep your vehicle data safe and let you control what you share. It explains what information connected vehicles collect, why they need it, and how owners can manage their privacy settings. Ford says its connected vehicles collect three types of information: vehicle diagnostics, driving characteristics, and location data. The automaker uses this information to power features such as embedded navigation, real-time traffic updates, and Roadside Assistance. This data also helps Ford troubleshoot problems, improve future vehicles, and personalize your driving experience. Ford says it has built privacy protections for the data, such as anonymizing or grouping data to reduce exposure of personal information. According to industry polling , only 14% of customers fully understand what their car collects. Meanwhile, Ford surveyed over 1,000 consumers for this launch and found 91% believe data privacy is a key consideration when choosing a vehicle. Chief Privacy Officer Kristin Jones told TechCrunch it felt important to be upfront with customers, not just about Ford’s practices but with an actual commitment behind them. The timing is also notable, since Ford’s upcoming connected EVs will generate even more data than before. Ford says it will never sell your driving data to brokers or insurers, and its new website lets you adjust privacy settings anytime. However, opting out comes with trade-offs. Turning off connected services can disable features such as BlueCruise, internet connectivity, and vehicle location services in the Ford app. Real-time navigation and built-in roadside assistance may also stop working. You can adjust what you share anytime through your vehicle’s center display or the Ford app. If your Ford was built in 2018 or later, you can manage these settings right from your vehicle’s screen. Ford’s privacy resources for Lincoln owners, and those residing in Mexico & Canada, are rolling out in the coming weeks, with more countries expected afterward. sources.title: Coming in 2027: Apple’s $1,000 home robot for FaceTime and switching on lights
passages: Apple’s new CEO, John Ternus, is apparently pushing the tech company’s development of household robots—and the first to debut may be a home robot designed to autonomously roam around while supporting FaceTime calls and switching lights on whenever a person enters the room.
The company is reportedly aiming to launch the robotic product with a possible price tag of $1,000 or more by 2027, although development delays may push that back to 2028.
The earliest prototypes of the home robot first came out in 2018 and received approval from former Apple CEO Tim Cook to continue the project.

The Information describes Apple’s engineers as trying to give the robot more capabilities beyond being a “fancy way to make FaceTime calls” in order to justify a high price tag, even as the team has spent years refining the software and incorporating more AI technologies.

However, the robot’s few reported features seem underwhelming so far when compared with existing smart home devices and systems, or even a run-of-the-mill robot vacuum with a clearer use case for households.
Still, Ternus has been backing this home robot as well as a separate Apple project focused on developing robots for household tasks like folding clothes, according to The Information.

The latter would presumably require robotic arms and manipulators, though it’s unclear if that means Apple has ambitions to develop a general-purpose humanoid robot for household use like robotics startups 1X and Figure AI .
The question is whether Apple can find enough customers willing to pay whatever it charges for a limited-purpose home robot.
One of the Information’s sources also described Apple as having a very small team of about 10 “true roboticists,” with many members of the initial engineering team having departed over the years.
The software side boasts a significantly larger team of approximately 300 people.

passages: Apple is reportedly building a home robot that would cost around $1,000 and handle FaceTime calls and light control, and Ars Technica frames the device as a 2027 product.
No name, price, specification or date has come from the company, so everything below rests on press reports as of November 02, 2026.
Where we offer judgment instead of reporting, we say so.
Ars Technica carries that framing, and iThinkDiff and FourWeekMBA both ran price-focused write-ups around the same figure.
The takeaway: Apple’s home robot is a credible report with a lot of unknowns.
For buyers, the practical takeaway is to plan around 2028 and treat 2027 as the optimistic case.
Buyers will compare it against what they already own.
A family that has a tablet on the kitchen counter and a speaker in the living room will ask what the robot does that those two cannot.
The reports do not say which path Apple will take, so we treat both as open.
The Apple Watch and the home speaker line both followed that arc, and a robot at $1,000 would likely start the same way.
The same reports say development could delay the release until 2028.
That is a normal spread for a first-of-its-kind Apple device, and it echoes how other new categories at the company slid when the hardware outran the software.
Component costs, tariffs and the final feature set all move before launch.
The Apple Post, per its headline, reports that Apple has explored other home-robot concepts, including ones that follow users around and fold clothes.
It fits the company’s habit of testing many prototypes and shipping few.
This is also where the hardware category meets policy.
How Apple answers will shape trust in the whole premium home segment.
J595 is the reported internal code name for the home robot project.
Investors read new categories as proof that Apple can find growth beyond the phone.
The same logic drove attention to the foldable line, which our analysis of the iPhone Duo growth case covers.
The name matters because it signals positioning.
For accessory makers and smart-home brands, the question is compatibility.
Anyone selling lights, locks or sensors will want to know whether the robot can control their devices.
The light-control capability in the reports suggests Apple plans some home-control support, but the scope is unconfirmed.

The headline claim is simple. Apple is working on a home robot, it would sell for roughly $1,000 in the United States, and it is aimed at 2027. Ars Technica carries that framing, and iThinkDiff and FourWeekMBA both ran price-focused write-ups around the same figure.

MacRumors published its own piece on November 02 and describes the HomeView Ultra name with a 9-inch screen. That matches the roughly 9-inch display in the other reporting. Nobody in the coverage cites an Apple spokesperson, and we found no on-record quote from Apple or a named Apple representative.

J595 is the internal code name that appears in the reporting. Apple uses alphanumeric identifiers like it for unreleased hardware, and they rarely tell you much about the final marketing name. HomeView Ultra is the product name some reports use, and Apple has not confirmed it.

The name matters because it signals positioning. An Ultra label attached to HomeView would place the robot as the top tier of a home line, not as a separate product family. That reading is our inference. The reports do not say how Apple will brand the device, and Apple could pick something else entirely.

Two use cases dominate the coverage. The first is FaceTime. The second is turning on lights when someone enters a room. Both rely on the same underlying idea, which is that the device carries a camera-and-sensor system and uses it to understand the room around it.

FaceTime is the more natural fit. Apple owns the call experience end to end, and a home screen built for calls plays to that strength. The reports do not describe call features in detail, so how the device would frame or follow a speaker remains outside what any outlet has confirmed.

iThinkDiff reports the HomeView Ultra robot at about $1,000. FourWeekMBA says a tabletop version could cost about the same, citing a report. Ars Technica uses the same round number in its headline framing. Every outlet qualifies it as reported and subject to change.

A four-figure sticker puts the device in an unusual spot. It would cost far more than a typical smart display, and it would land in the price range Apple normally reserves for its top-tier products. Apple has shown it will charge that much when it believes a product is new. It has also shown it will cut features to hit a target price.

Our read is that $1,000 works as a planning anchor, not a promise. Component costs, tariffs and the final feature set all move before launch. If the price holds, Apple is betting that buyers see the robot as a new category and not a pricey screen. The pattern in the industry is that sensing, on-device intelligence and reliability testing eat schedules faster than industrial design. That is general context, not a claim about J595 specifically.

For buyers, the practical takeaway is to plan around 2028 and treat 2027 as the optimistic case. For competitors, the gap is a window. Anyone selling a home robot or a premium display has at least a year to establish habits before Apple shows a finished product.

Apple’s home business has looked like a soft spot. A Yahoo Finance analysis ties the robot plan to the state of Apple’s home segment and asks what it means for AAPL stock. That framing is useful. A robot at this price signals that Apple wants to reset the home category with a flagship, not just refresh the speakers.

The broader industry is also watching robotics shift from lab demos to factory floors. Our look at how Tesla cleared a Model S line for Optimus robots shows how seriously large hardware makers now treat the field. Home robots are a different problem from factory humanoids, but investor attention to both is rising together.

The Apple Post, per its headline, reports that Apple has explored other home-robot concepts, including ones that follow users around and fold clothes. A $1,000 device will not move Apple’s revenue on its own. Apple’s scale is large enough that a first-generation home robot is a rounding error against its core lines. Our breakdown of Apple’s first earnings under Ternus shows where the company’s margin pressure actually sits.

The real signal is strategic. Investors read new categories as proof that Apple can find growth beyond the phone. The same logic drove attention to the foldable line, which our analysis of the iPhone Duo growth case covers. A home robot would extend that story into a different part of the house.

Rivals face a different calculation. If Apple legitimizes the premium home robot, competitors gain a category reference point. If it stumbles, the whole segment looks riskier. Either outcome reshapes how smart-home vendors pitch their next generation.

One more thing about the price. At $1,000, an Apple home robot competes with a laptop or a mid-range phone for the same household budget. Buyers will compare it against what they already own. A family that has a tablet on the kitchen counter and a speaker in the living room will ask what the robot does that those two cannot. Apple’s answer, based on the reports, is awareness and hands-free calls, and that case has to feel obvious in a store demo.

Retail strategy will matter as much as hardware. Apple stores let shoppers try a device in a staged room, which suits a product built around reacting to people. A boxed robot on a shelf sells poorly, while a live demo of lights switching on as a visitor walks in sells itself. Expect Apple to lean on that kind of showing if the project reaches launch.

A device that watches a room to decide when to act raises obvious privacy questions. Apple has built a brand on privacy, and it will have to explain where camera data is processed, what is stored, and who can see it. None of the reports address these points, so they remain open.

The bar here is higher than for a phone. A phone camera points where the owner points it. A home device with autonomous awareness can capture guests, children and routines without anyone choosing to record. Buyers and regulators will want clear indicators, easy off switches and plain disclosures.

This is also where the hardware category meets policy. Home cameras have already drawn scrutiny from lawmakers and security researchers, and a $1,000 Apple device would draw more. How Apple answers will shape trust in the whole premium home segment.

Support and repair raise a final question. Our coverage of the foldable line already shows how repair costs shape perception of a new Apple category. A robot with moving or sensing parts would add service complexity, and buyers at this price expect strong support. Apple has not said anything about warranty or service for the device, so that stays an open item.

A device with a camera-and-sensor system and a screen creates a new surface for software. If Apple opens it to third parties, developers could build call, reminder and household-routine experiences for a display that reacts to people. If Apple keeps it closed, the robot stays a showcase for first-party features.

The reports do not say which path Apple will take, so we treat both as open. Apple’s pattern with new hardware is to launch with a tight first-party feature set and widen access later. The Apple Watch and the home speaker line both followed that arc, and a robot at $1,000 would likely start the same way.

For accessory makers and smart-home brands, the question is compatibility. Anyone selling lights, locks or sensors will want to know whether the robot can control their devices. The light-control capability in the reports suggests Apple plans some home-control support, but the scope is unconfirmed. Vendors should watch Apple’s developer documentation for clues, since new hardware often shows up there before it ships.

Also track how the reported price evolves. If outlets converge on a different figure, that is a stronger signal than any single report. And watch whether Apple comments at all, because silence is the default until the company is ready to sell.

passages: Apple is preparing to enter the home robotics market, with a robotic smart-home device code-named J595 that could carry a price tag of roughly $1,000 or more and reach customers as early as 2027, according to reporting from The Information.

The product, which people familiar with the effort expect to be branded HomeView Ultra, would sit alongside Apple's new HomeView stationary smart display, a device that arrives in users' homes within days.
For Apple investors, the project represents a long-horizon bet on a category the company has never sold into, and one whose revenue would not materialize before the end of the decade.
The timing also matters because Apple has been selective about extending its "Ultra" branding to new products.
Component prices could push the final retail figure above the $1,000 target, and the launch could slip to 2028 if software work falls behind.
Rivals in home automation and consumer robotics would have time to respond, and any delay would leave Apple's smart-home lineup anchored by the HomeView display shipping this month.

Beyond the HomeView Ultra, he is backing a separate effort aimed at machines that can handle household chores such as folding laundry, a project that would presumably require robotic arms and manipulators.
It is unclear whether that work points toward a general-purpose humanoid robot of the kind being developed by startups 1X and Figure AI.

The report describes a core group of only about 10 "true roboticists," with many members of the original engineering team having left over the years, while the software organization counts roughly 300 people.
Apple has not publicly confirmed the project, the name, or the price.
Much of the physical hardware has been ready for about two years, but software remains the bottleneck.

The delay stems from Apple's decision to pursue a more ambitious set of AI-powered capabilities than it originally planned, when the device was conceived mostly as a way to make FaceTime calls more engaging by following a person from room to room.
The project's origins trace back to 2018 prototypes, and former Apple chief executive Tim Cook approved continued work on it.
Equipped with cameras and sensors, the robot is meant to understand its surroundings and act on its own, such as turning on lights when someone walks in or shooing a cat off a table.

The open question is commercial rather than technical: whether buyers will pay four figures for a moving screen whose demonstrated functions overlap with far cheaper smart-home gear and robot vacuums.

coreStoryFacts.text: Apple’s new CEO, John Ternus, is apparently pushing the tech company’s development of household robots—and the first to debut may be a home robot designed to autonomously roam around while supporting FaceTime calls and switching lights on whenever a person enters the room.
The company is reportedly aiming to launch the robotic product with a possible price tag of $1,000 or more by 2027, although development delays may push that back to 2028.
The earliest prototypes of the home robot first came out in 2018 and received approval from former Apple CEO Tim Cook to continue the project.

The Information describes Apple’s engineers as trying to give the robot more capabilities beyond being a “fancy way to make FaceTime calls” in order to justify a high price tag, even as the team has spent years refining the software and incorporating more AI technologies.

However, the robot’s few reported features seem underwhelming so far when compared with existing smart home devices and systems, or even a run-of-the-mill robot vacuum with a clearer use case for households.
Still, Ternus has been backing this home robot as well as a separate Apple project focused on developing robots for household tasks like folding clothes, according to The Information.

The latter would presumably require robotic arms and manipulators, though it’s unclear if that means Apple has ambitions to develop a general-purpose humanoid robot for household use like robotics startups 1X and Figure AI .
The question is whether Apple can find enough customers willing to pay whatever it charges for a limited-purpose home robot.
One of the Information’s sources also described Apple as having a very small team of about 10 “true roboticists,” with many members of the initial engineering team having departed over the years.
The software side boasts a significantly larger team of approximately 300 people.
Apple is reportedly building a home robot that would cost around $1,000 and handle FaceTime calls and light control, and Ars Technica frames the device as a 2027 product.
No name, price, specification or date has come from the company, so everything below rests on press reports as of November 02, 2026.
Where we offer judgment instead of reporting, we say so.
Ars Technica carries that framing, and iThinkDiff and FourWeekMBA both ran price-focused write-ups around the same figure.
The takeaway: Apple’s home robot is a credible report with a lot of unknowns.
For buyers, the practical takeaway is to plan around 2028 and treat 2027 as the optimistic case.
Buyers will compare it against what they already own.
A family that has a tablet on the kitchen counter and a speaker in the living room will ask what the robot does that those two cannot.
The reports do not say which path Apple will take, so we treat both as open.
The Apple Watch and the home speaker line both followed that arc, and a robot at $1,000 would likely start the same way.
The same reports say development could delay the release until 2028.
That is a normal spread for a first-of-its-kind Apple device, and it echoes how other new categories at the company slid when the hardware outran the software.
Component costs, tariffs and the final feature set all move before launch.
The Apple Post, per its headline, reports that Apple has explored other home-robot concepts, including ones that follow users around and fold clothes.

However, the robot’s few reported features seem underwhelming so far when compared with existing smart home devices and systems, or even a run-of-the-mill robot vacuum with a clearer use case for households. Is there a market for a smart home device costing more than $1,000 that moves around while hosting FaceTime calls, automatically handling room lights, and occasionally ordering the family cat to get off the dining table? One of the Information’s sources also described Apple as having a very small team of about 10 “true roboticists,” with many members of the initial engineering team having departed over the years. From a technical and safety standpoint, Apple’s initial focus on a limited-purpose home robot still makes much more sense right now than any attempt to develop a general-purpose autonomous robot that could pose greater risks when operating near humans . The question is whether Apple can find enough customers willing to pay whatever it charges for a limited-purpose home robot. The headline claim is simple. Apple is working on a home robot, it would sell for roughly $1,000 in the United States, and it is aimed at 2027. Ars Technica carries that framing, and iThinkDiff and FourWeekMBA both ran price-focused write-ups around the same figure.

MacRumors published its own piece on November 02 and describes the HomeView Ultra name with a 9-inch screen. That matches the roughly 9-inch display in the other reporting. Nobody in the coverage cites an Apple spokesperson, and we found no on-record quote from Apple or a named Apple representative.

J595 is the internal code name that appears in the reporting. Apple uses alphanumeric identifiers like it for unreleased hardware, and they rarely tell you much about the final marketing name. HomeView Ultra is the product name some reports use, and Apple has not confirmed it.

The name matters because it signals positioning. An Ultra label attached to HomeView would place the robot as the top tier of a home line, not as a separate product family. That reading is our inference. The reports do not say how Apple will brand the device, and Apple could pick something else entirely.

Two use cases dominate the coverage. The first is FaceTime. The second is turning on lights when someone enters a room. Both rely on the same underlying idea, which is that the device carries a camera-and-sensor system and uses it to understand the room around it.

FaceTime is the more natural fit. Apple owns the call experience end to end, and a home screen built for calls plays to that strength. The reports do not describe call features in detail, so how the device would frame or follow a speaker remains outside what any outlet has confirmed.

iThinkDiff reports the HomeView Ultra robot at about $1,000. FourWeekMBA says a tabletop version could cost about the same, citing a report. Ars Technica uses the same round number in its headline framing. Every outlet qualifies it as reported and subject to change.

A four-figure sticker puts the device in an unusual spot. It would cost far more than a typical smart display, and it would land in the price range Apple normally reserves for its top-tier products. Apple has shown it will charge that much when it believes a product is new. It has also shown it will cut features to hit a target price.

Our read is that $1,000 works as a planning anchor, not a promise. Component costs, tariffs and the final feature set all move before launch. If the price holds, Apple is betting that buyers see the robot as a new category and not a pricey screen. If it climbs, the device narrows to early adopters, which may be exactly the point for a first generation.

The target in the reports is 2027. The same reports say development could delay the release until 2028. That is a normal spread for a first-of-its-kind Apple device, and it echoes how other new categories at the company slid when the hardware outran the software.

We did not find a stated reason for the possible slip in the verified coverage, so we will not assign one. The pattern in the industry is that sensing, on-device intelligence and reliability testing eat schedules faster than industrial design. That is general context, not a claim about J595 specifically.

For buyers, the practical takeaway is to plan around 2028 and treat 2027 as the optimistic case. For competitors, the gap is a window. Anyone selling a home robot or a premium display has at least a year to establish habits before Apple shows a finished product.

Apple’s home business has looked like a soft spot. A Yahoo Finance analysis ties the robot plan to the state of Apple’s home segment and asks what it means for AAPL stock. That framing is useful. A robot at this price signals that Apple wants to reset the home category with a flagship, not just refresh the speakers.

The broader industry is also watching robotics shift from lab demos to factory floors. Our look at how Tesla cleared a Model S line for Optimus robots shows how seriously large hardware makers now treat the field. Home robots are a different problem from factory humanoids, but investor attention to both is rising together.

The Apple Post, per its headline, reports that Apple has explored other home-robot concepts, including ones that follow users around and fold clothes. That suggests the J595 is the product that survived a wider exploration, not Apple’s only idea. It fits the company’s habit of testing many prototypes and shipping few.

A $1,000 device will not move Apple’s revenue on its own. Apple’s scale is large enough that a first-generation home robot is a rounding error against its core lines. Our breakdown of Apple’s first earnings under Ternus shows where the company’s margin pressure actually sits.

The real signal is strategic. Investors read new categories as proof that Apple can find growth beyond the phone. The same logic drove attention to the foldable line, which our analysis of the iPhone Duo growth case covers. A home robot would extend that story into a different part of the house.

Rivals face a different calculation. If Apple legitimizes the premium home robot, competitors gain a category reference point. If it stumbles, the whole segment looks riskier. Either outcome reshapes how smart-home vendors pitch their next generation.

One more thing about the price. At $1,000, an Apple home robot competes with a laptop or a mid-range phone for the same household budget. Buyers will compare it against what they already own. A family that has a tablet on the kitchen counter and a speaker in the living room will ask what the robot does that those two cannot. Apple’s answer, based on the reports, is awareness and hands-free calls, and that case has to feel obvious in a store demo.

Retail strategy will matter as much as hardware. Apple stores let shoppers try a device in a staged room, which suits a product built around reacting to people. A boxed robot on a shelf sells poorly, while a live demo of lights switching on as a visitor walks in sells itself. Expect Apple to lean on that kind of showing if the project reaches launch.

A device that watches a room to decide when to act raises obvious privacy questions. Apple has built a brand on privacy, and it will have to explain where camera data is processed, what is stored, and who can see it. None of the reports address these points, so they remain open.

The bar here is higher than for a phone. A phone camera points where the owner points it. A home device with autonomous awareness can capture guests, children and routines without anyone choosing to record. Buyers and regulators will want clear indicators, easy off switches and plain disclosures.

This is also where the hardware category meets policy. Home cameras have already drawn scrutiny from lawmakers and security researchers, and a $1,000 Apple device would draw more. How Apple answers will shape trust in the whole premium home segment.

Support and repair raise a final question. Our coverage of the foldable line already shows how repair costs shape perception of a new Apple category. A robot with moving or sensing parts would add service complexity, and buyers at this price expect strong support. Apple has not said anything about warranty or service for the device, so that stays an open item.

A device with a camera-and-sensor system and a screen creates a new surface for software. If Apple opens it to third parties, developers could build call, reminder and household-routine experiences for a display that reacts to people. If Apple keeps it closed, the robot stays a showcase for first-party features.

The reports do not say which path Apple will take, so we treat both as open. Apple’s pattern with new hardware is to launch with a tight first-party feature set and widen access later. The Apple Watch and the home speaker line both followed that arc, and a robot at $1,000 would likely start the same way.

For accessory makers and smart-home brands, the question is compatibility. Anyone selling lights, locks or sensors will want to know whether the robot can control their devices. The light-control capability in the reports suggests Apple plans some home-control support, but the scope is unconfirmed. Vendors should watch Apple’s developer documentation for clues, since new hardware often shows up there before it ships.

Also track how the reported price evolves. If outlets converge on a different figure, that is a stronger signal than any single report. And watch whether Apple comments at all, because silence is the default until the company is ready to sell.

extraction.body: OpenAI has hired former U.S. Army Secretary Dan Driscoll as senior counselor for national security modernization, a newly created role at the company . Driscoll will focus on how artificial intelligence can be used to strengthen U.S. national security and cybersecurity, OpenAI said, while his updated LinkedIn profile also lists his new position. He will work with OpenAI's senior leadership and external partners, with a particular focus on helping U.S. allies adopt advanced AI responsibly. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said the U.S. has "an extraordinary opportunity to work with other countries to spread the adoption of democratic AI," and that Driscoll's appointment would help strengthen American leadership in the technology. "National security requirements are changing faster than at any time in the past fifty years," Driscoll said. He added that AI could help reduce paperwork, process information and deliver answers more quickly to those working in national security. The appointment comes after Driscoll stepped down as Army secretary earlier this year after months of reported tensions with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. An Iraq war veteran, Driscoll pushed efforts to modernize the U.S. military, including expanding access to drone and counter-drone technologies among U.S. allies, according to a previous U.S. Army announcement. Driscoll also met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Kyiv in November 2025 to discuss a U.S.-proposed peace plan aimed at ending the war with Russia, according to a statement from the Presidential Office of Ukraine. At OpenAI, Driscoll will work with government officials, industry leaders, academic institutions and allied organizations to advance what the company calls "democratic AI." He will also help internal teams understand the operational needs of national security institutions, building on OpenAI's efforts to strengthen cyber resilience and protect essential services through its Daybreak program . passages: Dan Driscoll, a former US Secretary of the Army has been appointed by OpenAI as its senior counselor for national security modernisation.
The company created a new position for Driscoll for advancing the responsible use of artificial intelligence in national security, cybersecurity and defense.
Driscoll, whose appointment was announced on Monday will work with OpenAI's senior leadership, government officials, industry executives to strengthen national security capabilities.
The announcement by OpenAI comes after Driscoll stepped down as the 26th Army secretary earlier this year over his reported differences with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
Driscoll described his appointment as an opportunity to help military personnel and national security institutions benefit from technology that is advancing rapidly.
"I’m joining OpenAI to help the United States and our allies put this technology to work responsibly, for the people who keep us safe," he said.
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman welcomed the appointment of Driscoll and spoke about the importance of international cooperation in strengthening artificial intelligence further.
The fall out between Driscoll and Hegseth was largely over Army leadership and modernization priorities.

extraction.body: OpenAI has hired former U.S. Army Secretary Dan Driscoll as senior counselor for national security modernization, a newly created role at the company . Driscoll will focus on how artificial intelligence can be used to strengthen U.S. national security and cybersecurity, OpenAI said, while his updated LinkedIn profile also lists his new position. He will work with OpenAI's senior leadership and external partners, with a particular focus on helping U.S. allies adopt advanced AI responsibly. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said the U.S. has "an extraordinary opportunity to work with other countries to spread the adoption of democratic AI," and that Driscoll's appointment would help strengthen American leadership in the technology. "National security requirements are changing faster than at any time in the past fifty years," Driscoll said. He added that AI could help reduce paperwork, process information and deliver answers more quickly to those working in national security. The appointment comes after Driscoll stepped down as Army secretary earlier this year after months of reported tensions with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. An Iraq war veteran, Driscoll pushed efforts to modernize the U.S. military, including expanding access to drone and counter-drone technologies among U.S. allies, according to a previous U.S. Army announcement. Driscoll also met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Kyiv in November 2025 to discuss a U.S.-proposed peace plan aimed at ending the war with Russia, according to a statement from the Presidential Office of Ukraine. At OpenAI, Driscoll will work with government officials, industry leaders, academic institutions and allied organizations to advance what the company calls "democratic AI." He will also help internal teams understand the operational needs of national security institutions, building on OpenAI's efforts to strengthen cyber resilience and protect essential services through its Daybreak program . passages: Apple had a record-breaking quarter for iPhone sales — despite not releasing a standard model during its latest refresh.
In its fourth-quarter earnings report released on Monday, Apple says it earned $57.58 billion in iPhone revenue, a 17 percent jump from the same time last year.

Its Mac business grew 24 percent to $10.79 billion, while Apple’s services division, which includes App Store commissions along with subscriptions to services like Apple TV and Apple Music, grew to $31.57 billion. iPad revenue declined 10 percent year over year, with $6.23 billion in sales.
The increase in revenue follows the launch of Apple’s iPhone 18 lineup in September, which included a pricier iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max model.
Apple also took the wraps off its first folding phone, the iPhone Duo, but its preorder sales aren’t included in this earnings report.
Meanwhile, Apple only had a “limited” number of iPhone Duos available in store at launch, with some estimated shipment dates extending into 2027.
Apple shook up other areas of its product lineup with some other major launches over the past several weeks.
Like other device-makers, Apple has been dealing with supply chain constraints and rising memory costs, leading it to raise prices across its products.
Last week, Apple also revealed a MacBook Pro with a touchscreen — a design choice that its executives famously resisted.

Notably, the company reported US$57.58 billion (about C$80.5 billion) in iPhone revenue, a 17 per cent jump from the same time last year. Overall, Apple reported US$114.5 billion (about C$160 billion) in revenue, marking a 12 percent increase. The Mac and services businesses grew during Q4, the latter of which actually reaching an all-time high of US$31.57 billion (about C$44.1 billion), although iPad revenue declined 10 per cent year-over-year. Looking ahead to the next quarter, Apple has the aforementioned Duo and a new touchscreen MacBook . It will also be John Ternus’ first full quarter as CEO, as he took over from Apple veteran Tim Cook on Sept. 1 . extraction.body: Apple is rewriting its playbook for the iPhone lineup, and the iPhone 17 is the unexpected beneficiary. With the standard iPhone 18 delayed until spring 2027, the iPhone 17 is set to become the longest-lived standard model in the company’s history. The move comes alongside Apple’s best-ever March quarter revenue, driven by what CEO Tim Cook described as “extraordinary demand” for the iPhone 17 series. For years, Apple has followed a predictable rhythm: new iPhones every September. That rhythm is about to change. According to multiple reports, Apple will launch only the iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, and the much-anticipated iPhone Ultra foldable at its September 2026 event. The standard iPhone 18 will not appear until the following spring. This delay means the iPhone 17, which debuted in September 2025, will remain on sale for roughly 18 months—an unusually long lifecycle for a non-Pro model. Apple has already ramped up production capacity for the iPhone 17, signaling its intention to keep the device in the spotlight through the 2026 holiday season and beyond. The extended production run is expected to allow the phone to participate in major sales events like China’s Double 11 shopping festival later this year. The iPhone 17’s staying power is not just about timing—it is also about hardware. For the first time, a standard iPhone model includes ProMotion technology, giving it a 120Hz variable refresh rate display that matches the Pro lineup. This upgrade addresses one of the most persistent criticisms of Apple’s base models. Apple also eliminated the 128GB entry-level storage tier, starting the iPhone 17 at 256GB. Despite the upgrade, the starting price remains at $876 USD (converted from CNY 5,999 at the reference rate of 0.146). In China, government subsidies of up to $73 USD (CNY 500) can bring the effective price down to about $803 USD. This pricing strategy positions the iPhone 17 as a value-driven option in the premium segment. The strategy is working. According to Counterpoint Research, iPhone sales surged 22% in the first month after the iPhone 17’s launch, even as the overall smartphone market contracted by 2.7%. This growth helped Apple report its best March quarter ever, with total revenue of $111.2 billion—a 17% year-over-year increase. iPhone-specific revenue reached $56.99 billion, slightly above analyst expectations. Tim Cook attributed the results to double-digit growth across every geographic segment and strong demand for the entire iPhone 17 lineup, including the iPhone 17e, which launched during the quarter. Apple also set new March quarter records for operating cash flow (over $28 billion) and earnings per share. Not everything is smooth sailing. Cook warned that memory costs are expected to rise significantly in the coming quarter, driven by an ongoing memory shortage that has already impacted other tech companies. Rising component prices could pressure Apple’s margins, especially as it continues to offer competitive pricing on the iPhone 17. Additionally, Cook is set to step down as CEO later this year, marking the end of an era. His departure adds an element of uncertainty to Apple’s future product and pricing strategies, though the company’s current momentum remains strong. The iPhone 17’s extended lifecycle is a clear sign that Apple is willing to break its own traditions to maximize returns on a winning product. For consumers, it means a well-equipped phone at a stable price—and a longer wait before the next standard model arrives. coreStoryFacts.text: Apple had a record-breaking quarter for iPhone sales — despite not releasing a standard model during its latest refresh.
In its fourth-quarter earnings report released on Monday, Apple says it earned $57.58 billion in iPhone revenue, a 17 percent jump from the same time last year.

Its Mac business grew 24 percent to $10.79 billion, while Apple’s services division, which includes App Store commissions along with subscriptions to services like Apple TV and Apple Music, grew to $31.57 billion. iPad revenue declined 10 percent year over year, with $6.23 billion in sales.
The increase in revenue follows the launch of Apple’s iPhone 18 lineup in September, which included a pricier iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max model.
Apple also took the wraps off its first folding phone, the iPhone Duo, but its preorder sales aren’t included in this earnings report.
Meanwhile, Apple only had a “limited” number of iPhone Duos available in store at launch, with some estimated shipment dates extending into 2027.
Apple shook up other areas of its product lineup with some other major launches over the past several weeks.
Like other device-makers, Apple has been dealing with supply chain constraints and rising memory costs, leading it to raise prices across its products.
Last week, Apple also revealed a MacBook Pro with a touchscreen — a design choice that its executives famously resisted.

Traditionally, Apple has launched the standard and premium versions of its phones in the same September window, but for this year’s iPhone 18 family, it only debuted the 18 Pro and Pro Max , as well as its first-ever foldable, the Duo .
The base iPhone 18 has yet to be released, with reports suggesting it will come in early 2027 alongside the lower-cost 18e and Air 2.
In other words, Apple still managed to have a record iPhone quarter on the back of its more expensive phones.
Looking ahead to the next quarter, Apple has the aforementioned Duo and a new touchscreen MacBook .
It will also be John Ternus’ first full quarter as CEO, as he took over from Apple veteran Tim Cook on Sept.
Apple just had released its fourth-quarter earnings report, and it was a particularly big one.
Overall, Apple reported US$114.5 billion (about C$160 billion) in revenue, marking a 12 percent increase.

extraction.body: Apple is rewriting its playbook for the iPhone lineup, and the iPhone 17 is the unexpected beneficiary. With the standard iPhone 18 delayed until spring 2027, the iPhone 17 is set to become the longest-lived standard model in the company’s history. The move comes alongside Apple’s best-ever March quarter revenue, driven by what CEO Tim Cook described as “extraordinary demand” for the iPhone 17 series. For years, Apple has followed a predictable rhythm: new iPhones every September. That rhythm is about to change. According to multiple reports, Apple will launch only the iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, and the much-anticipated iPhone Ultra foldable at its September 2026 event. The standard iPhone 18 will not appear until the following spring. This delay means the iPhone 17, which debuted in September 2025, will remain on sale for roughly 18 months—an unusually long lifecycle for a non-Pro model. Apple has already ramped up production capacity for the iPhone 17, signaling its intention to keep the device in the spotlight through the 2026 holiday season and beyond. The extended production run is expected to allow the phone to participate in major sales events like China’s Double 11 shopping festival later this year. The iPhone 17’s staying power is not just about timing—it is also about hardware. For the first time, a standard iPhone model includes ProMotion technology, giving it a 120Hz variable refresh rate display that matches the Pro lineup. This upgrade addresses one of the most persistent criticisms of Apple’s base models. Apple also eliminated the 128GB entry-level storage tier, starting the iPhone 17 at 256GB. Despite the upgrade, the starting price remains at $876 USD (converted from CNY 5,999 at the reference rate of 0.146). In China, government subsidies of up to $73 USD (CNY 500) can bring the effective price down to about $803 USD. This pricing strategy positions the iPhone 17 as a value-driven option in the premium segment. The strategy is working. According to Counterpoint Research, iPhone sales surged 22% in the first month after the iPhone 17’s launch, even as the overall smartphone market contracted by 2.7%. This growth helped Apple report its best March quarter ever, with total revenue of $111.2 billion—a 17% year-over-year increase. iPhone-specific revenue reached $56.99 billion, slightly above analyst expectations. Tim Cook attributed the results to double-digit growth across every geographic segment and strong demand for the entire iPhone 17 lineup, including the iPhone 17e, which launched during the quarter. Apple also set new March quarter records for operating cash flow (over $28 billion) and earnings per share. Not everything is smooth sailing. Cook warned that memory costs are expected to rise significantly in the coming quarter, driven by an ongoing memory shortage that has already impacted other tech companies. Rising component prices could pressure Apple’s margins, especially as it continues to offer competitive pricing on the iPhone 17. Additionally, Cook is set to step down as CEO later this year, marking the end of an era. His departure adds an element of uncertainty to Apple’s future product and pricing strategies, though the company’s current momentum remains strong. The iPhone 17’s extended lifecycle is a clear sign that Apple is willing to break its own traditions to maximize returns on a winning product. For consumers, it means a well-equipped phone at a stable price—and a longer wait before the next standard model arrives. extraction.body: OpenAI just made its most aggressive move yet into the defense sector, hiring former U.S. Army Secretary Dan Driscoll for a newly created national security modernization role. The appointment signals the ChatGPT maker's determination to compete with Palantir and Microsoft for lucrative government AI contracts, coming just days after CEO Sam Altman returned from courting Middle Eastern allies and Asian chipmakers. The company announced it's bringing former U.S. Army Secretary Dan Driscoll on board for a brand-new role focused on national security modernization, marking its most explicit push yet into the defense and intelligence markets that have long been dominated by contractors like Palantir and tech giants like Microsoft. Just last week, CEO Sam Altman was in Abu Dhabi signing four separate deals with the crown prince covering energy, government services, and investment. The pattern is clear: OpenAI is racing to build the infrastructure and relationships needed to compete at nation-state scale. Driscoll's appointment creates a direct channel into Pentagon procurement and classified AI development. His tenure leading the Army gives him exactly the kind of clearance levels and institutional knowledge that OpenAI needs to navigate the labyrinthine world of defense contracting. It's a world where Palantir has been cleaning up lately, though interestingly the data analytics firm just reported that commercial revenue overtook government sales for the first time, suggesting the market dynamics are shifting fast. The national security modernization mandate is deliberately broad. These aren't the kind of flashy consumer features that made ChatGPT a household name, but they're potentially far more lucrative on a per-contract basis. OpenAI's move also reflects growing pressure to diversify revenue beyond its core consumer and API businesses. The company recently slashed its fundraising targets as investor enthusiasm for sky-high AI valuations cooled. Government contracts offer something the consumer market doesn't: multi-year commitments worth hundreds of millions, with built-in switching costs that make them stickier than any subscription service. Microsoft already has massive defense contracts through Azure Government Cloud and its longstanding relationships with intelligence agencies. Google famously backed away from defense AI work after employee protests over Project Maven, then quietly reversed course. And Palantir has spent two decades building exactly the kind of trust with defense and intelligence communities that OpenAI is now trying to establish overnight. Its models are widely considered state-of-the-art for language understanding and generation, capabilities that map directly onto intelligence analysis, strategic planning, and cybersecurity defense. The company's recent Shepherd model for AI research validation and its Dots personal assistant show it's pushing beyond basic chatbots into more sophisticated reasoning systems. OpenAI has faced criticism over safety practices, with its own monitoring systems failing a third-party audit just last month. Defense contracts will bring even more scrutiny, both from government overseers who demand ironclad security and from employees and researchers who may object to military applications of AI technology. Driscoll will also inherit thorny questions about how OpenAI's technology should and shouldn't be used in national security contexts. Does the company allow its models to help plan military operations? These aren't hypothetical questions but real decisions that will define OpenAI's role in the defense ecosystem and its broader reputation. For the past two years, companies competed mainly on model capabilities and consumer traction. Now they're competing on geopolitical relationships, infrastructure deals, and government access. Altman's globe-trotting diplomacy, the Abu Dhabi energy partnerships, the Seoul chip talks, and now the Driscoll hire all point to the same conclusion: OpenAI believes the next trillion dollars in AI value will come from nations, not individuals. What makes this particularly interesting is how it inverts the usual tech industry playbook. Normally companies build consumer traction first, then gradually move upmarket into enterprise and eventually government. OpenAI is trying to do both simultaneously, maintaining its ChatGPT consumer brand while also positioning itself as a trusted partner for the most sensitive national security applications. Driscoll's appointment marks OpenAI's clearest signal yet that it sees government AI as a strategic imperative, not just an opportunistic revenue stream. As the company navigates funding pressures and competitive threats, defense contracts offer stability that consumer markets can't match. But success will require more than just hiring the right people—it'll demand navigating security clearances, building trust with skeptical agencies, and resolving internal debates about AI's role in national security. The real test isn't whether OpenAI can land its first Pentagon contract, but whether it can do so without fracturing the research culture that made its technology valuable in the first place.

extraction.body: OpenAI just made its most aggressive move yet into the defense sector, hiring former U.S. Army Secretary Dan Driscoll for a newly created national security modernization role. The appointment signals the ChatGPT maker's determination to compete with Palantir and Microsoft for lucrative government AI contracts, coming just days after CEO Sam Altman returned from courting Middle Eastern allies and Asian chipmakers. The company announced it's bringing former U.S. Army Secretary Dan Driscoll on board for a brand-new role focused on national security modernization, marking its most explicit push yet into the defense and intelligence markets that have long been dominated by contractors like Palantir and tech giants like Microsoft. Just last week, CEO Sam Altman was in Abu Dhabi signing four separate deals with the crown prince covering energy, government services, and investment. The pattern is clear: OpenAI is racing to build the infrastructure and relationships needed to compete at nation-state scale. Driscoll's appointment creates a direct channel into Pentagon procurement and classified AI development. His tenure leading the Army gives him exactly the kind of clearance levels and institutional knowledge that OpenAI needs to navigate the labyrinthine world of defense contracting. It's a world where Palantir has been cleaning up lately, though interestingly the data analytics firm just reported that commercial revenue overtook government sales for the first time, suggesting the market dynamics are shifting fast. The national security modernization mandate is deliberately broad. These aren't the kind of flashy consumer features that made ChatGPT a household name, but they're potentially far more lucrative on a per-contract basis. OpenAI's move also reflects growing pressure to diversify revenue beyond its core consumer and API businesses. The company recently slashed its fundraising targets as investor enthusiasm for sky-high AI valuations cooled. Government contracts offer something the consumer market doesn't: multi-year commitments worth hundreds of millions, with built-in switching costs that make them stickier than any subscription service. Microsoft already has massive defense contracts through Azure Government Cloud and its longstanding relationships with intelligence agencies. Google famously backed away from defense AI work after employee protests over Project Maven, then quietly reversed course. And Palantir has spent two decades building exactly the kind of trust with defense and intelligence communities that OpenAI is now trying to establish overnight. Its models are widely considered state-of-the-art for language understanding and generation, capabilities that map directly onto intelligence analysis, strategic planning, and cybersecurity defense. The company's recent Shepherd model for AI research validation and its Dots personal assistant show it's pushing beyond basic chatbots into more sophisticated reasoning systems. OpenAI has faced criticism over safety practices, with its own monitoring systems failing a third-party audit just last month. Defense contracts will bring even more scrutiny, both from government overseers who demand ironclad security and from employees and researchers who may object to military applications of AI technology. Driscoll will also inherit thorny questions about how OpenAI's technology should and shouldn't be used in national security contexts. Does the company allow its models to help plan military operations? These aren't hypothetical questions but real decisions that will define OpenAI's role in the defense ecosystem and its broader reputation. For the past two years, companies competed mainly on model capabilities and consumer traction. Now they're competing on geopolitical relationships, infrastructure deals, and government access. Altman's globe-trotting diplomacy, the Abu Dhabi energy partnerships, the Seoul chip talks, and now the Driscoll hire all point to the same conclusion: OpenAI believes the next trillion dollars in AI value will come from nations, not individuals. What makes this particularly interesting is how it inverts the usual tech industry playbook. Normally companies build consumer traction first, then gradually move upmarket into enterprise and eventually government. OpenAI is trying to do both simultaneously, maintaining its ChatGPT consumer brand while also positioning itself as a trusted partner for the most sensitive national security applications. Driscoll's appointment marks OpenAI's clearest signal yet that it sees government AI as a strategic imperative, not just an opportunistic revenue stream. As the company navigates funding pressures and competitive threats, defense contracts offer stability that consumer markets can't match. But success will require more than just hiring the right people—it'll demand navigating security clearances, building trust with skeptical agencies, and resolving internal debates about AI's role in national security. The real test isn't whether OpenAI can land its first Pentagon contract, but whether it can do so without fracturing the research culture that made its technology valuable in the first place.

passages: Binance customers withdrew more than $4.6 billion from the cryptocurrency exchange after it suffered what security experts said was the largest digital coin theft ever.In a post on social media, Binance said customers also deposited just over $1 billion after the company allowed people to resume transactions on Sunday for Bitcoin, Ethereum and other cryptocurrencies, resulting in a net outflow of $3.64 billion.

Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange with more than 300 million users, said the value of crypto holdings being withdrawn represents just 2.1% of its $171 billion in total assets."Our top priority right now is to ensure the environment is secure, after which users can withdraw their funds, and Binance can resume operations," Binance cofounder Yi He said in an X post early Monday.Binance did not immediately respond to a request for comment.The fund withdrawals came after cybercriminals, whom the FBI linked to North Korea, stole $6.3 billion in digital currency from Binance.

TraderTraitor was also responsible for a February 2025 attack on another crypto exchange, Bybit, that resulted in a $1.5 billion loss, according to the FBI.Following the Binance attack, the FBI encouraged private-sector entities "to block transactions with or derived from addresses TraderTraitor actors are using to launder these stolen assets."Binance has promised to cover the full losses using company funds.

Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange with more than 300 million users, said the value of crypto holdings being withdrawn represents just 2.1% of its $171 billion in total assets."Our top priority right now is to ensure the environment is secure, after which users can withdraw their funds, and Binance can resume operations," Binance cofounder Yi He said in an X post early Monday.Binance did not immediately respond to a request for comment.The fund withdrawals came after cybercriminals, whom the FBI linked to North Korea, stole $6.3 billion in digital currency from Binance.

TraderTraitor was also responsible for a February 2025 attack on another crypto exchange, Bybit, that resulted in a $1.5 billion loss, according to the FBI.Following the Binance attack, the FBI encouraged private-sector entities "to block transactions with or derived from addresses TraderTraitor actors are using to launder these stolen assets."Binance has promised to cover the full losses using company funds.

extraction.body: BTCPay warns of unauthorized withdrawals from hot wallets. Developers of the payment service BTCPay Server have warned about unauthorized withdrawals from users’ hot wallets. The team has urged owners to temporarily shut down servers until the investigation is complete. 🚨 We are receiving reports of hot wallets on BTCPay Servers being swept by unauthorized attackers. If you’re running an instance, please shut it down (./btcpay-down.sh) until we complete the investigation. — BTCPay Server (@BtcpayServer) November 1, 2026 The first warning appeared on November 1 at 22:25 UTC. Developers suggested using the script ./btcpay-down.sh for shutdown. BTCPay Server is a free, open-source payment system that allows online stores and other organizations to accept the leading cryptocurrency independently, without intermediaries. Users host the software on their own or rented servers. The project does not centrally manage this infrastructure, so it cannot disable all installations itself. BTCPay supports hot wallets: the seed phrase is stored on an internet-connected server and used for automatically signing outgoing transactions. This approach simplifies payments but poses risks if an attacker gains server access. Project founder Nicolas Dorier reported that, according to preliminary data, servers with software older than version 2.4.2 were attacked. Update on my part: Our public servers were not attacked (on 2.4.7), it seems reports are on before 2.4.2. According to him, the attacker logged in with admin rights, but the project’s public servers on version 2.4.7 were not affected. Developers have yet to determine how the hacker gained access. Later, the BTCPay team confirmed these findings: the attack method affects versions 2.4.1 and earlier. The latest of these was released on July 23. Meanwhile, developers have not received credible reports of thefts from servers running the current version 2.4.7. The team again urged timely updates of BTCPay. Affected users were asked to send incident details and server logs to security@btcpayserver.org . Servers operating through hosting providers could be automatically shut down to prevent attackers from exploiting vulnerabilities in older versions. Developers thanked LunaNode and other providers for their quick response to the initial warning. The number of affected installations, the total damage, and the identities of the attackers remain unknown at the time of publication. On October 29, BTCPay developers released version 2.4.7, which fixed 85 issues identified using the Anthropic OSS Scanner program. According to the developers’ report, one issue was rated critical, 13 high, 52 medium, and 19 low in severity. The changes affected authorization mechanisms, payment management, invoice processing, software interfaces, and other components of the payment server. Experts strongly recommended installing the update, especially for server owners managing multiple stores. The connection between the current thefts and any of the fixed issues or previously discovered vulnerabilities has not yet been confirmed. In August, hackers emptied Lightning nodes of hardware wallet manufacturer Foundation and Bitcoin publication Citadel21 through a critical vulnerability in BTCPay Server. Attackers obtained LND authorization files—software for working with the Lightning Network . These files allowed them to control nodes and withdraw funds. The vulnerability was fixed in version 2.4.2. Developers then urged LND users to urgently update or disable servers. extraction.body: The payment software provider warns that installing security updates may not remove attackers' access, as Bitcoin and Litecoin thefts continue. BTCPay Server has urged merchants to rebuild outdated payment servers and replace wallets after attackers stole Bitcoin and Litecoin . In a Nov. 2 security advisory , the open-source Bitcoin payment software provider warned that installing the latest update may not protect funds if hackers have already gained access to a server. The warning follows a series of attacks targeting installations running version 2.4.1 or earlier, using a different method to exploit a vulnerability that BTCPay patched on Aug. 7. Blockchain analytics firm Bitquery traced approximately $1.63 million in suspected thefts involving 18.38 BTC and 3,405 LTC across 682 wallet sweeps between Oct. 30 and Nov. 2. Its investigation found that 87% of the funds moved during an eight-hour window on Nov. 1, with the busiest hour accounting for approximately $725,000 in transfers. The findings provide an early indication of the attack's financial scale, although BTCPay has not confirmed a total loss figure or established how many merchants were compromised. BTCPay said it regretted not doing more to reach operators still running outdated installations after its August security advisory. The project has issued several additional security updates since then, including version 2.4.7 on Oct. 29. The suspected thefts continued even after BTCPay publicly warned operators to shut down their servers. According to Bitquery, another 267 wallet sweeps worth approximately $150,000 occurred after BTCPay's Nov. 1 warning at 22:25 UTC. The transfers continued through the night and were still being recorded when the analytics firm stopped counting at 06:00 UTC on Nov. 2. BTCPay said it contacted hosting providers, including LunaNode, to take affected installations offline as a precaution. The project had received its first emailed theft report at 20:56 UTC, although its investigation documented a wallet drain earlier that afternoon. The company said it had seen no impact from these attacks on servers already running version 2.4.2 or later when the November warning was issued. It also confirmed that wallets whose spending keys were stored outside the server, including hardware wallets, were unaffected by the reported thefts. However, BTCPay is urging operators who previously ran vulnerable versions to migrate to entirely new server installations, even if they have since updated their software or have not noticed any missing funds. The concern is that attackers who previously gained administrative access may have obtained credentials or wallet secrets that remain usable after the underlying vulnerability is patched. Consequently, the project recommends generating a new wallet with a fresh seed phrase on a trusted device and transferring any remaining funds from the old hot wallet. Operators must also retire their existing servers, preserve transaction records and relevant logs, and install the latest supported software on a fresh virtual machine without restoring the old system. Potentially exposed hosting passwords, SSH credentials, application access keys, API keys and Lightning credentials should also be replaced from a trusted device. Meanwhile, Bitquery's tracking showed that more than 99% of the suspected stolen funds remained at addresses first used during the thefts as of early Nov. 2, with no identified transfers to known exchanges. The analytics firm cautioned that its 682 recorded sweeps do not represent an equivalent number of affected merchants, as individual wallets could have been drained through multiple transactions. BTCPay has also warned that some activity involving the identified addresses appears to predate the reported incidents. It has yet to establish the complete attack timeline or determine which transactions can be conclusively attributed to the thefts. The project is continuing to collect reports and transaction records from affected operators as it investigates the intrusions. Oluwapelumi values Bitcoin's potential. A hot wallet is one whose private keys sit on an internet-connected server, so it can send funds automatically, for example to pay out refunds.
That makes the latest reports notable, because they point to the type of wallet that was outside the scope of the August flaw.

extraction.body: BTCPay Server, the open-source software many merchants use to accept Bitcoin payments without a third-party processor, has told operators to shut down their instances after receiving reports that hot wallets on multiple servers were being drained by unauthorized attackers. In a post on X, the project asked anyone running an instance to take it offline with its shutdown command until the investigation is complete. BTCPay has not yet disclosed the cause of the attack, how many servers were affected or how much was taken. A hot wallet is one whose private keys sit on an internet-connected server, so it can send funds automatically, for example to pay out refunds. That convenience makes it a bigger target than offline storage. The incident involves software built around Bitcoin, not the Bitcoin network itself. The warning follows two recent security events at the project. On October 29, BTCPay released emergency version 2.4.7 to fix one critical and several medium-risk vulnerabilities. In August, attackers exploited a separate flaw to steal Lightning Network credentials and drain nodes running behind BTCPay, including one operated by hardware wallet maker Foundation. At that time, BTCPay said its standard on-chain wallets, including hot wallets created inside the software, were not affected. That makes the latest reports notable, because they point to the type of wallet that was outside the scope of the August flaw. BTCPay has not said whether the new attacks are linked to the vulnerabilities fixed last week. The key questions are whether BTCPay ties the attacks to a specific software version, and whether servers running the October 29 update were affected. Loss figures and reports from named merchants will show the scale of the problem. In August, BTCPay narrowed the scope considerably after its first alert, so the initial warning may not reflect the final picture. Developers of the payment service BTCPay Server have warned about unauthorized withdrawals from users’ hot wallets.
🚨 We are receiving reports of hot wallets on BTCPay Servers being swept by unauthorized attackers.
— BTCPay Server (@BtcpayServer) November 1, 2026
BTCPay supports hot wallets: the seed phrase is stored on an internet-connected server and used for automatically signing outgoing transactions.
BTCPay Server is a free, open-source payment system that allows online stores and other organizations to accept the leading cryptocurrency independently, without intermediaries.
Hackers Target JavaScript Ecosystem to Hijack Crypto Wallets
BTCPay Server has urged merchants to rebuild outdated payment servers and replace wallets after attackers stole Bitcoin and Litecoin .
According to Bitquery, another 267 wallet sweeps worth approximately $150,000 occurred after BTCPay's Nov.
The transfers continued through the night and were still being recorded when the analytics firm stopped counting at 06:00 UTC on Nov.
BTCPay said it contacted hosting providers, including LunaNode, to take affected installations offline as a precaution.
The project had received its first emailed theft report at 20:56 UTC, although its investigation documented a wallet drain earlier that afternoon.
2 security advisory , the open-source Bitcoin payment software provider warned that installing the latest update may not protect funds if hackers have already gained access to a server.
The findings provide an early indication of the attack's financial scale, although BTCPay has not confirmed a total loss figure or established how many merchants were compromised.
The project has issued several additional security updates since then, including version 2.4.7 on Oct.
Blockchain analytics firm Bitquery traced approximately $1.63 million in suspected thefts involving 18.38 BTC and 3,405 LTC across 682 wallet sweeps between Oct.
BTCPay has also warned that some activity involving the identified addresses appears to predate the reported incidents.
It has yet to establish the complete attack timeline or determine which transactions can be conclusively attributed to the thefts.

sources.title: BTCPay Server Hack: Bitcoin Hot Wallets Drained, Shut Your Server Down Now
passages: Every crypto hack since the Binance hack, with status and safety tips, is in Crypto hack news.What happened to BTCPay Server?Late on Saturday, 1 November, the BTCPay Server team posted an emergency alert: it was receiving reports of hot wallets connected to BTCPay instances being emptied by unauthorized attackers.

BTCPay Server, the most widely used self-hosted Bitcoin payment processor, has confirmed that attackers are sweeping hot wallets on older installations and has asked every operator to take their instance offline until the investigation is complete.
Shut your server down with the ./btcpay-down.sh script and wait.By Sunday, the incident response team had narrowed the attack vector.

The message from three separate incidents in three months is the same: Bitcoin payment infrastructure that is not updated is being actively scanned and attacked.What should BTCPay Server operators do right now?Shut the instance down until BTCPay Server gives the all clear, even if you are on a recent version.
In August, BTCPay Server warned of an actively exploited flaw that let attackers lift LND administrator credentials and reach connected Lightning wallets.
That bug was patched in 2.4.2, and the project put up a recovery bounty of 10 percent of recovered funds, capped at 3 BTC.The August flaw explicitly did not touch on-chain hot wallets.
There are no credible reports of drained wallets on the current 2.4.7 release.
LunaNode and others began shutting down older instances automatically, so if your BTCPay dashboard suddenly went dark over the weekend, that may be why.
BTCPay has long recommended keeping only operating float in a hot wallet.Preserve your logs.

That bug was patched in 2.4.2, and the project put up a recovery bounty of 10 percent of recovered funds, capped at 3 BTC.The August flaw explicitly did not touch on-chain hot wallets. And it comes six weeks after Core Lightning warned that attackers were hunting older, unpatched Lightning nodes. The message from three separate incidents in three months is the same: Bitcoin payment infrastructure that is not updated is being actively scanned and attacked.What should BTCPay Server operators do right now?Shut the instance down until BTCPay Server gives the all clear, even if you are on a recent version. The project says 2.4.7 is not affected, but the root cause of the admin login is unknown.Check your hot wallet balances and move whatever is left into cold storage. BTCPay has long recommended keeping only operating float in a hot wallet.Preserve your logs. If you see unexplained transactions, do not wipe the server. Send the logs to BTCPay’s security team.Update before you restart. When you bring the instance back, do it on 2.4.7 or whatever patched release follows.Rotate credentials for every admin account on the server, and for any service that shared a password with it.

sources.title: BTCPay Server tells operators to shut down after reports of hot wallets being drained - investingLive
passages: BTCPay Server, the open-source software many merchants use to accept Bitcoin payments without a third-party processor, has told operators to shut down their instances after receiving reports that hot wallets on multiple servers were being drained by unauthorized attackers.
In August, attackers exploited a separate flaw to steal Lightning Network credentials and drain nodes running behind BTCPay, including one operated by hardware wallet maker Foundation.
At that time, BTCPay said its standard on-chain wallets, including hot wallets created inside the software, were not affected.
The key questions are whether BTCPay ties the attacks to a specific software version, and whether servers running the October 29 update were affected.
Until the project gives an all-clear, operators holding funds in a BTCPay hot wallet should follow its shutdown advice.
BTCPay has not yet disclosed the cause of the attack, how many servers were affected or how much was taken.
A hot wallet is one whose private keys sit on an internet-connected server, so it can send funds automatically, for example to pay out refunds.
That makes the latest reports notable, because they point to the type of wallet that was outside the scope of the August flaw.
