extraction.body: BTCPay Server, the open-source software many merchants use to accept Bitcoin payments without a third-party processor, has told operators to shut down their instances after receiving reports that hot wallets on multiple servers were being drained by unauthorized attackers. In a post on X, the project asked anyone running an instance to take it offline with its shutdown command until the investigation is complete. BTCPay has not yet disclosed the cause of the attack, how many servers were affected or how much was taken. A hot wallet is one whose private keys sit on an internet-connected server, so it can send funds automatically, for example to pay out refunds. That convenience makes it a bigger target than offline storage. The incident involves software built around Bitcoin, not the Bitcoin network itself. The warning follows two recent security events at the project. On October 29, BTCPay released emergency version 2.4.7 to fix one critical and several medium-risk vulnerabilities. In August, attackers exploited a separate flaw to steal Lightning Network credentials and drain nodes running behind BTCPay, including one operated by hardware wallet maker Foundation. At that time, BTCPay said its standard on-chain wallets, including hot wallets created inside the software, were not affected. That makes the latest reports notable, because they point to the type of wallet that was outside the scope of the August flaw. BTCPay has not said whether the new attacks are linked to the vulnerabilities fixed last week. The key questions are whether BTCPay ties the attacks to a specific software version, and whether servers running the October 29 update were affected. Loss figures and reports from named merchants will show the scale of the problem. In August, BTCPay narrowed the scope considerably after its first alert, so the initial warning may not reflect the final picture. extraction.body: The Apple Watch Ultra 4 is the company’s most capable smartwatch. Of note, those include Sound Recognition, which alerts you to noises like alarms and doorbells, and the Live Rewind feature that lets you revisit the last 15 seconds of an in-person conversation. This model has broader health and fitness capabilities than previous models, too. Its sensors promise more accurate EKG measurements, while the watch can track your heart rate as often as every five seconds. The new Readiness feature (not available on the Ultra 3 and earlier models) also analyzes your recent activity, sleep quality, and other health metrics to generate a score from zero to 10, helping you determine whether to push yourself or take it easy. On the hardware front, battery life is perhaps the biggest highlight, with Apple promising up to 50 hours on a charge — twice as long as the Series 12. Like its predecessor, this model features Apple’s brightest watch display and a rugged design that’s water-resistant up to 100 meters and IP6X-rated for dust resistance. It also retains conveniences like the second-generation Ultra Wideband chip for Precision Finding, and helpful gesture controls so you can you can perform actions with a double tap or flick of your wrist. Read our hands-on impressions of the Apple Watch Ultra 4. Three more ways to save * Ugreen’s FineTrack2 Bluetooth tracker is on sale for $13.99 at Amazon, just a few cents shy of its best price to date. The soccer ball-shaped tracker stands out with its playful design, but it also offers some useful features including a non-rechargeable battery can last up to seven years. It works with Apple’s expansive Find My network to help you locate misplaced belongings, while its lanyard makes it easy to attach to your keys, bag, or other items. * If you’re looking to spruce up your Apple Watch Ultra or Series smartwatch, a variety of Apple’s official bands are on sale for up to 69 percent off at Woot. The silicone Sport Band is down to $14.99 ($35 off), while the soft, breathable Sport Loop is available for $19.99 ($29 off). You can also grab the rugged Trail Loop for $34.99 ($64 off). * Hoto’s new Pulse 4-in-1 Cordless Staple Gun is on sale for $69.99 ($10 off) at Amazon. It works with four types of staples and nails, letting you switch between them depending on the task, while offering two firing modes. It also features a built-in display that shows battery life and alerts you when you can safely fire the stapler and when it’s time to reload it.

Of note, those include Sound Recognition, which alerts you to noises like alarms and doorbells, and the Live Rewind feature that lets you revisit the last 15 seconds of an in-person conversation. Its sensors promise more accurate EKG measurements, while the watch can track your heart rate as often as every five seconds. The new Readiness feature (not available on the Ultra 3 and earlier models) also analyzes your recent activity, sleep quality, and other health metrics to generate a score from zero to 10, helping you determine whether to push yourself or take it easy. On the hardware front, battery life is perhaps the biggest highlight, with Apple promising up to 50 hours on a charge — twice as long as the Series 12. sources.title: Ford Introduces the Ford Privacy Promise to Protect Customer Data - DBusiness Magazine
passages: Ford Motor Co. in Dearborn is launching the Ford Privacy Promise to make an “explicit commitment to customers that their vehicle data is safe” and they’re in control of what they share.
As Ford created the Privacy Promise, it surveyed more than 1,000 U.S. consumers — both Ford and non-Ford owners.
It learned that while privacy is important to them, customers understand the value of data sharing.

“Even for a tech-savvy consumer, it can be hard to understand the relationship between your vehicle, the data it generates, and your privacy and rights,” says Kristin Jones, chief privacy officer and deputy general counsel for data and privacy at Ford.
“With our connected vehicle and app user communities growing every day, Ford takes its responsibility in safeguarding customer data seriously.”
Ford says it designs and builds its products with privacy in mind — from collection of data to its use, storage, and disposal.
This can include privacy-enhancing technologies like anonymizing or aggregating data to further protect a customer’s privacy.
As a result, Ford offers vehicle privacy settings that allow customers to control what data they want to share, subject to the features and services they wish to enjoy.
Ford stresses that it never sells data about how customers drive their vehicle to data brokers.

“Even for a tech-savvy consumer, it can be hard to understand the relationship between your vehicle, the data it generates, and your privacy and rights,” says Kristin Jones, chief privacy officer and deputy general counsel for data and privacy at Ford. “With our connected vehicle and app user communities growing every day, Ford takes its responsibility in safeguarding customer data seriously.”

As Ford created the Privacy Promise, it surveyed more than 1,000 U.S. consumers — both Ford and non-Ford owners. It learned that while privacy is important to them, customers understand the value of data sharing. A value survey respondents kept returning to, according to Jones, was control: the ability to adjust their settings on demand and in detail.
As a result, Ford offers vehicle privacy settings that allow customers to control what data they want to share, subject to the features and services they wish to enjoy.
Ford stresses that it never sells data about how customers drive their vehicle to data brokers.
“We know that trust is earned,” Jones says. “Protecting your personal information is one way we intend to earn it every day.”

extraction.body: Data privacy has become an uncomfortable subject for America’s automakers. Within days of General Motors agreeing to a $220 million settlement over how it handled driver information, Ford announced a new customer-facing commitment on the same issue. The contrast is hard to miss. GM stood accused of letting driving data reach insurance companies, while Ford is now telling owners that they decide what their vehicles share. Here is what led to the settlement, and what Ford is promising in response. The data came from Smart Driver, a program that enrolled millions of motorists from 2016 until GM discontinued it in 2024. Many participants also subscribed to OnStar. GM must now restrict the driving data it collects and obtain a driver’s explicit consent before gathering or sharing it. According to a report by MotorBiscuit , an outside party will also audit its privacy programs. GM said the agreement reinforces steps it has already taken. This is not the company’s first penalty on the subject. It paid $12.75 million to settle a California investigation in May. Earlier, in January 2025, it agreed with the Federal Trade Commission to stop sharing geolocation and driving-behavior data with consumer reporting agencies for five years. It is not yet clear whether affected owners will receive any of the $220 million. According to Ford Authority , Ford maintains that it does not sell driving data to third parties, although a recent study found that it shares some personal vehicle data with outside companies. Against that backdrop, Ford has introduced the Ford Privacy Promise, which is meant to assure owners that their information is protected and that they decide what to share. The company has built a dedicated website explaining how to change data settings, either inside the vehicle or through the Ford App. Ford says it develops its products with privacy in mind and tries to make clear how personal details are used. The pledge also states that Ford never sells data on how customers drive to data brokers. That is the practice at the center of GM’s legal trouble. To support the effort, Ford surveyed more than 1,000 U.S. customers about their understanding of data privacy. passages: Data privacy has become an uncomfortable subject for America’s automakers. Within days of General Motors agreeing to a $220 million settlement over how it handled driver information, Ford announced a new customer-facing commitment on the same issue.

The contrast is hard to miss. GM stood accused of letting driving data reach insurance companies, while Ford is now telling owners that they decide what their vehicles share. Here is what led to the settlement, and what Ford is promising in response.
The data came from Smart Driver, a program that enrolled millions of motorists from 2016 until GM discontinued it in 2024. Many participants also subscribed to OnStar.

GM must now restrict the driving data it collects and obtain a driver’s explicit consent before gathering or sharing it. According to a report by MotorBiscuit , an outside party will also audit its privacy programs.
GM said the agreement reinforces steps it has already taken. This is not the company’s first penalty on the subject. It paid $12.75 million to settle a California investigation in May.

Earlier, in January 2025, it agreed with the Federal Trade Commission to stop sharing geolocation and driving-behavior data with consumer reporting agencies for five years. It is not yet clear whether affected owners will receive any of the $220 million.

According to Ford Authority , Ford maintains that it does not sell driving data to third parties, although a recent study found that it shares some personal vehicle data with outside companies. Against that backdrop, Ford has introduced the Ford Privacy Promise, which is meant to assure owners that their information is protected and that they decide what to share.

The company has built a dedicated website explaining how to change data settings, either inside the vehicle or through the Ford App. Ford says it develops its products with privacy in mind and tries to make clear how personal details are used.
The pledge also states that Ford never sells data on how customers drive to data brokers. That is the practice at the center of GM’s legal trouble.

To support the effort, Ford surveyed more than 1,000 U.S. customers about their understanding of data privacy. Respondents overwhelmingly said they want the ability to control and adjust their privacy settings whenever they choose.

Control comes with a catch. Owners can decline to share certain categories of data, but some features reportedly stop working properly without it. BlueCruise, internet connectivity, and vehicle location services in the Ford App are among the features that may not function as intended without data sharing. Anyone adjusting their privacy settings should weigh what they are giving up.

passages: November’s Critical Infrastructure Security and Resilience Month highlights preparations that infrastructure owners and operators can make to maintain essential services and recover from disruptions.
Chelsey Arries is assistant editor of Security Today, Campus Security Today, Occupational Health & Safety and Environmental Protection Online.
CISA’s monthlong campaign brings together guidance and resources addressing physical security, cybersecurity and service continuity.
Among them is the Infrastructure Resilience Planning Framework, which supports efforts to identify essential infrastructure, evaluate risks and develop resilience measures.

The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) is emphasizing four priorities: identifying essential systems and their dependencies, determining the most consequential risks, developing practical response plans and evaluating improvements.
The agency’s observance toolkit directs organizations to existing resources for assessing vulnerabilities, preparing for incidents and strengthening recovery capabilities.
The toolkit also encourages organizations to incorporate cybersecurity into facility protection and operational planning.
For cybersecurity, CISA identifies its Cross-Sector Cybersecurity Performance Goals as voluntary guidance for prioritizing security investments.
CISA recommends that organizations determine how long customers can tolerate service interruptions, develop recovery plans around those limits and test their ability to restore operations.

sources.title: CISA urges critical infrastructure firms to ‘fortify’ before it’s too late - Cybersecurity Dive
passages: The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) wants to help critical infrastructure operators keep their systems running during a major cyberattack or other serious incident.
CI Fortify also includes recommendations for how other companies in the critical infrastructure ecosystem can support operators.
Equipment vendors should remove barriers to isolation and recovery, CISA said, while managed service providers and integrators should help operators with engineering and planning work.

CISA on Tuesday released guidance as part of an international “CI Fortify” initiative focused on activities that infrastructure operators can take to isolate the effects of a cyber intrusion and recover from them.

The administration has approved CISA’s request to hire 329 new employees to fill critical vacancies, and Andersen told reporters that the regional teams “are high on that priority [list]” for the hiring plan.

The new guidance, modeled on advice that the Australian government published in 2025, comes as intelligence agencies warn that China might sabotage Western critical infrastructure to keep the U.S. and its allies from interfering with Beijing’s long-rumored invasion of Taiwan.

China’s Volt Typhoon hacking campaign indicated that Beijing had already begun laying the groundwork for such disruption, prompting U.S. officials to step up warnings about the dangers of interdependencies in operational technology.

Editor’s note: This story has been updated with information from a CISA press briefing.

The isolation advice includes identifying “critical customers,” such as nearby military bases, establishing service delivery expectations for them, identifying the OT assets necessary to provide that service and maintaining up-to-date “business continuity plans and engineering processes” to facilitate safe isolated operations “for weeks to months.”
Each infrastructure facility assessment will prioritize different outcomes depending on the sector and operator in question, Andersen said.

CISA’s monthlong campaign brings together guidance and resources addressing physical security, cybersecurity and service continuity. The agency’s observance toolkit directs organizations to existing resources for assessing vulnerabilities, preparing for incidents and strengthening recovery capabilities. Among them is the Infrastructure Resilience Planning Framework, which supports efforts to identify essential infrastructure, evaluate risks and develop resilience measures. sources.title: Bitcoin price rebounds after Binance hack, but can it reclaim $80K?
passages: Bitcoin price has recovered to around $78,000 following last week's sell-off triggered by the record $6.3 billion Binance hack, although technical indicators suggest the cryptocurrency is still struggling to regain bullish momentum.
On the downside, failure to reclaim $78,219 could leave Bitcoin vulnerable to another decline towards its 100-day EMA at $77,761, followed by the 200-day EMA at $76,460.
US spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded approximately $643 million in net outflows on October 30, while Bitcoin maintained its seventh consecutive weekly close above the 50 week moving average near $75,728.
As previously reported by crypto.news, Bitcoin fell below $77,000 during the subsequent sell-off, while traders monitored the $76,200 to $76,800 region for signs of support.
Bitcoin continues to trade below its 20 day and 50 day exponential moving averages near $80,200, while the daily RSI at 38.97 suggests sellers still have the upper hand.
2, Bitcoin (BTC) was trading near $78,053, having recovered from a recent low of around $76,173.
Meanwhile, Binance said on Monday that customer withdrawals were stabilizing after users withdrew a net $3.64 billion following the attack.
The reading suggests sellers continue to hold the advantage, although Bitcoin has not entered the conventional oversold region below 30.
Bitcoin's four-hour chart offers a somewhat more encouraging picture, with the moving average convergence divergence indicator showing early signs of improving buying momentum.

The flagship cryptocurrency has managed to regain some ground after falling from above $80,000 following the Oct. 29 security breach, but its latest recovery has yet to clear several important resistance levels. BTC briefly climbed towards $78,600 during early Asian trading on Monday before giving back some of those gains. The recovery followed three consecutive days of gains, with Asian equities and US stock futures also moving higher after Friday's technology stock sell-off. Despite the recent volatility, Bitcoin has maintained its position above the 50-week moving average at $75,728 for seven consecutive weeks. The latest weekly close came in at approximately $78,229, leaving the cryptocurrency around 3.3% above that longer-term technical level. Bitcoin price struggles to recover after Binance hack The latest recovery follows one of the cryptocurrency market's biggest security incidents, after hackers stole approximately $6.3 billion in digital assets from Binance on Oct. As previously reported by crypto.news, Bitcoin fell below $77,000 during the subsequent sell-off, while traders monitored the $76,200 to $76,800 region for signs of support. Selling pressure was particularly heavy in the derivatives market, where more than $1.5 billion in liquidations were recorded as leveraged positions were closed during the downturn. The selling extended into US spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds, which recorded $643.2 million in outflows on Oct. BlackRock's IBIT accounted for $233.7 million of the withdrawals, while Fidelity's FBTC and ARK 21Shares' ARKB lost $201 million and $129.5 million, respectively. The outflows erased four consecutive sessions of inflows and left the funds with a combined weekly loss of $202.4 million. Meanwhile, Binance said on Monday that customer withdrawals were stabilizing after users withdrew a net $3.64 billion following the attack. The exchange said it had replaced approximately 95% of the stolen assets and was working to restore the remaining tokens. What do Bitcoin's daily technical indicators suggest? On the daily chart, Bitcoin continues to trade below its 20-day and 50-day exponential moving averages, which stood at $80,155 and $80,212, respectively, at the time of writing. Source: crypto.news Both indicators are positioned close together, making the $80,000 to $80,200 region an important resistance area that buyers would need to reclaim before a stronger recovery could develop. However, Bitcoin remains above its 100-day EMA at $77,761 and its 200-day EMA at $76,460, leaving two important support levels beneath the current price. A sustained decline below these averages would weaken the longer-term technical structure and could bring the recent lows back into focus. The daily relative strength index stood at 38.97, below its signal average of 43.23 and the neutral threshold of 50. The reading suggests sellers continue to hold the advantage, although Bitcoin has not entered the conventional oversold region below 30. According to Coinbase Institutional's October 30 market commentary, the $80,000 to $82,000 range remains a major resistance zone, while the $73,000 to $75,000 region could provide support if selling resumes. Bitcoin's four-hour chart offers a somewhat more encouraging picture, with the moving average convergence divergence indicator showing early signs of improving buying momentum. Source: crypto.news The MACD line stood at negative 356, above its signal line at negative 553, while the histogram had turned positive at 197. The bullish crossover suggests selling momentum has weakened and buyers are attempting to regain control. The Fibonacci retracement drawn between the recent $84,843 swing high and $76,173 low places immediate resistance at $78,219, corresponding to the 23.6% retracement level. A sustained move above this level could allow Bitcoin to approach $79,485, followed by the 50% retracement at $80,508. A stronger recovery beyond those levels would bring $81,531 and potentially $82,987 into focus. On the downside, failure to reclaim $78,219 could leave Bitcoin vulnerable to another decline towards its 100-day EMA at $77,761, followed by the 200-day EMA at $76,460.

The average entry price across the spot ETF investor base sits at $84,714.
At $77,749, the average ETF holder is underwater by 8.2%.
That creates a natural ceiling: as Bitcoin approaches $84,714, holders who bought the summer rally have a chance to exit at breakeven, and that supply will slow any recovery.
ET on Monday, November 2, down $165.70 or 0.21% over 24 hours, with $8.81 billion in spot volume across major venues.
Binance’s BTC-USDT pair traded at $77,928, a premium of under $140 to the dollar benchmark, which says the exchange at the center of last week’s hack is trading normally again.
The network’s market value stands at $1.56 trillion on a circulating supply of 20,105,365 coins, and Bitcoin’s share of the total $2.69 trillion crypto market sits at 58.5%.
The price of Bitcoin across the whole episode tells the same story.
A $6.4 billion theft, absorbed with a 2% net move from Thursday’s pre-hack level, shows the market structure is deeper and more institutional than in prior cycles.
That low marks the point where the hack, the ETF exit and the Nasdaq’s 2.86% collapse all hit at once.
If Bitcoin breaks below a low set under maximum stress, the market has found new sellers beyond the event-driven ones, and that changes the forecast.
The forecast rests on one thesis: Bitcoin has absorbed the supply shock and now needs demand to return.
The overhang is a sentiment problem first and a supply problem second.
Binance suspended deposits and withdrawals for 30 hours to secure its systems and coordinate recovery.
It reinforces the base case that Bitcoin trades a range rather than trending in either direction through November.
Strategy disclosed in an 8-K filed Monday that it bought 811 Bitcoin for $65.5 million between October 26 and November 1, an average purchase price of $80,764 per coin.
Bitcoin moved between $77,600 and $78,500 on Sunday as Binance restored withdrawals network by network, with Bitcoin the first chain reopened.
Bitcoin sits 2.1% above the bear trigger and 9% below the bull target, while the macro backdrop of falling oil, easing input costs and a recovering equity market leans constructive.

extraction.body: Bitcoin traded at $77,749.01 at 10:24 a.m. ET on Monday, November 2, down $165.70 or 0.21% over 24 hours, with $8.81 billion in spot volume across major venues. Coinbase printed $77,791.26. Binance’s BTC-USDT pair traded at $77,928, a premium of under $140 to the dollar benchmark, which says the exchange at the center of last week’s hack is trading normally again. The network’s market value stands at $1.56 trillion on a circulating supply of 20,105,365 coins, and Bitcoin’s share of the total $2.69 trillion crypto market sits at 58.5%. The price action is the problem. U.S. equities ripped higher at the open, with the Nasdaq Composite up 0.82% and the Dow up 510 points as crude oil collapsed 6% on Iran-Qatar peace talks. Bitcoin did not join the move. It traded in a $77,000 to $78,700 band all weekend, touched $78,727 in early Asian hours and gave it back. When a risk asset fails to rally on a morning when oil, yields and the VIX all fall, the market is telling you the marginal buyer is missing, not that the seller has disappeared. That distinction drives this forecast. The supply side of Bitcoin’s problem has been absorbed. A record $6.4 billion exchange theft, $4.7 billion in exchange withdrawals and a $643.3 million single-day exit from spot ETFs all hit within 72 hours, and the price never broke October’s $76,141 low. The demand side has not recovered. Spot ETFs logged a losing week, the Fear and Greed Index sits at 37 after dropping to 30 on Friday, and Bitcoin remains 5.3% below its 50-day moving average. The weekend showed resilience rather than strength. Bitcoin moved between $77,600 and $78,500 on Sunday as Binance restored withdrawals network by network, with Bitcoin the first chain reopened. There was no capitulation wick, no liquidation cascade and no break of the 200-day exponential moving average at $76,459. That is the best news in the tape. The largest theft in crypto history hit Binance on the evening of Thursday, October 29. Attackers drained $6.4 billion in tokens from the exchange’s hot wallets in under 20 minutes. The company’s initial investigation traced the breach to a compromised engineer’s laptop that gave the attacker access to a service container and let them submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions. passages: Before the hack, exchange balances rose to roughly 3.37 million BTC, which we read as a potential headwind: more coins on exchanges means more potential supply for sale.

When Binance reopened withdrawals on November 1, it processed $4.65 billion of withdrawals against $1.01 billion of deposits in the first nine and a half hours, a net outflow of $3.64 billion, or about 2.1% of its $171 billion in reported assets, with tracked net outflows reaching about $5.8 billion over 24 hours.

So far this looks like an orderly withdrawal rather than a run: Binance says it has replaced about 95% of the stolen assets, and bitcoin fell about 6% from its October 28 close to the October 30 low, a fraction of the 15% to 39% drawdowns around Celsius, FTX, BlockFi and Bybit.
If those coins are moving into self-custody, lower exchange balances would reduce sellable supply.
Withdrawal pauses have historically been a bad sign, though, so the test for November is whether Binance completes its withdrawal phases and its proof of reserves confirms full backing.

relevantPassages.text: Before the hack, exchange balances rose to roughly 3.37 million BTC, which we read as a potential headwind: more coins on exchanges means more potential supply for sale.

When Binance reopened withdrawals on November 1, it processed $4.65 billion of withdrawals against $1.01 billion of deposits in the first nine and a half hours, a net outflow of $3.64 billion, or about 2.1% of its $171 billion in reported assets, with tracked net outflows reaching about $5.8 billion over 24 hours.

So far this looks like an orderly withdrawal rather than a run: Binance says it has replaced about 95% of the stolen assets, and bitcoin fell about 6% from its October 28 close to the October 30 low, a fraction of the 15% to 39% drawdowns around Celsius, FTX, BlockFi and Bybit.
If those coins are moving into self-custody, lower exchange balances would reduce sellable supply.
Withdrawal pauses have historically been a bad sign, though, so the test for November is whether Binance completes its withdrawal phases and its proof of reserves confirms full backing.
A second-order effect is where trading goes next.
What we find most encouraging is how the market handled the worst of it.

The largest hack in crypto’s history caused a far smaller drawdown than past crises; the protocols kept running, and none of the structural drivers broke: banks, payment networks, and asset managers kept shipping onchain products through the drawdown, and regulators kept writing rules.

For allocators, we are watching four things into November: bitcoin holding $76,000 to $78,000 and reclaiming $80,000 to $82,000, Binance completing withdrawals and proving its reserves, credit spreads, oil and long-end yields, and whether ETF flows return.
If those turn, the setup for the final weeks of the year remains constructive.
How did the Binance hack affect the bitcoin price?
The Bitcoin and Ethereum networks kept producing blocks as normal: what failed was one exchange’s access controls, not the protocols themselves.
The script held for the first few days, then macro took over.

An early inflation scare, with the consumer price index (CPI) and producer price index (PPI) running hot and the 10-year Treasury yield touching 5.37%, its highest since 2002, gave way to something more damaging: worries about growth and default risk.
With the Federal Reserve (Fed) offering no prospect of relief, financial conditions tightened through credit.
Bitcoin closed October down 7.3% at about $77,500, its first back-to-back red Octobers since 2011 and 2012.
What bitcoin price levels matter in November 2026?

Flows stayed two-way for most of the month, with inflows of $653 million on October 19 and $436 million on October 21 against a $540 million withdrawal on October 22, but the hack tipped the balance at month-end: ETFs shed $380 million on October 30, the day after Binance froze withdrawals.

Treasury companies split: Strive bought about 13,500 BTC in October, roughly $1.1 billion, taking its holdings to 43,000 BTC (Bitcoin Treasuries, 2026), while Strategy skipped bitcoin purchases for a week to spend $205 million buying back its STRC preferred shares (SEC, 2026).
November has historically been one of bitcoin’s strongest months, with a median gain of 10.3% since 2010, and this year the November 3 US midterms open it.
Polymarket puts the odds of Democrats taking the House at around 92% and of a sweep of both chambers at about 66%, so the vote should remove an overhang rather than add one.
History backs that up: since 1950, the S&P 500 has never posted a negative 12-month return after a midterm election, averaging about 15%.
Past performance is not a reliable indicator of future results.
A Democratic Congress would slow legislation, but the rulemaking under way at the SEC, CFTC, and OCC does not need Congress.
The Fed leaves December open, credit spreads stop widening, oil stabilizes, and the midterms deliver the expected result.
A monthly close above $87,500 would flip 2026 to green, with the mean Market-Value-to-Realized-Value (MVRV) price near $94,000 as the next objective.
Capital rotates back into themes with visible revenue rather than the speculative long tail.
The hack’s second-order effects surface: Binance’s remaining withdrawal phases slip, the attacker starts selling unfrozen BTC and ETH, or outflows turn from self-custody into flight.

ETF holders keep cutting losses below their cost basis, and with leverage still elevated, bitcoin loses the True Market Mean and the $76,000 cluster before testing the 200-day near $73,000, with MSCI exclusions adding an overhang.
Is November historically a good month for bitcoin?
October tested whether the September recovery could survive a hostile macro tape and then a record hack, and the answer was largely no.
The seasonal tailwind we flagged did not show up, a reminder that seasonality only matters when the backdrop allows it.
Binance hack: the largest robbery in financial history
Forced index selling would hit the equity, not the coins, but could weigh on sentiment and on Strategy’s buying, which already slowed this month.

coreStoryFacts.text: Bitcoin price has recovered to around $78,000 following last week's sell-off triggered by the record $6.3 billion Binance hack, although technical indicators suggest the cryptocurrency is still struggling to regain bullish momentum.
On the downside, failure to reclaim $78,219 could leave Bitcoin vulnerable to another decline towards its 100-day EMA at $77,761, followed by the 200-day EMA at $76,460.
US spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded approximately $643 million in net outflows on October 30, while Bitcoin maintained its seventh consecutive weekly close above the 50 week moving average near $75,728.
As previously reported by crypto.news, Bitcoin fell below $77,000 during the subsequent sell-off, while traders monitored the $76,200 to $76,800 region for signs of support.
Bitcoin continues to trade below its 20 day and 50 day exponential moving averages near $80,200, while the daily RSI at 38.97 suggests sellers still have the upper hand.
2, Bitcoin (BTC) was trading near $78,053, having recovered from a recent low of around $76,173.
Meanwhile, Binance said on Monday that customer withdrawals were stabilizing after users withdrew a net $3.64 billion following the attack.
The reading suggests sellers continue to hold the advantage, although Bitcoin has not entered the conventional oversold region below 30.
Bitcoin's four-hour chart offers a somewhat more encouraging picture, with the moving average convergence divergence indicator showing early signs of improving buying momentum.
The cost basis math sets the key upside level.
The average entry price across the spot ETF investor base sits at $84,714.
At $77,749, the average ETF holder is underwater by 8.2%.
That creates a natural ceiling: as Bitcoin approaches $84,714, holders who bought the summer rally have a chance to exit at breakeven, and that supply will slow any recovery.
ET on Monday, November 2, down $165.70 or 0.21% over 24 hours, with $8.81 billion in spot volume across major venues.
Binance’s BTC-USDT pair traded at $77,928, a premium of under $140 to the dollar benchmark, which says the exchange at the center of last week’s hack is trading normally again.
The network’s market value stands at $1.56 trillion on a circulating supply of 20,105,365 coins, and Bitcoin’s share of the total $2.69 trillion crypto market sits at 58.5%.
The price of Bitcoin across the whole episode tells the same story.
A $6.4 billion theft, absorbed with a 2% net move from Thursday’s pre-hack level, shows the market structure is deeper and more institutional than in prior cycles.
That low marks the point where the hack, the ETF exit and the Nasdaq’s 2.86% collapse all hit at once.
If Bitcoin breaks below a low set under maximum stress, the market has found new sellers beyond the event-driven ones, and that changes the forecast.
The forecast rests on one thesis: Bitcoin has absorbed the supply shock and now needs demand to return.
Binance suspended deposits and withdrawals for 30 hours to secure its systems and coordinate recovery.
It reinforces the base case that Bitcoin trades a range rather than trending in either direction through November.
Strategy disclosed in an 8-K filed Monday that it bought 811 Bitcoin for $65.5 million between October 26 and November 1, an average purchase price of $80,764 per coin.

Bitcoin sits 2.1% above the bear trigger and 9% below the bull target, while the macro backdrop of falling oil, easing input costs and a recovering equity market leans constructive.
U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded $643.3 million in net outflows on October 30, ending a four-day inflow streak and posting the largest single-day withdrawal since June 25.

Every fund that moved posted a loss: BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust led with $233.7 million out, Fidelity’s Wise Origin Bitcoin Fund lost $201.0 million, ARK 21Shares Bitcoin ETF lost $129.5 million, Grayscale Bitcoin Trust shed $53.3 million and Bitwise Bitcoin ETF gave up $25.7 million.
Before the hack, exchange balances rose to roughly 3.37 million BTC, which we read as a potential headwind: more coins on exchanges means more potential supply for sale.

When Binance reopened withdrawals on November 1, it processed $4.65 billion of withdrawals against $1.01 billion of deposits in the first nine and a half hours, a net outflow of $3.64 billion, or about 2.1% of its $171 billion in reported assets, with tracked net outflows reaching about $5.8 billion over 24 hours.

So far this looks like an orderly withdrawal rather than a run: Binance says it has replaced about 95% of the stolen assets, and bitcoin fell about 6% from its October 28 close to the October 30 low, a fraction of the 15% to 39% drawdowns around Celsius, FTX, BlockFi and Bybit.
If those coins are moving into self-custody, lower exchange balances would reduce sellable supply.
Withdrawal pauses have historically been a bad sign, though, so the test for November is whether Binance completes its withdrawal phases and its proof of reserves confirms full backing.
A second-order effect is where trading goes next.
What we find most encouraging is how the market handled the worst of it.

The largest hack in crypto’s history caused a far smaller drawdown than past crises; the protocols kept running, and none of the structural drivers broke: banks, payment networks, and asset managers kept shipping onchain products through the drawdown, and regulators kept writing rules.

For allocators, we are watching four things into November: bitcoin holding $76,000 to $78,000 and reclaiming $80,000 to $82,000, Binance completing withdrawals and proving its reserves, credit spreads, oil and long-end yields, and whether ETF flows return.
If those turn, the setup for the final weeks of the year remains constructive.
How did the Binance hack affect the bitcoin price?
The Bitcoin and Ethereum networks kept producing blocks as normal: what failed was one exchange’s access controls, not the protocols themselves.
The script held for the first few days, then macro took over.

An early inflation scare, with the consumer price index (CPI) and producer price index (PPI) running hot and the 10-year Treasury yield touching 5.37%, its highest since 2002, gave way to something more damaging: worries about growth and default risk.
With the Federal Reserve (Fed) offering no prospect of relief, financial conditions tightened through credit.
Bitcoin closed October down 7.3% at about $77,500, its first back-to-back red Octobers since 2011 and 2012.
What bitcoin price levels matter in November 2026?

Treasury companies split: Strive bought about 13,500 BTC in October, roughly $1.1 billion, taking its holdings to 43,000 BTC (Bitcoin Treasuries, 2026), while Strategy skipped bitcoin purchases for a week to spend $205 million buying back its STRC preferred shares (SEC, 2026).
November has historically been one of bitcoin’s strongest months, with a median gain of 10.3% since 2010, and this year the November 3 US midterms open it.
Polymarket puts the odds of Democrats taking the House at around 92% and of a sweep of both chambers at about 66%, so the vote should remove an overhang rather than add one.
History backs that up: since 1950, the S&P 500 has never posted a negative 12-month return after a midterm election, averaging about 15%.
Past performance is not a reliable indicator of future results.
A Democratic Congress would slow legislation, but the rulemaking under way at the SEC, CFTC, and OCC does not need Congress.
The Fed leaves December open, credit spreads stop widening, oil stabilizes, and the midterms deliver the expected result.
A monthly close above $87,500 would flip 2026 to green, with the mean Market-Value-to-Realized-Value (MVRV) price near $94,000 as the next objective.
Capital rotates back into themes with visible revenue rather than the speculative long tail.
The hack’s second-order effects surface: Binance’s remaining withdrawal phases slip, the attacker starts selling unfrozen BTC and ETH, or outflows turn from self-custody into flight.

ETF holders keep cutting losses below their cost basis, and with leverage still elevated, bitcoin loses the True Market Mean and the $76,000 cluster before testing the 200-day near $73,000, with MSCI exclusions adding an overhang.
Is November historically a good month for bitcoin?
October tested whether the September recovery could survive a hostile macro tape and then a record hack, and the answer was largely no.
The seasonal tailwind we flagged did not show up, a reminder that seasonality only matters when the backdrop allows it.
Binance hack: the largest robbery in financial history
Forced index selling would hit the equity, not the coins, but could weigh on sentiment and on Strategy’s buying, which already slowed this month.

Bitcoin price struggles to recover after Binance hack The latest recovery follows one of the cryptocurrency market's biggest security incidents, after hackers stole approximately $6.3 billion in digital assets from Binance on Oct. As previously reported by crypto.news, Bitcoin fell below $77,000 during the subsequent sell-off, while traders monitored the $76,200 to $76,800 region for signs of support. The selling extended into US spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds, which recorded $643.2 million in outflows on Oct. BlackRock's IBIT accounted for $233.7 million of the withdrawals, while Fidelity's FBTC and ARK 21Shares' ARKB lost $201 million and $129.5 million, respectively. The outflows erased four consecutive sessions of inflows and left the funds with a combined weekly loss of $202.4 million. Meanwhile, Binance said on Monday that customer withdrawals were stabilizing after users withdrew a net $3.64 billion following the attack. The exchange said it had replaced approximately 95% of the stolen assets and was working to restore the remaining tokens. What do Bitcoin's daily technical indicators suggest? On the daily chart, Bitcoin continues to trade below its 20-day and 50-day exponential moving averages, which stood at $80,155 and $80,212, respectively, at the time of writing. Source: crypto.news Both indicators are positioned close together, making the $80,000 to $80,200 region an important resistance area that buyers would need to reclaim before a stronger recovery could develop. However, Bitcoin remains above its 100-day EMA at $77,761 and its 200-day EMA at $76,460, leaving two important support levels beneath the current price. A sustained decline below these averages would weaken the longer-term technical structure and could bring the recent lows back into focus. The daily relative strength index stood at 38.97, below its signal average of 43.23 and the neutral threshold of 50. The reading suggests sellers continue to hold the advantage, although Bitcoin has not entered the conventional oversold region below 30. According to Coinbase Institutional's October 30 market commentary, the $80,000 to $82,000 range remains a major resistance zone, while the $73,000 to $75,000 region could provide support if selling resumes. Bitcoin's four-hour chart offers a somewhat more encouraging picture, with the moving average convergence divergence indicator showing early signs of improving buying momentum. Source: crypto.news The MACD line stood at negative 356, above its signal line at negative 553, while the histogram had turned positive at 197. The bullish crossover suggests selling momentum has weakened and buyers are attempting to regain control. The Fibonacci retracement drawn between the recent $84,843 swing high and $76,173 low places immediate resistance at $78,219, corresponding to the 23.6% retracement level. A sustained move above this level could allow Bitcoin to approach $79,485, followed by the 50% retracement at $80,508. A stronger recovery beyond those levels would bring $81,531 and potentially $82,987 into focus. On the downside, failure to reclaim $78,219 could leave Bitcoin vulnerable to another decline towards its 100-day EMA at $77,761, followed by the 200-day EMA at $76,460.

sources.title: Bitcoin post-Binance hack: What recovery needs in November - 21Shares
passages: Before the hack, exchange balances rose to roughly 3.37 million BTC, which we read as a potential headwind: more coins on exchanges means more potential supply for sale.

When Binance reopened withdrawals on November 1, it processed $4.65 billion of withdrawals against $1.01 billion of deposits in the first nine and a half hours, a net outflow of $3.64 billion, or about 2.1% of its $171 billion in reported assets, with tracked net outflows reaching about $5.8 billion over 24 hours.

So far this looks like an orderly withdrawal rather than a run: Binance says it has replaced about 95% of the stolen assets, and bitcoin fell about 6% from its October 28 close to the October 30 low, a fraction of the 15% to 39% drawdowns around Celsius, FTX, BlockFi and Bybit.
If those coins are moving into self-custody, lower exchange balances would reduce sellable supply.
Withdrawal pauses have historically been a bad sign, though, so the test for November is whether Binance completes its withdrawal phases and its proof of reserves confirms full backing.
A second-order effect is where trading goes next.
What we find most encouraging is how the market handled the worst of it.

The largest hack in crypto’s history caused a far smaller drawdown than past crises; the protocols kept running, and none of the structural drivers broke: banks, payment networks, and asset managers kept shipping onchain products through the drawdown, and regulators kept writing rules.

For allocators, we are watching four things into November: bitcoin holding $76,000 to $78,000 and reclaiming $80,000 to $82,000, Binance completing withdrawals and proving its reserves, credit spreads, oil and long-end yields, and whether ETF flows return.
If those turn, the setup for the final weeks of the year remains constructive.
How did the Binance hack affect the bitcoin price?
The Bitcoin and Ethereum networks kept producing blocks as normal: what failed was one exchange’s access controls, not the protocols themselves.
The script held for the first few days, then macro took over.

An early inflation scare, with the consumer price index (CPI) and producer price index (PPI) running hot and the 10-year Treasury yield touching 5.37%, its highest since 2002, gave way to something more damaging: worries about growth and default risk.
With the Federal Reserve (Fed) offering no prospect of relief, financial conditions tightened through credit.
Bitcoin closed October down 7.3% at about $77,500, its first back-to-back red Octobers since 2011 and 2012.
What bitcoin price levels matter in November 2026?

Flows stayed two-way for most of the month, with inflows of $653 million on October 19 and $436 million on October 21 against a $540 million withdrawal on October 22, but the hack tipped the balance at month-end: ETFs shed $380 million on October 30, the day after Binance froze withdrawals.

Treasury companies split: Strive bought about 13,500 BTC in October, roughly $1.1 billion, taking its holdings to 43,000 BTC (Bitcoin Treasuries, 2026), while Strategy skipped bitcoin purchases for a week to spend $205 million buying back its STRC preferred shares (SEC, 2026).
November has historically been one of bitcoin’s strongest months, with a median gain of 10.3% since 2010, and this year the November 3 US midterms open it.
Polymarket puts the odds of Democrats taking the House at around 92% and of a sweep of both chambers at about 66%, so the vote should remove an overhang rather than add one.
History backs that up: since 1950, the S&P 500 has never posted a negative 12-month return after a midterm election, averaging about 15%.
Past performance is not a reliable indicator of future results.
A Democratic Congress would slow legislation, but the rulemaking under way at the SEC, CFTC, and OCC does not need Congress.
The Fed leaves December open, credit spreads stop widening, oil stabilizes, and the midterms deliver the expected result.
A monthly close above $87,500 would flip 2026 to green, with the mean Market-Value-to-Realized-Value (MVRV) price near $94,000 as the next objective.
Capital rotates back into themes with visible revenue rather than the speculative long tail.
The hack’s second-order effects surface: Binance’s remaining withdrawal phases slip, the attacker starts selling unfrozen BTC and ETH, or outflows turn from self-custody into flight.

ETF holders keep cutting losses below their cost basis, and with leverage still elevated, bitcoin loses the True Market Mean and the $76,000 cluster before testing the 200-day near $73,000, with MSCI exclusions adding an overhang.
Is November historically a good month for bitcoin?
October tested whether the September recovery could survive a hostile macro tape and then a record hack, and the answer was largely no.
The seasonal tailwind we flagged did not show up, a reminder that seasonality only matters when the backdrop allows it.
Binance hack: the largest robbery in financial history
Forced index selling would hit the equity, not the coins, but could weigh on sentiment and on Strategy’s buying, which already slowed this month.
Bitcoin’s Q3 2026: ETF inflows replaced treasury company buying

extraction.body: They will apply to apps that allow AI companion relationships, as well. Apple will start asking developers more questions about their apps to help the company ensure that their age ratings accurately reflect their content. Specifically, it will add new content descriptor questions to App Store Connect, the company's web-based management platform for developers. One of the new descriptors will require them to declare whether their app shares the real-world location of the user with another person or group. The other one will require them to disclose whether their app has features, which enable dating "between real people and/or a virtual companion that engages a user in sexual or romantic content." All apps declared to have dating and relationship content will get a minimum age rating of 18+. That means they will not appear in the App Store for kids under 18 if their parents or guardians have set app content restrictions on their device. If underage users who can see them on the store try to purchase or download them, they will be required to provide Apple proof that they're adult. As for apps that share location, they will not be affected by age ratings in most regions. Some countries do have rules for apps like that, however, like Brazil that requires apps that share locations to have an age rating of 16-years-old and up. The new content descriptors will show up in the management platform on November 16. Developers will have to answer both inquiries in the age rating questionnaire when submitting a new app or making changes to an existing one. By January 12, 2027, they must have already answered both questions for all their applications.

passages: Apple will introduce a minimum 18+ age rating for apps that contain dating features or relationships between real people or with a virtual AI companion featuring romantic or sexual content.

Apple will also separately ask whether the app shares a user's real location with another person or a group of people.

extraction.body: CFPB, Federal Agencies, State Agencies, and Attorneys General Pennsylvania has enacted legislation imposing new disclosure requirements on certain advertisements that use artificial intelligence (AI)-generated or AI-modified content. Senate Bill 806, now Act 99 of 2026 , was signed into law by Governor Josh Shapiro on October 22, 2026. The statute, titled the Artificial Intelligence Deceptive Advertising Act , establishes a disclosure requirement for advertisers whose use of synthetic content creates a false consumer perception about the nature, origin, or authenticity of the goods or services being advertised. The law is particularly relevant to businesses that use AI-generated images, videos, or audio in their marketing and advertising campaigns, including financial services providers that employ synthetic content to promote lending products, deposit accounts, payment services, or other consumer financial products. Although the statute is directed at deceptive advertising rather than AI use generally, its broad definitions and disclosure requirements warrant attention from businesses using generative AI in consumer-facing advertising. The statute defines “synthetic content” as information, including an image, video, audio clip, or text, that has been significantly modified or generated by AI. Its definition of AI expressly includes generative AI. The law does not impose a blanket disclosure requirement whenever an advertiser uses AI. Rather, the disclosure obligation is tied to the use of synthetic content in a manner that creates a false consumer perception about the advertised goods or services. For example, an advertiser using an AI-generated video that appears to depict a real customer describing an actual experience with a financial product could face questions under the statute if the presentation creates a false impression about the authenticity of the testimonial. Similarly, synthetic audio or imagery that falsely suggests a product, service, or endorsement is genuine could trigger the disclosure requirement. Whether a particular advertisement falls within the statute will depend on its content, context, and presentation. What Constitutes a Clear and Conspicuous Disclosure? The statute imposes detailed requirements governing the placement and presentation of disclosures. A disclosure must satisfy the following requirements: The statute also requires the disclosure to appear the first time the synthetic content is presented to the consumer, in the same medium as the synthetic content, and, to the extent technically feasible, in a form that is permanent or extraordinarily difficult to remove. These requirements make the manner of disclosure as important as its substance. A disclosure that is technically present but difficult to see, hear, or understand may not satisfy the statute. The statute excludes three categories of content from its disclosure requirement: The text-only exception is notable. Although the statute’s definition of synthetic content encompasses text significantly modified or generated by AI, the disclosure provision expressly excludes content limited to text. Consequently, AI-generated text alone does not trigger this particular disclosure requirement, even though other laws governing deceptive advertising may remain applicable. The exception for evidently fictional content also suggests that the law is principally concerned with synthetic depictions that could mislead consumers into believing that an advertisement or its underlying representation is authentic. The statute does not, however, define a specific test for determining when content is evidently fictional. The statute authorizes the Pennsylvania Attorney General or the appropriate district attorney to seek injunctive relief when the official has reason to believe that a prohibited practice is occurring or is about to occur and proceedings would be in the public interest. The Attorney General or appropriate district attorney may also bring a civil action for violations. A court may award a civil fine of up to $3,000, as well as actual attorney fees and court costs. The statute does not expressly create a private right of action. Its enforcement provisions identify the Attorney General and appropriate district attorneys as the officials authorized to bring actions under the Act. The provision authorizing a court to award damages does not, standing alone, resolve every question concerning who may pursue a claim, but the text does not expressly authorize consumers to sue directly under the new law. Importantly, the Act provides that disclosure of AI use does not limit any other recourse available under law. Thus, compliance with the new disclosure requirement does not immunize an advertiser from otherwise applicable claims based on deceptive advertising or other unlawful conduct. The most immediate concern is not the use of AI itself, but the potential for synthetic content to create a misleading impression about a product, service, customer experience, endorsement, or other material representation. Advertisers should consider whether their campaigns include AI-generated or materially AI-modified testimonials, spokespersons, product demonstrations, audio, or video. Businesses should consider taking the following steps: Businesses should also distinguish this law’s specific disclosure obligation from their broader compliance obligations. The Act does not authorize deceptive advertising merely because an advertiser discloses the use of AI, nor does it establish a general safe harbor for AI-generated marketing. The Act provides that it takes effect 60 days after enactment. Because Governor Shapiro approved it on October 22, 2026, the new requirements are scheduled to take effect on December 21, 2026. Pennsylvania’s Artificial Intelligence Deceptive Advertising Act adds another state-level requirement to the evolving legal framework governing the use of generative AI in commercial communications. Its scope is narrower than a general AI transparency mandate: the disclosure requirement applies to specified uses of synthetic content that create a false consumer perception about advertised goods or services, subject to the statute’s stated exceptions. Nevertheless, businesses using AI-generated imagery, audio, or video in consumer advertising should not assume that a disclosure buried in fine print or added after the content has already been presented will suffice. Similarly, synthetic audio or imagery that falsely suggests a product, service, or endorsement is genuine could trigger the disclosure requirement.
Whether a particular advertisement falls within the statute will depend on its content, context, and presentation.

The text-only exception is notable. Although the statute’s definition of synthetic content encompasses text significantly modified or generated by AI, the disclosure provision expressly excludes content limited to text. Consequently, AI-generated text alone does not trigger this particular disclosure requirement, even though other laws governing deceptive advertising may remain applicable.

The exception for evidently fictional content also suggests that the law is principally concerned with synthetic depictions that could mislead consumers into believing that an advertisement or its underlying representation is authentic. The statute does not, however, define a specific test for determining when content is evidently fictional.

extraction.body: CFPB, Federal Agencies, State Agencies, and Attorneys General Pennsylvania has enacted legislation imposing new disclosure requirements on certain advertisements that use artificial intelligence (AI)-generated or AI-modified content. Senate Bill 806, now Act 99 of 2026 , was signed into law by Governor Josh Shapiro on October 22, 2026. The statute, titled the Artificial Intelligence Deceptive Advertising Act , establishes a disclosure requirement for advertisers whose use of synthetic content creates a false consumer perception about the nature, origin, or authenticity of the goods or services being advertised. The law is particularly relevant to businesses that use AI-generated images, videos, or audio in their marketing and advertising campaigns, including financial services providers that employ synthetic content to promote lending products, deposit accounts, payment services, or other consumer financial products. Although the statute is directed at deceptive advertising rather than AI use generally, its broad definitions and disclosure requirements warrant attention from businesses using generative AI in consumer-facing advertising. The statute defines “synthetic content” as information, including an image, video, audio clip, or text, that has been significantly modified or generated by AI. Its definition of AI expressly includes generative AI. The law does not impose a blanket disclosure requirement whenever an advertiser uses AI. Rather, the disclosure obligation is tied to the use of synthetic content in a manner that creates a false consumer perception about the advertised goods or services. For example, an advertiser using an AI-generated video that appears to depict a real customer describing an actual experience with a financial product could face questions under the statute if the presentation creates a false impression about the authenticity of the testimonial. Similarly, synthetic audio or imagery that falsely suggests a product, service, or endorsement is genuine could trigger the disclosure requirement. Whether a particular advertisement falls within the statute will depend on its content, context, and presentation. What Constitutes a Clear and Conspicuous Disclosure? The statute imposes detailed requirements governing the placement and presentation of disclosures. A disclosure must satisfy the following requirements: The statute also requires the disclosure to appear the first time the synthetic content is presented to the consumer, in the same medium as the synthetic content, and, to the extent technically feasible, in a form that is permanent or extraordinarily difficult to remove. These requirements make the manner of disclosure as important as its substance. A disclosure that is technically present but difficult to see, hear, or understand may not satisfy the statute. The statute excludes three categories of content from its disclosure requirement: The text-only exception is notable. Although the statute’s definition of synthetic content encompasses text significantly modified or generated by AI, the disclosure provision expressly excludes content limited to text. Consequently, AI-generated text alone does not trigger this particular disclosure requirement, even though other laws governing deceptive advertising may remain applicable. The exception for evidently fictional content also suggests that the law is principally concerned with synthetic depictions that could mislead consumers into believing that an advertisement or its underlying representation is authentic. The statute does not, however, define a specific test for determining when content is evidently fictional. The statute authorizes the Pennsylvania Attorney General or the appropriate district attorney to seek injunctive relief when the official has reason to believe that a prohibited practice is occurring or is about to occur and proceedings would be in the public interest. The Attorney General or appropriate district attorney may also bring a civil action for violations. A court may award a civil fine of up to $3,000, as well as actual attorney fees and court costs. The statute does not expressly create a private right of action. Its enforcement provisions identify the Attorney General and appropriate district attorneys as the officials authorized to bring actions under the Act. The provision authorizing a court to award damages does not, standing alone, resolve every question concerning who may pursue a claim, but the text does not expressly authorize consumers to sue directly under the new law. Importantly, the Act provides that disclosure of AI use does not limit any other recourse available under law. Thus, compliance with the new disclosure requirement does not immunize an advertiser from otherwise applicable claims based on deceptive advertising or other unlawful conduct. The most immediate concern is not the use of AI itself, but the potential for synthetic content to create a misleading impression about a product, service, customer experience, endorsement, or other material representation. Advertisers should consider whether their campaigns include AI-generated or materially AI-modified testimonials, spokespersons, product demonstrations, audio, or video. Businesses should consider taking the following steps: Businesses should also distinguish this law’s specific disclosure obligation from their broader compliance obligations. The Act does not authorize deceptive advertising merely because an advertiser discloses the use of AI, nor does it establish a general safe harbor for AI-generated marketing. The Act provides that it takes effect 60 days after enactment. Because Governor Shapiro approved it on October 22, 2026, the new requirements are scheduled to take effect on December 21, 2026. Its scope is narrower than a general AI transparency mandate: the disclosure requirement applies to specified uses of synthetic content that create a false consumer perception about advertised goods or services, subject to the statute’s stated exceptions. sources.title: North Carolina launches PATH NC to modernize child welfare in all 100 counties
passages: On Wednesday, June 18, the North Carolina Department of Health and Human Services announced the start of PATH NC, the Partnership and Technology Hub for North Carolina, a new statewide information system designed to modernize the administration of child welfare services.

By streamlining documentation processes and providing real-time access to child welfare data for users across the system, PATH NC offers more opportunity for state and county staff to pinpoint trends or challenges in child welfare practice and address them sooner – ultimately leading to a stronger system and better outcomes for children and families.
PATH NC aims to bring a unified system to all 100 counties for the first time.
Over the next eight months, all remaining counties will transition to PATH NC for intake and assessment.

Key features of PATH NC include: Mobile-Friendly Design – The system supports documentation from the field, including some offline functionality, so that staff can update case records while conducting assessments, facilitating family visits, attending court and more.

extraction.body: On Wednesday, June 18, the North Carolina Department of Health and Human Services announced the start of PATH NC, the Partnership and Technology Hub for North Carolina, a new statewide information system designed to modernize the administration of child welfare services. The program works to get child welfare staff with real-time data and decision-making tools in order to protect children better and improve outcomes for children and families across the state. Up until this time, officials say, North Carolina's 100 county departments of social services, which administer child welfare services, operate with a patchwork of independent data systems, with nearly half of counties still largely reliant on manual processes and paper records for child welfare operations. PATH NC aims to bring a unified system to all 100 counties for the first time. PATH NC is more than a technology upgrade – it’s an investment in North Carolina’s children and families,” said NC Health and Human Services Secretary Dev Sangvai. “By providing social services staff with better tools, clearer data and integrated support, we are laying the foundation for a safer, more responsive child welfare system that delivers better, more consistent results – no matter where you live. The NCDHHS says the following in a release: NCDHHS' goal for PATH NC was not merely to create a system that collects information, but also to improve child welfare practice through evidence-based tools and actionable insights for the workforce. While developing the new system, the department worked in close collaboration with county leaders to fully redesign the state’s Structured Decision-Making (SDM) tools. Nationally certified by Evident Change for accuracy and consistent results, the new SDM tools within PATH NC help frontline staff better identify and assess risk and safety concerns when responding to reports of child abuse or neglect. Over the last five years, NCDHHS has worked hand-in-hand with North Carolina’s county departments of social services to plan, develop and test both PATH NC and the SDM tools. The department’s projected total investment for the new system’s design, development, training and implementation is approximately $65 million. An early review of cases supported by PATH NC and the new SDM tools shows promising results – county intake decisions are consistently aligned with state policies and best practice in child protective services. “We’ve built PATH NC from the ground up in collaboration with county leaders to ensure it meets the current, real-world needs of North Carolina’s child welfare social workers,” said NCDHHS Deputy Secretary for Opportunity and Well-Being Michael Leighs. “It’s designed to improve the everyday experience of staff while making it easier to track, report and respond to what’s happening in real time. PATH NC is a critical part of our work to transform the child welfare system and improve the lives of children and families in North Carolina.” The new system aligns with NCDHHS’ broader efforts to strengthen system oversight and modernize service delivery. Key features of PATH NC include: Mobile-Friendly Design – The system supports documentation from the field, including some offline functionality, so that staff can update case records while conducting assessments, facilitating family visits, attending court and more. Decision-Making Tools – PATH NC’s new certified SDM tools provide built-in risk and safety assessments, dashboards and real-time alerts for county staff and supervisors. The platform also has the capability to add automated policy support functions and dedicated portals for providers and families in the future. Comprehensive Case Management – Fully implemented, PATH NC will include modules for intake, assessment, in-home services, foster care, adoption, financials, licensing and eligibility all together in one system. Data Accessibility – Once all counties have transitioned to PATH NC, staff will be able to access statewide data, including a family’s full history with child welfare services, regardless of whether they move or transfer to a different county. Integrated Systems – PATH NC is designed to interface with other child-serving systems such as NC Medicaid, the NC Department of Public Instruction and other partner agencies in the future, which will streamline information sharing and reduce administrative burden across the system. The statewide rollout of PATH NC began June 2, 2025, with an initial cohort of 15 counties using the system to support child welfare intakes and assessments. Over the next eight months, all remaining counties will transition to PATH NC for intake and assessment. This phased rollout allows NCDHHS to provide targeted training and individualized support as each cohort of counties prepares to transition to PATH NC. The department will continue to update and improve the system based on user feedback throughout the implementation process. “PATH NC is going to be a game changer for the state, and we’re excited to be among the first counties leading the way,” said Christa Smith, Director of Forsyth County DSS. “The system gives our staff the right tools to make timely, informed decisions, and it gives our supervisors the data they need to identify trends and improve practice. We look forward to seeing everything PATH NC will do for us and our DSS partners across the state.” PATH NC is a critical step forward in NCDHHS’ ongoing effort to transform child welfare in North Carolina through systemic change, increased access to services, better data and stronger alignment among state and county systems. By streamlining documentation processes and providing real-time access to child welfare data for users across the system, PATH NC offers more opportunity for state and county staff to pinpoint trends or challenges in child welfare practice and address them sooner – ultimately leading to a stronger system and better outcomes for children and families.

extraction.body: For decades, child welfare workers have struggled to follow the lives and progress of children in the state’s child welfare system. Families in financial and emotional crisis can have chaotic lives, and case workers often end up a step behind. Sometimes that time lag can have tragic results. Child advocates have long wished for a better way to consistently assess, follow and manage the progress of children caught up in the system, and track what’s happening with their families. In 2025 — after a decade of failed attempts — the state’s Department of Health and Human Services started rolling out a software package to do just that . Now all of the state’s counties have the Partnership and Technology Hub, or PATH NC, to track the intake and assessment portion of each child’s case. More than two-thirds of North Carolina’s county departments of social services are also now using the case management portion of the information system, state health officials said during an Oct. 20 North Carolina Child Fatality Task Force meeting. And by early 2027, all counties are expected to be using the full software suite, including case management. Last year, state officials said they hoped to have the system fully operational by this past summer. But adding the ongoing case management — tracking foster care, in-home services, adoption, and the like — was complicated for county social services departments, said Donna Fayko, deputy director for child welfare with NC DHHS. “It’s just a more complex system to train and implement than intake and assessment,” she told Child Fatality Task Force members. “So we’re seeing more challenges with implementation with this phase at the county level.” The expansion of PATH NC is one of many efforts North Carolina has made as it overhauls its child welfare system, said Lisa Tucker Cauley, a division director for human services with NC DHHS. That work has included redesigning worker training and expanding prevention services to “strengthen statewide infrastructure and support counties in their daily work,” Cauley said. “These initiatives have laid a stronger foundation for child welfare services across the state,” she said. “But at the same time, this infrastructure alone can’t meet the needs of children and families without enough qualified workers, supervisors, funding and services to support its use.” The improvements can’t come soon enough. Data show that 8,163 children were involved in child welfare cases where maltreatment allegations were substantiated. In that group, there were 22 cases where a child died of suspected maltreatment.
