extraction.body: On Wednesday, June 18, the North Carolina Department of Health and Human Services announced the start of PATH NC, the Partnership and Technology Hub for North Carolina, a new statewide information system designed to modernize the administration of child welfare services. The program works to get child welfare staff with real-time data and decision-making tools in order to protect children better and improve outcomes for children and families across the state. Up until this time, officials say, North Carolina's 100 county departments of social services, which administer child welfare services, operate with a patchwork of independent data systems, with nearly half of counties still largely reliant on manual processes and paper records for child welfare operations. PATH NC aims to bring a unified system to all 100 counties for the first time. PATH NC is more than a technology upgrade – it’s an investment in North Carolina’s children and families,” said NC Health and Human Services Secretary Dev Sangvai. “By providing social services staff with better tools, clearer data and integrated support, we are laying the foundation for a safer, more responsive child welfare system that delivers better, more consistent results – no matter where you live. The NCDHHS says the following in a release: NCDHHS' goal for PATH NC was not merely to create a system that collects information, but also to improve child welfare practice through evidence-based tools and actionable insights for the workforce. While developing the new system, the department worked in close collaboration with county leaders to fully redesign the state’s Structured Decision-Making (SDM) tools. Nationally certified by Evident Change for accuracy and consistent results, the new SDM tools within PATH NC help frontline staff better identify and assess risk and safety concerns when responding to reports of child abuse or neglect. Over the last five years, NCDHHS has worked hand-in-hand with North Carolina’s county departments of social services to plan, develop and test both PATH NC and the SDM tools. The department’s projected total investment for the new system’s design, development, training and implementation is approximately $65 million. An early review of cases supported by PATH NC and the new SDM tools shows promising results – county intake decisions are consistently aligned with state policies and best practice in child protective services. “We’ve built PATH NC from the ground up in collaboration with county leaders to ensure it meets the current, real-world needs of North Carolina’s child welfare social workers,” said NCDHHS Deputy Secretary for Opportunity and Well-Being Michael Leighs. “It’s designed to improve the everyday experience of staff while making it easier to track, report and respond to what’s happening in real time. PATH NC is a critical part of our work to transform the child welfare system and improve the lives of children and families in North Carolina.” The new system aligns with NCDHHS’ broader efforts to strengthen system oversight and modernize service delivery. Key features of PATH NC include: Mobile-Friendly Design – The system supports documentation from the field, including some offline functionality, so that staff can update case records while conducting assessments, facilitating family visits, attending court and more. Decision-Making Tools – PATH NC’s new certified SDM tools provide built-in risk and safety assessments, dashboards and real-time alerts for county staff and supervisors. The platform also has the capability to add automated policy support functions and dedicated portals for providers and families in the future. Comprehensive Case Management – Fully implemented, PATH NC will include modules for intake, assessment, in-home services, foster care, adoption, financials, licensing and eligibility all together in one system. Data Accessibility – Once all counties have transitioned to PATH NC, staff will be able to access statewide data, including a family’s full history with child welfare services, regardless of whether they move or transfer to a different county. Integrated Systems – PATH NC is designed to interface with other child-serving systems such as NC Medicaid, the NC Department of Public Instruction and other partner agencies in the future, which will streamline information sharing and reduce administrative burden across the system. The statewide rollout of PATH NC began June 2, 2025, with an initial cohort of 15 counties using the system to support child welfare intakes and assessments. Over the next eight months, all remaining counties will transition to PATH NC for intake and assessment. This phased rollout allows NCDHHS to provide targeted training and individualized support as each cohort of counties prepares to transition to PATH NC. The department will continue to update and improve the system based on user feedback throughout the implementation process. “PATH NC is going to be a game changer for the state, and we’re excited to be among the first counties leading the way,” said Christa Smith, Director of Forsyth County DSS. “The system gives our staff the right tools to make timely, informed decisions, and it gives our supervisors the data they need to identify trends and improve practice. passages: On Wednesday, June 18, the North Carolina Department of Health and Human Services announced the start of PATH NC, the Partnership and Technology Hub for North Carolina, a new statewide information system designed to modernize the administration of child welfare services.
The program works to get child welfare staff with real-time data and decision-making tools in order to protect children better and improve outcomes for children and families across the state.

Up until this time, officials say, North Carolina's 100 county departments of social services, which administer child welfare services, operate with a patchwork of independent data systems, with nearly half of counties still largely reliant on manual processes and paper records for child welfare operations.
PATH NC aims to bring a unified system to all 100 counties for the first time.

PATH NC is more than a technology upgrade – it’s an investment in North Carolina’s children and families,” said NC Health and Human Services Secretary Dev Sangvai. “By providing social services staff with better tools, clearer data and integrated support, we are laying the foundation for a safer, more responsive child welfare system that delivers better, more consistent results – no matter where you live.

The NCDHHS says the following in a release: NCDHHS' goal for PATH NC was not merely to create a system that collects information, but also to improve child welfare practice through evidence-based tools and actionable insights for the workforce.
While developing the new system, the department worked in close collaboration with county leaders to fully redesign the state’s Structured Decision-Making (SDM) tools.

Nationally certified by Evident Change for accuracy and consistent results, the new SDM tools within PATH NC help frontline staff better identify and assess risk and safety concerns when responding to reports of child abuse or neglect.
Over the last five years, NCDHHS has worked hand-in-hand with North Carolina’s county departments of social services to plan, develop and test both PATH NC and the SDM tools.
The department’s projected total investment for the new system’s design, development, training and implementation is approximately $65 million.

An early review of cases supported by PATH NC and the new SDM tools shows promising results – county intake decisions are consistently aligned with state policies and best practice in child protective services. “We’ve built PATH NC from the ground up in collaboration with county leaders to ensure it meets the current, real-world needs of North Carolina’s child welfare social workers,” said NCDHHS Deputy Secretary for Opportunity and Well-Being Michael Leighs. “It’s designed to improve the everyday experience of staff while making it easier to track, report and respond to what’s happening in real time.

PATH NC is a critical part of our work to transform the child welfare system and improve the lives of children and families in North Carolina.” The new system aligns with NCDHHS’ broader efforts to strengthen system oversight and modernize service delivery.

Key features of PATH NC include: Mobile-Friendly Design – The system supports documentation from the field, including some offline functionality, so that staff can update case records while conducting assessments, facilitating family visits, attending court and more.
Decision-Making Tools – PATH NC’s new certified SDM tools provide built-in risk and safety assessments, dashboards and real-time alerts for county staff and supervisors.
The platform also has the capability to add automated policy support functions and dedicated portals for providers and families in the future.

Comprehensive Case Management – Fully implemented, PATH NC will include modules for intake, assessment, in-home services, foster care, adoption, financials, licensing and eligibility all together in one system.

Data Accessibility – Once all counties have transitioned to PATH NC, staff will be able to access statewide data, including a family’s full history with child welfare services, regardless of whether they move or transfer to a different county.

Integrated Systems – PATH NC is designed to interface with other child-serving systems such as NC Medicaid, the NC Department of Public Instruction and other partner agencies in the future, which will streamline information sharing and reduce administrative burden across the system.
The statewide rollout of PATH NC began June 2, 2025, with an initial cohort of 15 counties using the system to support child welfare intakes and assessments.
Over the next eight months, all remaining counties will transition to PATH NC for intake and assessment.
This phased rollout allows NCDHHS to provide targeted training and individualized support as each cohort of counties prepares to transition to PATH NC.

The department will continue to update and improve the system based on user feedback throughout the implementation process. “PATH NC is going to be a game changer for the state, and we’re excited to be among the first counties leading the way,” said Christa Smith, Director of Forsyth County DSS. “The system gives our staff the right tools to make timely, informed decisions, and it gives our supervisors the data they need to identify trends and improve practice.

We look forward to seeing everything PATH NC will do for us and our DSS partners across the state.” PATH NC is a critical step forward in NCDHHS’ ongoing effort to transform child welfare in North Carolina through systemic change, increased access to services, better data and stronger alignment among state and county systems.

By streamlining documentation processes and providing real-time access to child welfare data for users across the system, PATH NC offers more opportunity for state and county staff to pinpoint trends or challenges in child welfare practice and address them sooner – ultimately leading to a stronger system and better outcomes for children and families.

extraction.body: For decades, child welfare workers have struggled to follow the lives and progress of children in the state’s child welfare system. Families in financial and emotional crisis can have chaotic lives, and case workers often end up a step behind. Sometimes that time lag can have tragic results. Child advocates have long wished for a better way to consistently assess, follow and manage the progress of children caught up in the system, and track what’s happening with their families. In 2025 — after a decade of failed attempts — the state’s Department of Health and Human Services started rolling out a software package to do just that . Now all of the state’s counties have the Partnership and Technology Hub, or PATH NC, to track the intake and assessment portion of each child’s case. More than two-thirds of North Carolina’s county departments of social services are also now using the case management portion of the information system, state health officials said during an Oct. 20 North Carolina Child Fatality Task Force meeting. And by early 2027, all counties are expected to be using the full software suite, including case management. Last year, state officials said they hoped to have the system fully operational by this past summer. But adding the ongoing case management — tracking foster care, in-home services, adoption, and the like — was complicated for county social services departments, said Donna Fayko, deputy director for child welfare with NC DHHS. “It’s just a more complex system to train and implement than intake and assessment,” she told Child Fatality Task Force members. “So we’re seeing more challenges with implementation with this phase at the county level.” The expansion of PATH NC is one of many efforts North Carolina has made as it overhauls its child welfare system, said Lisa Tucker Cauley, a division director for human services with NC DHHS. That work has included redesigning worker training and expanding prevention services to “strengthen statewide infrastructure and support counties in their daily work,” Cauley said. “These initiatives have laid a stronger foundation for child welfare services across the state,” she said. “But at the same time, this infrastructure alone can’t meet the needs of children and families without enough qualified workers, supervisors, funding and services to support its use.” The improvements can’t come soon enough. In the first five months that the entire state has been on the system for intake and assessment, 22 children have died of maltreatment. The goal is that better tracking of cases could help prevent these tragedies. North Carolina is one of only nine states in the U.S. where the child welfare system is supervised by the state but county workers do the actual work. That’s led to a patchwork of independent data systems in county departments of social services, who administer child welfare services. Tracking a child or a family who moved across county lines, for instance, could easily become a bureaucratic nightmare. Before PATH NC, more than half of North Carolina counties relied on manual processes and paper records, DHHS officials said. Coupled with high staff turnover keeping track of everything was often difficult. Now, social workers have easier access to up-to-date information on any child in the system. They can access PATH NC on their phones, tablets or computers while out in the field working with families. “This is a big deal for child welfare because families … they move across county lines frequently,” she said. “Tracking them, being able to see their history, really adds to the safety decision making and assessment.” Before PATH NC, one of the state’s biggest challenges had been inconsistent screening decisions, she said. Now, as social workers enter information into PATH NC, they are prompted by the system through structured decision-making tools to improve how they identify, assess and respond to safety concerns, she said. Trishana Jones, a task force member from the North Carolina Coalition Against Domestic Violence , asked if there is county-by-county data on the number of children involved in the child welfare system with domestic violence as a contributing factor in their referral. “That really helps whenever I’m doing trainings talking about childhood exposure to domestic violence for people to understand prevalence,” she said. Morrell said that is a data point that can be tracked and shared with her. During the five months that all of North Carolina’s counties have been using the PATH NC system: Data show that 8,163 children were involved in child welfare cases where maltreatment allegations were substantiated. In that group, there were 22 cases where a child died of suspected maltreatment. State health officials said counties are struggling with high turnover among social workers and supervisors. They often leave over low pay and high workloads, Cauley said. Very few counties are fully staffed to meet the state’s caseload standards of no more than 10 for Child Protective Services or 15 for foster care, she said. “They report that they can’t recruit and find enough … people to fill positions,” Cauley said. She noted that caseworkers frequently leave lower paying counties in search of higher pay in neighboring counties. Other reasons for leaving include secondary trauma, stress and personal safety concerns, Cauley said. That turnover contributes to longer stays in foster care, a lower likelihood of timely reunification and a lack of stability for children and families, Cauley said. “New workers need time and supervision to build judgment in assessing safety, engaging families, documenting decisions and working with courts,” she said. “When supervisors are stretched thin or frequently turned over, they have less capacity to provide the coaching and consultation necessary for effective practice.” To strengthen the workforce pipeline, the department has reintroduced a stipend for students at some schools within the Child Welfare Education Collaborative , a long-held goal for the department to restore a program that was terminated in 2016. Out of 21 social work programs in universities and colleges statewide, the stipend — which covers tuition and fees — is now offered at three universities — Appalachian State, East Carolina and N.C. A&T. Fayko said it will be expanded to more sites. Students receive pre-service training and get hands-on experience in county child welfare agencies. When they finish the program, they’re ready to start work immediately, she said. In the most recent school year, the program graduated 45 child welfare professionals. “These students are entering the workforce equipped to support children and families with skill, empathy, and professionalism,” said Kayla Warren, a social work professor at Appalachian, in a news release about the program . “Investing in programs like [the Child Welfare Education Collaborative] is critical to building and sustaining a strong child welfare workforce in North Carolina.” This work is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution-NoDerivatives 4.0 International License . The awards programme gathered leaders credited for innovation in the Asia Pacific retail industry.

As Asia Pacific’s retail sector evolves rapidly, businesses are adapting to consumer expectations, digital disruption, and demand for seamless customer experiences. These factors have redefined industry standards, pushing retailers and brands to innovate in terms of customer engagement, sustainability initiatives, omnichannel strategies, and operational excellence.

These achievements were celebrated at the Retail Asia Awards 2026, held on 3 June 2026 at the Marina Bay Sands Expo & Convention Centre, honouring companies and organisations whose efforts shape the future of retail in the Asia Pacific region.

The Retail Asia Awards 2026 celebrated transformative business practices whilst also providing a platform for businesses to strengthen their industry presence. Amongst those recognised was Vipul Chawla, Group Chief Executive Officer of FairPrice Group , who was honoured with the CEO of the Year award . In his acceptance speech, Chawla dedicated the accolade to the people behind FairPrice Group’s success, saying: “Whilst I am honoured to receive this award, this award actually belongs to my colleagues, my friends, my brothers and sisters who work so hard every day for so many years and who continue to work hard late into the evening, early in the morning, so that you can get your daily essentials every day.”

The award winners were selected by an esteemed panel of judges composed of respected industry experts and consultants. The panel included Olivier Gergele , Asia Pacific EY-Parthenon Consumer Leader at EY; Quan Yao Peh , Research Consultant, Retail and Digital Consumer at Euromonitor International; Cath Jowett , National Sector Lead, Consumer & Retail and Partner, Workforce & HR Advisory at KPMG; David Eu , Partner, F&B, Retail and Consumer Products at RSM Singapore; Siddharth Pathak , Senior Partner and APAC Leader for Consumer and Retail Practice at Kearney; and Brian Man , Partner and Retail and Consumer Industry Leader at PwC Australia.
Congratulations to all the winners for their exceptional contributions to advancing excellence across Asia Pacific.

The awards programme gathered leaders credited for innovation in the Asia Pacific retail industry.

As Asia Pacific’s retail sector evolves rapidly, businesses are adapting to consumer expectations, digital disruption, and demand for seamless customer experiences. These factors have redefined industry standards, pushing retailers and brands to innovate in terms of customer engagement, sustainability initiatives, omnichannel strategies, and operational excellence.

These achievements were celebrated at the Retail Asia Awards 2026, held on 3 June 2026 at the Marina Bay Sands Expo & Convention Centre, honouring companies and organisations whose efforts shape the future of retail in the Asia Pacific region.

The Retail Asia Awards 2026 celebrated transformative business practices whilst also providing a platform for businesses to strengthen their industry presence. Amongst those recognised was Vipul Chawla, Group Chief Executive Officer of FairPrice Group , who was honoured with the CEO of the Year award . In his acceptance speech, Chawla dedicated the accolade to the people behind FairPrice Group’s success, saying: “Whilst I am honoured to receive this award, this award actually belongs to my colleagues, my friends, my brothers and sisters who work so hard every day for so many years and who continue to work hard late into the evening, early in the morning, so that you can get your daily essentials every day.”

The award winners were selected by an esteemed panel of judges composed of respected industry experts and consultants. The panel included Olivier Gergele , Asia Pacific EY-Parthenon Consumer Leader at EY; Quan Yao Peh , Research Consultant, Retail and Digital Consumer at Euromonitor International; Cath Jowett , National Sector Lead, Consumer & Retail and Partner, Workforce & HR Advisory at KPMG; David Eu , Partner, F&B, Retail and Consumer Products at RSM Singapore; Siddharth Pathak , Senior Partner and APAC Leader for Consumer and Retail Practice at Kearney; and Brian Man , Partner and Retail and Consumer Industry Leader at PwC Australia.
Congratulations to all the winners for their exceptional contributions to advancing excellence across Asia Pacific.

passages: Ethereum Foundation has framed Ethereum as a potential base layer for digital public infrastructure, arguing that public services can share digital systems without handing control of the underlying network to a single operator.

In a blog post published on 3 November 2026, the foundation said the network’s open-source and publicly verifiable design could help institutions collaborate across organizational and national boundaries while preserving more control over their own policies and systems.
The foundation also described a humanitarian assistance proof of concept developed by its Technical Foundations team after discussions with humanitarian organizations and engineers.
It said the model explores how aid coordination could work on Ethereum’s public network while protecting sensitive personal information through decentralized identity and private payment mechanisms.

According to the post, participating organizations can coordinate through shared infrastructure without exchanging personal records or relying on a single agency to operate the network, and each organization remains responsible for the information it collects and the assistance it provides.
The post pointed to Bhutan’s National Digital Identity system as an example of this approach.

It said Bhutan’s NDI supports remote identity verification using digital credentials issued by authorized organizations, with individuals holding the credentials in their NDI Wallets and deciding what information to share.
It also did not state that Ethereum itself guarantees sovereignty, regulatory compliance or specific implementation outcomes.
The foundation distinguished between institutional and individual sovereignty.
For institutions, it said shared infrastructure can create dependency if one provider operates the system and can affect continued access or verification of records.

Ethereum Foundation has framed Ethereum as a potential base layer for digital public infrastructure, arguing that public services can share digital systems without handing control of the underlying network to a single operator. In a blog post published on 3 November 2026, the foundation said the network’s open-source and publicly verifiable design could help institutions collaborate across organizational and national boundaries while preserving more control over their own policies and systems. The post said the issue is not only technical interoperability, but also governance: who controls the infrastructure that public services depend on. According to the Ethereum Foundation, Ethereum is a global network that no single organization controls, and its software is open source for inspection and reuse. The foundation said a new website, publicsector.ethereum.foundation, collects explanations, case studies and practical resources for governments, multilateral organizations, NGOs and other public-interest institutions. The foundation distinguished between institutional and individual sovereignty. For institutions, it said shared infrastructure can create dependency if one provider operates the system and can affect continued access or verification of records. Ethereum, it argued, allows institutions to independently verify records and choose different service providers or their own infrastructure, while retaining authority over their policies. For individuals, it said applications can be designed so people hold their own digital credentials and decide what to disclose, while services verify those credentials without publishing underlying personal information on Ethereum. The post pointed to Bhutan’s National Digital Identity system as an example of this approach. It said Bhutan’s NDI supports remote identity verification using digital credentials issued by authorized organizations, with individuals holding the credentials in their NDI Wallets and deciding what information to share. The foundation said a shared registry on Ethereum helps participating services verify the authenticity of those credentials without publishing them on the network, while Bhutanese institutions keep responsibility for deciding which organizations may issue trusted credentials. The foundation also described a humanitarian assistance proof of concept developed by its Technical Foundations team after discussions with humanitarian organizations and engineers. It said the model explores how aid coordination could work on Ethereum’s public network while protecting sensitive personal information through decentralized identity and private payment mechanisms. According to the post, participating organizations can coordinate through shared infrastructure without exchanging personal records or relying on a single agency to operate the network, and each organization remains responsible for the information it collects and the assistance it provides. The Technical Foundations team has published further articles on the proof of concept’s design, learnings and future development. The post did not say that Ethereum adoption is a requirement for public services, nor did it specify any timeline for broader deployment of the humanitarian model. It also did not state that Ethereum itself guarantees sovereignty, regulatory compliance or specific implementation outcomes. extraction.body: Public services increasingly rely on digital systems that enable institutions to collaborate across organizational and national boundaries. Such cooperation may involve government agencies verifying documents issued by other authorities, or humanitarian organizations coordinating assistance while safeguarding sensitive personal information. Yet technical interoperability alone does not resolve a more fundamental question: who controls the infrastructure on which this cooperation depends? Ethereum offers a different foundation for digital public infrastructure. It is a global network that no single organization controls, and its software is open source for anyone to inspect, use, and build on. When shared infrastructure is operated by a single organization, other participants may depend on that provider for continued access or verification of records. For public services expected to endure beyond individual contracts and political cycles, such dependencies can have significant consequences. Ethereum allows institutions to use shared infrastructure without granting any single organization control over the underlying network. They can independently verify records and choose how they access the network, including through different service providers or their own infrastructure. At the same time, they retain authority over their own policies and systems. For individuals, sovereignty concerns control over personal information and the freedom to decide what to disclose. Applications using Ethereum can be designed so people hold their own digital credentials and choose how to present them. Services can verify the authenticity of these credentials without requiring the underlying personal information to be published on Ethereum. This allows institutions to retain responsibility for the information they certify, while individuals exercise greater control over how that information is held and shared. For communities spread across Bhutan's mountainous terrain, accessing services in person can involve long and costly journeys. Bhutan's National Digital Identity (NDI) system supports remote identity verification using digital credentials issued by authorized organizations. Rather than storing these credentials in a centralized government database, individuals hold them in their own NDI Wallets and decide what information to share when accessing services. A shared registry on Ethereum helps participating services verify the authenticity of these credentials without publishing them on the network. Bhutanese institutions remain responsible for determining which organizations can issue trusted credentials, while individuals retain greater control over their personal information. A different challenge arises in humanitarian assistance, where organizations serving overlapping populations need to coordinate support without unnecessarily sharing sensitive personal records. Drawing on discussions with humanitarian organizations and work with engineers and product leads, the Ethereum Foundation's Technical Foundations team developed a proof of concept exploring how aid coordination could work on Ethereum's public network while protecting sensitive personal information. The approach combines decentralized identity and private payment mechanisms. Participating organizations can coordinate through shared infrastructure without needing to exchange the personal records they hold, or rely on a single agency to operate the underlying network. Each organization retains responsibility for the information it collects and the assistance it provides. The Technical Foundations team has published a series of articles examining the proof of concept in greater depth, including its technical design, key learnings, and directions for future development. The long-term promise of digital public infrastructure is not simply that more services can be connected. It is that institutions can cooperate without surrendering their independence, while individuals can participate in digital systems with greater control over their personal information. Ethereum can support both objectives through open, shared infrastructure that no single organization controls.

extraction.body: Public services increasingly rely on digital systems that enable institutions to collaborate across organizational and national boundaries. Such cooperation may involve government agencies verifying documents issued by other authorities, or humanitarian organizations coordinating assistance while safeguarding sensitive personal information. Yet technical interoperability alone does not resolve a more fundamental question: who controls the infrastructure on which this cooperation depends? Ethereum offers a different foundation for digital public infrastructure. It is a global network that no single organization controls, and its software is open source for anyone to inspect, use, and build on. When shared infrastructure is operated by a single organization, other participants may depend on that provider for continued access or verification of records. For public services expected to endure beyond individual contracts and political cycles, such dependencies can have significant consequences. Ethereum allows institutions to use shared infrastructure without granting any single organization control over the underlying network. They can independently verify records and choose how they access the network, including through different service providers or their own infrastructure. At the same time, they retain authority over their own policies and systems. For individuals, sovereignty concerns control over personal information and the freedom to decide what to disclose. Applications using Ethereum can be designed so people hold their own digital credentials and choose how to present them. Services can verify the authenticity of these credentials without requiring the underlying personal information to be published on Ethereum. This allows institutions to retain responsibility for the information they certify, while individuals exercise greater control over how that information is held and shared. For communities spread across Bhutan's mountainous terrain, accessing services in person can involve long and costly journeys. Bhutan's National Digital Identity (NDI) system supports remote identity verification using digital credentials issued by authorized organizations. Rather than storing these credentials in a centralized government database, individuals hold them in their own NDI Wallets and decide what information to share when accessing services. A shared registry on Ethereum helps participating services verify the authenticity of these credentials without publishing them on the network. Bhutanese institutions remain responsible for determining which organizations can issue trusted credentials, while individuals retain greater control over their personal information. A different challenge arises in humanitarian assistance, where organizations serving overlapping populations need to coordinate support without unnecessarily sharing sensitive personal records. Drawing on discussions with humanitarian organizations and work with engineers and product leads, the Ethereum Foundation's Technical Foundations team developed a proof of concept exploring how aid coordination could work on Ethereum's public network while protecting sensitive personal information. The approach combines decentralized identity and private payment mechanisms. Participating organizations can coordinate through shared infrastructure without needing to exchange the personal records they hold, or rely on a single agency to operate the underlying network. Each organization retains responsibility for the information it collects and the assistance it provides. The Technical Foundations team has published a series of articles examining the proof of concept in greater depth, including its technical design, key learnings, and directions for future development. The long-term promise of digital public infrastructure is not simply that more services can be connected. It is that institutions can cooperate without surrendering their independence, while individuals can participate in digital systems with greater control over their personal information. Ethereum can support both objectives through open, shared infrastructure that no single organization controls.

Artificial intelligence (AI) stocks have been getting hammered for weeks now, and the headlines all sound the same: bubble fears, AI financing anxiety, investors suddenly nervous that the hundreds of billions pouring into data centers won't pay off. None of that is made up; the sell-off is real, and some of these stocks have dropped 20%, 30%, even 40% from their highs. Here's the thing I keep coming back to, though: Price drops driven by fear tend to be the ones worth paying attention to, because they often have almost nothing to do with whether the underlying business is actually struggling. When a stock falls because its own numbers disappointed, that's one kind of signal. When it falls because the whole sector got spooked by a headline, that's a different kind of opportunity. These three companies are showing you exactly that gap right now, between what the stock price is doing and what the business is actually doing. Micron Technology ( MU -5.78% ) makes the memory chips that power AI processors, and it's been caught up in the broader memory-stock rout, like the rest of the industry. Here's what that sell-off is ignoring: Micron's high-bandwidth memory is sold out for all of 2026, the company has already locked in roughly $100 billion in take-or-pay contracts and $22 billion in customer deposits, and it still can't fill half the AI-driven demand coming its way. That's not a company bracing for a slowdown; it's really a company turning away business. Micron posted record quarterly revenue of $41.46 billion and guided to around $50 billion for the following quarter. A stock sliding on bubble fears while its own order book says the opposite is exactly the kind of disconnect worth buying into. Astera Labs ( ALAB -11.22% ) makes the connectivity chips that let AI processors talk to each other and to memory inside a data center rack, unglamorous plumbing that happens to be essential. Second-quarter revenue grew 104.5% year over year, and the company just unveiled a new rack-scale architecture, Orion, built to support up to 160 accelerators in a single pod, a sign it's racing to keep pace with how fast AI hardware is scaling. The honest risk here is customer concentration: a handful of hyperscalers account for most of Astera's revenue , so any pullback from one of them would sting. But a company growing revenue that fast while expanding its product line isn't the profile of a business that's run out of room, it's the profile of one that just got caught in a sectorwide mood swing. But that's a different risk than the one the market is currently pricing in, which is closer to panic than analysis. Each of these companies backed up its business with real numbers this earnings season: record demand, raised guidance, sold-out production, while the stock price moved in the opposite direction. That gap doesn't last forever. Buying into fear only works when the fear turns out to be bigger than the problem, and based on what these three companies just reported, that's exactly where we are right now. Artificial intelligence (AI) stocks have been getting hammered for weeks now, and the headlines all sound the same: bubble fears, AI financing anxiety, investors suddenly nervous that the hundreds of billions pouring into data centers won't pay off. None of that is made up; the sell-off is real, and some of these stocks have dropped 20%, 30%, even 40% from their highs. Here's the thing I keep coming back to, though: Price drops driven by fear tend to be the ones worth paying attention to, because they often have almost nothing to do with whether the underlying business is actually struggling. When a stock falls because its own numbers disappointed, that's one kind of signal. When it falls because the whole sector got spooked by a headline, that's a different kind of opportunity. These three companies are showing you exactly that gap right now, between what the stock price is doing and what the business is actually doing. Micron Technology ( MU -5.78% ) makes the memory chips that power AI processors, and it's been caught up in the broader memory-stock rout, like the rest of the industry. Here's what that sell-off is ignoring: Micron's high-bandwidth memory is sold out for all of 2026, the company has already locked in roughly $100 billion in take-or-pay contracts and $22 billion in customer deposits, and it still can't fill half the AI-driven demand coming its way. That's not a company bracing for a slowdown; it's really a company turning away business. Micron posted record quarterly revenue of $41.46 billion and guided to around $50 billion for the following quarter. A stock sliding on bubble fears while its own order book says the opposite is exactly the kind of disconnect worth buying into. Astera Labs ( ALAB -11.22% ) makes the connectivity chips that let AI processors talk to each other and to memory inside a data center rack, unglamorous plumbing that happens to be essential. Second-quarter revenue grew 104.5% year over year, and the company just unveiled a new rack-scale architecture, Orion, built to support up to 160 accelerators in a single pod, a sign it's racing to keep pace with how fast AI hardware is scaling. The honest risk here is customer concentration: a handful of hyperscalers account for most of Astera's revenue , so any pullback from one of them would sting. But a company growing revenue that fast while expanding its product line isn't the profile of a business that's run out of room, it's the profile of one that just got caught in a sectorwide mood swing. Vertiv Holdings ( VRT -3.55% ) sells the power and cooling systems that keep AI data centers from overheating, which sounds boring until you remember that every AI chip ever sold needs somewhere to run and something to keep it cool. Vertiv's third-quarter results beat estimates, and management raised full-year net sales guidance to $13.5 billion to $14 billion, yet the stock still sits well below its earlier high this year, dragged down by the same hyperscaler spending worries hitting everything AI-adjacent. The company has also been buying its way into adjacent capabilities, picking up a microgrid developer and two liquid-cooling specialists this year, building out a fuller stack of what a next-generation data center actually needs. A business raising guidance while its stock gets punished for sectorwide anxiety is the definition of a gap between price and reality. I'm not going to pretend none of this carries risk. AI capital spending could genuinely slow , and all three of these stocks would feel it if that happens. But that's a different risk than the one the market is currently pricing in, which is closer to panic than analysis. Each of these companies backed up its business with real numbers this earnings season: record demand, raised guidance, sold-out production, while the stock price moved in the opposite direction. That gap doesn't last forever. Buying into fear only works when the fear turns out to be bigger than the problem, and based on what these three companies just reported, that's exactly where we are right now. At the end of October, two of my top AI stocks sold off following earnings: Amazon ( AMZN +2.20% ) and Alphabet ( GOOG -0.07% ) ( GOOGL -0.30% ) . Both had earnings reports that investors reacted negatively to, but I believe the market missed the picture with them.

Another stock that hasn't gotten the respect it deserves is Nvidia ( NVDA -1.26% ) . Nvidia has been the market leader for a few years now, but in 2026, it has maintained a market-average growth rate despite business exploding. However, Nvidia has told investors what it expects for 2027, and it should be another year of huge gains.
I believe these three names are excellent stocks to buy in November, and they could deliver incredible growth to end the year.

Amazon and Alphabet may not seem like similar companies on the surface, but after further examination, you may find they're nearly identical. Each has a core business that drives solid profits. For Amazon, it's the commerce business. For Alphabet, it's Google Search. However, the most exciting segment for both is their cloud computing divisions , Google Cloud and Amazon Web Services (AWS). These businesses are the reason that both companies are planning to spend $200 billion or more on capital expenditures this year, as the growth coming from these two segments is impressive.

Google Cloud takes the cake as the fastest-growing, delivering 103% revenue growth during Q3. That helped boost Alphabet's overall growth rate to 25%, but the market didn't care. Instead, the market sold the stock off by over 10% the day following earnings. That's short-sighted thinking by the market, as the huge investments that Alphabet is making in cloud computing will provide strong and steady cash flows for years, if not decades.

The same goes for AWS. While it didn't grow as fast as Google Cloud, it still grew at a 39% year-over-year pace. The bigger deal with Amazon is that AWS makes up 63% of Amazon's operating profits. So, as AWS grows quicker, so do Amazon's operating profits as a whole. This will cause Amazon's earnings to grow faster than revenue, which is an excellent setup for long-term outperformance of the market. However, because the market is focused on short-term profitability, it sold Amazon's stock off following earnings.
Buying opportunities rarely come around for these two, and investors should take advantage of the market's short-sightedness and buy them in November .

Nvidia may be an even bigger buying opportunity than Amazon and Alphabet. Nvidia has been vocal about how strong long-term demand is for its GPUs, yet the market is pricing none of that in. During its Q2 earnings report, it told investors to expect 70% revenue growth in 2027. If you've followed Nvidia for any period of time, you know that it consistently underprojects and overperforms, which is a good thing. So the 70% growth call for 2027 is likely an underestimation. Still, the market hasn't priced any of that into its stock.

Nvidia trades for just 26 times trailing earnings, which is an average price to pay for a big tech stock. However, Nvidia's growth is anything but average. If you utilize next year's earnings projections to value the stock, Nvidia trades for just 13 times next year's earnings. So, if it hits analyst expectations and returns to its current 26 times earnings level, the stock would have to double.
That's a pretty promising rate of return in just a bit over a year, and makes Nvidia a top stock to buy in November.
Keithen Drury has positions in Alphabet, Amazon, and Nvidia. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Alphabet, Amazon, and Nvidia. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy .

sources.title: Binance covers 95% of $6.3B North Korean crypto hack
passages: Binance announced Monday it had secured assets covering approximately 95% of the $6.3 billion in digital currencies stolen last Thursday in the largest cryptocurrency breach on record.

He purchased various cryptocurrencies on the open market and published evidence based on cryptographically verified internal records and blockchain transactions to substantiate the recovery efforts.The Federal Bureau of Investigation and independent analysts have attributed the attack to TraderTraitor, a North Korean state-linked hacking group previously associated with several major cryptocurrency thefts.

The incident has renewed criticism of the cryptocurrency sector's lack of government-backed deposit insurance available to traditional banking customers — protections absent from an industry that remains largely unregulated compared with conventional financial institutions.Cryptocurrency exchanges have frequently been targeted by North Korean hackers, with some platforms unable to fully compensate users for their losses.

Indian exchange WazirX, for example, lost approximately $234 million — nearly half of its assets — in a 2024 hack and subsequently underwent restructuring, unlike Binance which maintains sufficient reserves to absorb the current breach.The hack has also raised questions about whether artificial intelligence could be used to identify and exploit vulnerabilities in financial systems, although there is currently no clear evidence that AI was used in the Binance attack.

The exchange said it would fully cover user losses through a combination of corporate assets, an insurance fund, and a $1 billion strategic bitcoin reserve.Changpeng Zhao, the company's former chief executive who remains its largest shareholder, sought to reassure customers as the platform resumed withdrawals following a temporary suspension.

extraction.body: Here’s a question straight out of sci-fi: What if AI could predict what you were going to do before you decided to, even in a completely new situation? Israeli startup 42AI says it is developing a “behavioral world model” that can do just that, and it has just come out of stealth with $62.5 million in seed funding. The company is initially running its predictive system at a handful of financial brokerages, where it says the model can help predict how individual traders will respond to volatile conditions. “Behavior is not deterministic; it’s constantly probabilistic,” 42AI’s CEO and co-founder Amit Gal-Or told TechCrunch when I asked him to justify his company’s tall claim. He argues that people have underlying psychological tendencies that influence their decisions even when their circumstances change, and that’s what the startup is trying to measure and convert into data that the model can understand. “A week from now, you might be a different person, but your tendencies will always play out in certain areas to a probability or distribution,” his co-founder and CTO Ehud Ezra added. And that, the company argues, is what the model does: show the probability of a person making a certain decision. 42AI says the model tries to figure out people’s internal motivations instead of extrapolating patterns based on their previous actions. To do that, 42AI examines how people react to seemingly unrelated events. For an investor or trader, for example, such events might include completing KYC processes, onboarding, support calls, money transfers, or trading stocks. “When the person is talking to support or sales in the initial process […] we’re looking at the sentiment, we’re looking at the voice, we’re looking at a lot of interactions that they’re doing, how many times do they call, and so forth,” added Ezra. “And all of those data points are going into the model. Later on, you have the interactions: how you buy and sell, and when, and we’re looking at the market at that stage.” “So we’re trying to look at how they’re looking at the world. In a world model, every individual is the world,” he added. The company then converts those observations into mathematical representations of traits, which are then fed into a transformer-based world model that lays out probabilities for possible decisions under different circumstances. (The company uses a separate language model to generate explanations for its predictions.) Ezra said the model is trained to preserve a person’s underlying tendencies during simulations. So if someone is usually risk-averse, but the model suddenly treats them as a risk-taker, “the target is off,” he said, explaining how the model’s training rewards are structured. 42AI spent three years developing this approach, combining psychological research with neuroscience and genetics, as well as advice from experts in psychology and PTSD, and Dan Shechtman, who was awarded the 2011 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Gal-Or said the team first studied thousands of people via psych assessments and behavioral scenarios, before adding government and biobank datasets covering more than 2 million people. Its customer datasets have since expanded to cover almost 30 million people, he said. In live deployments, the model analyzes customers’ existing records, including transactions and support calls. Gal-Or pointed out the system doesn’t need personally identifiable information, arguing that “the model never knows who the person is.” However, it seems the company still creates individual behavioral profiles from linked customer activity. In predicting market trades, 42AI claims its model achieves 98% accuracy, but Gal-Or clarified that this is more a measure of whether trading flows fall within a predicted range, not if each trade was predicted correctly. He also said the model consistently achieves an F1 score of 0.8 to 0.85 for predicting trading direction and volume. (F1 score is a metric in machine learning that measures how well a classification model can balance correct predictions against false alarms and missed events.) And it’s not like the model can work everywhere, given it’s still a machine in a box. “There’s a natural ceiling because you really don’t have access to everything that a person experiences,” Gal-Or said. Ezra explained that the system’s accuracy also suffers when it misses important situational context, like if someone chooses to change their trading choices based on advice from a friend or a colleague. Gal-Or said 42AI is working with 10 large brokerages, who are using it to manage liquidity, margin requirements, and hedging exposure. The company is onboarding more customers, he said, and is generating more than “seven figures” in revenue, though he wouldn’t specify a number. Customers pay the startup a flat fee, or a percentage of the value the platform helps them gain. He claimed one brokerage generated approximately $30 million in additional value through dynamic hedging. Israeli startup 42AI says it is developing a “behavioral world model” that can do just that, and it has just come out of stealth with $62.5 million in seed funding. The company is initially running its predictive system at a handful of financial brokerages, where it says the model can help predict how individual traders will respond to volatile conditions.

“Behavior is not deterministic; it’s constantly probabilistic,” 42AI’s CEO and co-founder Amit Gal-Or told TechCrunch when I asked him to justify his company’s tall claim. He argues that people have underlying psychological tendencies that influence their decisions even when their circumstances change, and that’s what the startup is trying to measure and convert into data that the model can understand.

“A week from now, you might be a different person, but your tendencies will always play out in certain areas to a probability or distribution,” his co-founder and CTO Ehud Ezra added. And that, the company argues, is what the model does: show the probability of a person making a certain decision.

42AI says the model tries to figure out people’s internal motivations instead of extrapolating patterns based on their previous actions. To do that, 42AI examines how people react to seemingly unrelated events. For an investor or trader, for example, such events might include completing KYC processes, onboarding, support calls, money transfers, or trading stocks.

“When the person is talking to support or sales in the initial process […] we’re looking at the sentiment, we’re looking at the voice, we’re looking at a lot of interactions that they’re doing, how many times do they call, and so forth,” added Ezra. “And all of those data points are going into the model. Later on, you have the interactions: how you buy and sell, and when, and we’re looking at the market at that stage.”
“So we’re trying to look at how they’re looking at the world. In a world model, every individual is the world,” he added.

The company then converts those observations into mathematical representations of traits, which are then fed into a transformer-based world model that lays out probabilities for possible decisions under different circumstances. (The company uses a separate language model to generate explanations for its predictions.)

Ezra said the model is trained to preserve a person’s underlying tendencies during simulations. So if someone is usually risk-averse, but the model suddenly treats them as a risk-taker, “the target is off,” he said, explaining how the model’s training rewards are structured.

In live deployments, the model analyzes customers’ existing records, including transactions and support calls. Gal-Or pointed out the system doesn’t need personally identifiable information, arguing that “the model never knows who the person is.” However, it seems the company still creates individual behavioral profiles from linked customer activity.

In predicting market trades, 42AI claims its model achieves 98% accuracy, but Gal-Or clarified that this is more a measure of whether trading flows fall within a predicted range, not if each trade was predicted correctly.

He also said the model consistently achieves an F1 score of 0.8 to 0.85 for predicting trading direction and volume. (F1 score is a metric in machine learning that measures how well a classification model can balance correct predictions against false alarms and missed events.)

And it’s not like the model can work everywhere, given it’s still a machine in a box. “There’s a natural ceiling because you really don’t have access to everything that a person experiences,” Gal-Or said. Ezra explained that the system’s accuracy also suffers when it misses important situational context, like if someone chooses to change their trading choices based on advice from a friend or a colleague.

Gal-Or said 42AI is working with 10 large brokerages, who are using it to manage liquidity, margin requirements, and hedging exposure. The company is onboarding more customers, he said, and is generating more than “seven figures” in revenue, though he wouldn’t specify a number.

Customers pay the startup a flat fee, or a percentage of the value the platform helps them gain. He claimed one brokerage generated approximately $30 million in additional value through dynamic hedging.

But that may be a ways off yet: Ezra acknowledged that the model needs to be trained on rules and context for each new domain.

And like with all AI tools, there’s a potentially troubling side to 42AI’s technology: If a brokerage can anticipate what its customers may do, what’s to stop someone from using that knowledge to their own benefit? And like with all AI tools, there’s a potentially troubling side to 42AI’s technology: If a brokerage can anticipate what its customers may do, what’s to stop someone from using that knowledge to their own benefit? Ezra admitted that this was “a valid concern” when I raised it, and the founders pointed to regulations, monitoring, and an internal ethics committee, though they didn’t explain what, if anything, would stop their customers from using the technology to gain an advantage over the very people it’s profiling.

He argues that people have underlying psychological tendencies that influence their decisions even when their circumstances change, and that’s what the startup is trying to measure and convert into data that the model can understand.
Here’s a question straight out of sci-fi: What if AI could predict what you were going to do before you decided to, even in a completely new situation?
Gal-Or said 42AI is working with 10 large brokerages, who are using it to manage liquidity, margin requirements, and hedging exposure.
The company is onboarding more customers, he said, and is generating more than “seven figures” in revenue, though he wouldn’t specify a number.
To do that, 42AI examines how people react to seemingly unrelated events.
For an investor or trader, for example, such events might include completing KYC processes, onboarding, support calls, money transfers, or trading stocks.
In live deployments, the model analyzes customers’ existing records, including transactions and support calls.

In predicting market trades, 42AI claims its model achieves 98% accuracy, but Gal-Or clarified that this is more a measure of whether trading flows fall within a predicted range, not if each trade was predicted correctly.

Our initial investigation suggested that the security incident may have involved a compromised laptop, however our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach." Teng also describes how the hackers used "a self-destruct mechanism that destroyed tooling and traces as they went, making it more difficult for us to trace and investigate". Initially, the company had indicated the breach "may have started with a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop" but later statements have pointed to a broader breach. Pyongyang has systematically built its cyber operations, recruiting promising students from universities and sending them to hacker units overseen by North Korea's intelligence agency, research groups like the S Rajaratnam School of International Studies think tank have said. coreStoryFacts.text: North Korea has denied claims that it was behind the record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) hack of cryptocurrency exchange Binance , calling the allegations "absurd rhetoric".
Binance did not respond to the BBC's queries about North Korea's alleged involvement in the hack.
This is the latest hack to be linked to North Korea, which has been accused of relying on cyber-crime to help finance its sanctioned economy.
Who could be behind the Binance hack and what we know so far
Trading in major cryptocurrencies on Binance has since resumed after the exchange worked with issuers to freeze assets impacted by the hack.
The TraderTraitor unit, which is also known as the Lazarus Group, was blamed for a then-record $1.5bn hack of crypto exchange Bybit in 2025.
The net outflow represents a "relatively limited portion" of Binance's total assets, which stand at approximately $157bn, the spokesperson told the BBC on Tuesday.

Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, says it has frozen around half of the funds stolen in a "complex" hack, after $6.3bn (£4.7bn) was accessed in what is believed to be a record heist .
Chainalysis, a crypto analytics firm, said it had "high confidence" that a North Korean is linked to the hack.
Several experts have warned customers not to regard Binance's promise to cover losses as legally binding and said they may need to pursue litigation to recover them.
In nearly all cases investigators have blamed hackers from North Korea, pointing to the infamous Lazarus Group - also know as TraderTraitor.
The names refer to clusters of cyber criminals accused of working directly for the regime.
North Korea is an impoverished country with very little industry and heavy international sanctions and experts say the regime uses cyber crime as a way to bring money in.
Who could be behind the Binance hack and what we know so far
Binance, which was founded in China in 2017, allows users to trade digital assets and is estimated to have more than 300 million registered users worldwide.
A lot of the fear right now from Binance users - and the crypto industry at large - is whether or not Binance will actually be capable of covering this enormous financial loss.

America's lead federal agency for investigating financial crimes added that it would "identify the cyber criminals responsible and bring them to justice", while Binance also said it was working with the FBI.

While Binance said its US-facing exchange was unaffected, the US would still have jurisdiction to investigate the hack and help track down stolen funds - an effort which generally involves a global law enforcement effort.
Binance told its users "your money is safe, and we're covering every loss".
Binance's co-CEO Richard Teng said: "This was not carried out by one person.
Our initial investigation suggested that the security incident may have involved a compromised laptop, however our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach."

Daniel Tunkel, of the London-based Edwin Coe law firm, said that would "come down to what [customers] have been promised in their contracts", and "where Binance can be sued for non-performance, if it comes to it".
Binance has been subject of regulatory scrutiny around the world.

extraction.body: Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, says it has frozen around half of the funds stolen in a "complex" hack, after $6.3bn (£4.7bn) was accessed in what is believed to be a record heist . The firm said $3bn of its stolen digital assets had been secured - but many were still in the hands of unidentified hackers. It initially thought an engineer's laptop had been compromised, allowing unauthorised withdrawals, but later said the attack was wider. Several analytics firms have linked the hack, which eclipses a $1.5bn (£1.12bn) heist on the Bybit exchange in 2025, to a North Korean hacking unit. The US Secret Service said it was "working around the clock" "to identify, freeze, trace, and recover" stolen funds. America's lead federal agency for investigating financial crimes added that it would "identify the cyber criminals responsible and bring them to justice", while Binance also said it was working with the FBI. While Binance said its US-facing exchange was unaffected, the US would still have jurisdiction to investigate the hack and help track down stolen funds - an effort which generally involves a global law enforcement effort. The hack also involved some US-linked assets, such as stablecoins Tether and Circle – cryptocurrencies pegged to the dollar. Binance told its users "your money is safe, and we're covering every loss". It had initially suspended all deposits and withdrawals - but then said in an update that "deposits remain unaffected". Who could be behind the Binance hack and what we know so far Binance's co-CEO Richard Teng said: "This was not carried out by one person. Our initial investigation suggested that the security incident may have involved a compromised laptop, however our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach." Teng also describes how the hackers used "a self-destruct mechanism that destroyed tooling and traces as they went, making it more difficult for us to trace and investigate". Initially, the company had indicated the breach "may have started with a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop" but later statements have pointed to a broader breach. In a later update, the firm said it had "set aside" more than $6.34B in company funds to cover the stolen assets and was "actively buying" a range of crypto tokens. The Binance hack spooked cryptocurrency markets on Friday. The price of Bitcoin was down 5% to $76,800 in Friday afternoon trading in New York. Cryptocurrency exchange Coinbase was down 12% as investors also reacted to earnings results in which the firm reported revenue slightly below expectations. Robinhood, a financial services company that trades in cryptocurrency, was down 7.8%. Binance, which was founded in China in 2017, allows users to trade digital assets and is estimated to have more than 300 million registered users worldwide. Daniel Tunkel, of the London-based Edwin Coe law firm, said that would "come down to what [customers] have been promised in their contracts", and "where Binance can be sued for non-performance, if it comes to it". Binance has been subject of regulatory scrutiny around the world. story.title: North Korea denies being behind record $6.3bn Binance hack - BBC

facts.text: North Korea has denied claims that it was behind the record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) hack of cryptocurrency exchange Binance , calling the allegations "absurd rhetoric".
Binance did not respond to the BBC's queries about North Korea's alleged involvement in the hack.
This is the latest hack to be linked to North Korea, which has been accused of relying on cyber-crime to help finance its sanctioned economy.
Who could be behind the Binance hack and what we know so far
Trading in major cryptocurrencies on Binance has since resumed after the exchange worked with issuers to freeze assets impacted by the hack.
The TraderTraitor unit, which is also known as the Lazarus Group, was blamed for a then-record $1.5bn hack of crypto exchange Bybit in 2025.
The net outflow represents a "relatively limited portion" of Binance's total assets, which stand at approximately $157bn, the spokesperson told the BBC on Tuesday.

Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, says it has frozen around half of the funds stolen in a "complex" hack, after $6.3bn (£4.7bn) was accessed in what is believed to be a record heist .
Chainalysis, a crypto analytics firm, said it had "high confidence" that a North Korean is linked to the hack.
Several experts have warned customers not to regard Binance's promise to cover losses as legally binding and said they may need to pursue litigation to recover them.
In nearly all cases investigators have blamed hackers from North Korea, pointing to the infamous Lazarus Group - also know as TraderTraitor.
The names refer to clusters of cyber criminals accused of working directly for the regime.
North Korea is an impoverished country with very little industry and heavy international sanctions and experts say the regime uses cyber crime as a way to bring money in.
Who could be behind the Binance hack and what we know so far
Binance, which was founded in China in 2017, allows users to trade digital assets and is estimated to have more than 300 million registered users worldwide.
A lot of the fear right now from Binance users - and the crypto industry at large - is whether or not Binance will actually be capable of covering this enormous financial loss.

America's lead federal agency for investigating financial crimes added that it would "identify the cyber criminals responsible and bring them to justice", while Binance also said it was working with the FBI.

While Binance said its US-facing exchange was unaffected, the US would still have jurisdiction to investigate the hack and help track down stolen funds - an effort which generally involves a global law enforcement effort.
Binance told its users "your money is safe, and we're covering every loss".
Binance's co-CEO Richard Teng said: "This was not carried out by one person.
Our initial investigation suggested that the security incident may have involved a compromised laptop, however our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach."

Daniel Tunkel, of the London-based Edwin Coe law firm, said that would "come down to what [customers] have been promised in their contracts", and "where Binance can be sued for non-performance, if it comes to it".
Binance has been subject of regulatory scrutiny around the world.

sources.title: Musk is throttling Grok because its cost is 'unsustainably high' - Yahoo Finance
passages: "The cost of serving Grok Bot was unsustainably high relative to revenue," Musk wrote on his social media platform, X.
The sudden throttling highlights one of the biggest questions swirling around the AI revolution: whether demand from users will be enough to sustain a business.
It turns out, at least in Musk's case, that demand isn't the problem.
The tenor of the comments on Musk's own platform, filled with Grok users, turned noticeably sharp : "Yet another Elon rug-pull."
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
Elon Musk said on Sunday that Grok ( SPCX ) users would run up against usage limits more quickly than normal because servicing Grok Bot has become too expensive.
Musk suddenly changing Grok subscriptions so that the AI-usage meter runs faster has struck users and tech observers as unfair and worrisome for SpaceX's business.
Musk was responding to an X user complaining that their Grok Bot usage jumped to 100% before their reset date, when typically they never reached their cap while using the AI agent.
Now it's unsustainable and loses money (???)", wrote former xAI worker Benjamin De Kraker in a post on X .
Other commenters pointed to a bold and now ironic post Musk sent out a few days ago , saying, "Saving money for the distant future is pointless with the advent of super intelligent abundance."
That's why the revenue question is increasingly critical and why Musk's admission is so significant.
The AI business is running into real-world limitations.
Another way to think through the change is that Musk was simply offering an introductory rate to hook users.

Elon Musk said on Sunday that Grok ( SPCX ) users would run up against usage limits more quickly than normal because servicing Grok Bot has become too expensive. "The cost of serving Grok Bot was unsustainably high relative to revenue," Musk wrote on his social media platform, X. Musk was responding to an X user complaining that their Grok Bot usage jumped to 100% before their reset date, when typically they never reached their cap while using the AI agent. User demand is just one side of the AI market equation, and the businesses churning out sophisticated and expensive models have to — or will have to, eventually — generate revenue to cover their heightened costs. The economics of the still-new and messy AI industry suggest that even healthy demand can't always sustain the AI tools they're selling. Not at these prices — for the users (cheap) and for the corporate compute (expensive; just look at the computing bills ). That's why the revenue question is increasingly critical and why Musk's admission is so significant. The AI business is running into real-world limitations. Musk suddenly changing Grok subscriptions so that the AI-usage meter runs faster has struck users and tech observers as unfair and worrisome for SpaceX's business. "Two weeks ago Grok Bot was an incredible success story powering SpaceXai's revenue growth. Now it's unsustainable and loses money (???)", wrote former xAI worker Benjamin De Kraker in a post on X . Other commenters pointed to a bold and now ironic post Musk sent out a few days ago , saying, "Saving money for the distant future is pointless with the advent of super intelligent abundance." The tenor of the comments on Musk's own platform, filled with Grok users, turned noticeably sharp : "Yet another Elon rug-pull." "Just being sensible," he wrote on X , in response to a comment suggesting that investors would punish SpaceX for the decision. In fact, shares are up 5% on Monday. And why shouldn't they be? Wall Street has always loved fiscal responsibility and capitalizing on demand. Another way to think through the change is that Musk was simply offering an introductory rate to hook users. Perhaps AI subscriptions are going through their own version of the "VC subsidy," popularized when Uber, Lyft, and other venture-backed apps offered discounts and super-low rates to boost adoption and engagement, only for the apps to sharply increase prices once users became reliant on the services. But it’s unlikely that AI producers will be able to subsidize their products’ costs to users forever.

They additionally commented that “Normally I don’t even reach 100%.” Musk then replied to the post , stating: “The cost of serving Grok Bot was unsustainably high relative to revenue.” Many X users seemed irked by the situation, with several saying that their Grok Bot usage had hit the 100% limit while they were sleeping and not using any AI agents. Elon Musk’s comments come amid broader scrutiny of the financial sustainability of many AI products. Tech stocks — including those of many leading AI firms — fell sharply last week as investors grew concerned over the profitability of the industry , with Google revealing that its own AI summaries have hurt its search advertising revenue. Concerns have also been raised in recent months over the finances involved in many AI companies’ offerings. For instance, users of AI tools like ChatGPT and Claude Code can often spend many times more in tokens than they’re actually paying in monthly subscriptions, leading to questions over how sustainable many AI business models really are and whether things will need to be adjusted in the near future. This changing landscape hasn’t gone down well with many users, of course. One thread on Reddit dubbed Musk’s about-face an “indirect rug pull” of Grok Bot, with features and usage limited in a bid to cut costs. But it’s unlikely that AI producers will be able to subsidize their products’ costs to users forever. Usage limits will necessarily need to tighten (as OpenAI quietly announced recently, much to the frustration of users ) and prices will need to increase for these business models to make sense. So don’t be surprised if Grok Bot’s lower cap is just the first of many big changes looming on the horizon. sources.title: Elon Musk throttles Grok Bot limits due to ‘unsustainably high’ costs
passages: Grok Bot has been positioned as a success story for the newly public SpaceX, which said in a filing last month that AI now makes up 52% of company income.
Its renamed “Super Intelligence” division actually turned a profit of $431 million, which is a rarity in the AI industry.
Its profit would’ve been higher if not for $1.2 billion of one-time costs related to its acquisition of Cursor .
Musk recently referred to Grok Bot as having “the fastest growth of a product that I’ve ever seen in my life.”
Over Halloween weekend, some Grok Bot users awoke to something especially spooky: Their weekly usage limits were unexpectedly maxed out, even if they hadn’t been using SpaceX’s agentic AI overnight.
Some users reported on X that their usage jumped from as low as 50% to 100% .
He has not addressed the issue on his main feed but has continued boasting that Grok Bot can help you buy gifts for your family.
The cost of serving Grok Bot was unsustainably high relative to revenue
Musk has not yet shared how subscribers’ usage limits will be impacted moving forward.
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk confirmed in an X post on Sunday that this was not a glitch.
