Start your Independent Membership today. Users of Grok Bot, the personal assistant made by Elon Musk ’s artificial intelligence firm, are finding themselves cut off from their AI agents. SpaceXSI, which includes both Elon Musk’s rocket firm as well as its AI work and the social network X , introduced Grok Bot in August. It described the tool as “AI teammates you can give real work to”. It came amid a flurry of such personal AI assistants launched by many of the world’s biggest artificial intelligence firms. The most prominent among them is Meta ’s Muse , though OpenAI has also pushed its own system, called Dots. Now, however, Mr Musk has been hit by complaints from users of the service who say that they are rapidly running out of usage and so finding themselves unable to access the tool. As with many AI systems, each Grok Bot user is allocated a certain amount of work and any questions will run that down. In response to a complaint from a user who complained that they had hit their weekly maximum usage with four days until it was reset, Mr Musk said that the system was expensive and was not making enough money. “The cost of serving Grok Bot was unsustainably high relative to revenue,” he wrote in a reply on X. Such personal assistants are particularly resource intensive, because they can be asked to undertake complicated tasks and operate as a team of co-ordinated AI systems. But companies are nonetheless pushing them as the future of both our work and personal lives. Many of those companies – including SpaceXSI, Meta and OpenAI – are losing vast sums of money across their AI work. But they appear to be betting that the cost of running the systems will serve as an investment for the future, by allowing them to acquire users and build more complex systems. But it remains unclear how those companies will be able to keep running the tools and making money, given the vast expense required to actually offer them. While all of the companies have some kind of payment system – Grok Bot is only available to those who pay for SpaceXSI’s AI tools, and OpenAI has restricted Dots to users with its more expensive accounts – some, including Meta’s Muse, come with a free tier. At the moment, that is the primary way that companies make back some of the cost of offering those personal agents. But Meta may have offered a hint at how it could make money from its Muse service in other ways: in its latest results, the first since it released its agentic assistant, it noted that shopping was one of the top ways that users were interacting with it, which could presumably be used for advertising in the future. The sudden throttling highlights one of the biggest questions swirling around the AI revolution: whether demand from users will be enough to sustain a business.
It turns out, at least in Musk's case, that demand isn't the problem.
The tenor of the comments on Musk's own platform, filled with Grok users, turned noticeably sharp : "Yet another Elon rug-pull."

Musk was responding to an X user complaining that their Grok Bot usage jumped to 100% before their reset date, when typically they never reached their cap while using the AI agent.
Now it's unsustainable and loses money (???)", wrote former xAI worker Benjamin De Kraker in a post on X .
Other commenters pointed to a bold and now ironic post Musk sent out a few days ago , saying, "Saving money for the distant future is pointless with the advent of super intelligent abundance."

Elon Musk said on Sunday that Grok ( SPCX ) users would run up against usage limits more quickly than normal because servicing Grok Bot has become too expensive. "The cost of serving Grok Bot was unsustainably high relative to revenue," Musk wrote on his social media platform, X. The sudden throttling highlights one of the biggest questions swirling around the AI revolution: whether demand from users will be enough to sustain a business. It turns out, at least in Musk's case, that demand isn't the problem. The cost is. Musk was responding to an X user complaining that their Grok Bot usage jumped to 100% before their reset date, when typically they never reached their cap while using the AI agent. User demand is just one side of the AI market equation, and the businesses churning out sophisticated and expensive models have to — or will have to, eventually — generate revenue to cover their heightened costs. The economics of the still-new and messy AI industry suggest that even healthy demand can't always sustain the AI tools they're selling. Not at these prices — for the users (cheap) and for the corporate compute (expensive; just look at the computing bills ). That's why the revenue question is increasingly critical and why Musk's admission is so significant. The AI business is running into real-world limitations. Musk suddenly changing Grok subscriptions so that the AI-usage meter runs faster has struck users and tech observers as unfair and worrisome for SpaceX's business. "Two weeks ago Grok Bot was an incredible success story powering SpaceXai's revenue growth. Now it's unsustainable and loses money (???)", wrote former xAI worker Benjamin De Kraker in a post on X . Other commenters pointed to a bold and now ironic post Musk sent out a few days ago , saying, "Saving money for the distant future is pointless with the advent of super intelligent abundance." The tenor of the comments on Musk's own platform, filled with Grok users, turned noticeably sharp : "Yet another Elon rug-pull." "Just being sensible," he wrote on X , in response to a comment suggesting that investors would punish SpaceX for the decision. In fact, shares are up 5% on Monday. And why shouldn't they be? Wall Street has always loved fiscal responsibility and capitalizing on demand. Another way to think through the change is that Musk was simply offering an introductory rate to hook users. Perhaps AI subscriptions are going through their own version of the "VC subsidy," popularized when Uber, Lyft, and other venture-backed apps offered discounts and super-low rates to boost adoption and engagement, only for the apps to sharply increase prices once users became reliant on the services. story.title: Elon Musk throttles Grok Bot limits due to ‘unsustainably high’ costs

facts.text: "The cost of serving Grok Bot was unsustainably high relative to revenue," Musk wrote on his social media platform, X.
The sudden throttling highlights one of the biggest questions swirling around the AI revolution: whether demand from users will be enough to sustain a business.
It turns out, at least in Musk's case, that demand isn't the problem.
The tenor of the comments on Musk's own platform, filled with Grok users, turned noticeably sharp : "Yet another Elon rug-pull."
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
Elon Musk said on Sunday that Grok ( SPCX ) users would run up against usage limits more quickly than normal because servicing Grok Bot has become too expensive.
Musk suddenly changing Grok subscriptions so that the AI-usage meter runs faster has struck users and tech observers as unfair and worrisome for SpaceX's business.
Musk was responding to an X user complaining that their Grok Bot usage jumped to 100% before their reset date, when typically they never reached their cap while using the AI agent.
Now it's unsustainable and loses money (???)", wrote former xAI worker Benjamin De Kraker in a post on X .
Other commenters pointed to a bold and now ironic post Musk sent out a few days ago , saying, "Saving money for the distant future is pointless with the advent of super intelligent abundance."
That's why the revenue question is increasingly critical and why Musk's admission is so significant.
The AI business is running into real-world limitations.
Another way to think through the change is that Musk was simply offering an introductory rate to hook users.

If you noticed that you burned through your Grok Bot usage much faster than usual in recent days, there’s a reason for that: Elon Musk intentionally limited users’ AI agent allowances in the face of “unsustainably high costs.” And as you’d expect, a lot of people are unhappy with that.
This changing landscape hasn’t gone down well with many users, of course.
Users claimed their usage had suddenly gone from 50% to 100%, 35% to 78%, and 70% to 100%, all supposedly without using Grok Bot at all.
The revelation came about after an X user pinged platform owner Musk , asking for a Grok Bot reset after they surprisingly hit their 100% usage limit, four days before it was due to reset.
They additionally commented that “Normally I don’t even reach 100%.”
But it’s unlikely that AI producers will be able to subsidize their products’ costs to users forever.

sources.title: Crypto firm Binance covers 90% of losses after $6.3bn hack - BBC
passages: Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, says it has covered 90% of the $6.3bn (£4.7bn) assets stolen in a hack on Thursday.

Richard Teng, Binance's co-chief executive officer, said the hack was carried out by more than one person, and the hackers used sophisticated methods to hide their tracks, such as a "self-destruct mechanism".
In an update on Sunday, Binance said withdrawals had been restored on several of its networks, after they were suspended following the hack.
"Binance will absorb the financial impact of these stolen funds, not our users," the company said in a statement on Saturday.

Binance's initial investigation suggested an engineer's laptop was compromised, which allowed access to unauthorised withdrawals, but a later update said they had uncovered "additional points of breach".
The US Secret Service said on Friday it is "working around the clock" with private sector partners "to identify, freeze, trace, and recover funds" stolen from Binance.

Two analytics firms previously told the BBC they had robust intelligence pointing to North Korean state-backed hacking unit the Lazarus Group, also known as TraderTraitor - which was specifically named by the FBI - as the likely culprits.
Binance said it had replenished the stolen assets using various funds and its own corporate treasury.
Binance, founded in China in 2017, lets users buy, sell and trade digital assets - it is estimated to have hundreds of millions of users worldwide.
The hack is believed to be the largest in history, eclipsing the record of a $1.5bn heist on the Bybit exchange in 2025 - for which the FBI also said North Korea was responsible.
Crypto is a digital asset, which doesn't exist physically and is instead accessed via digital wallets or computers.

sources.title: Binance’s $6.3 billion hack raises questions about crypto wallet safety - CNBC
passages: A security incident at digital asset exchange Binance on Thursday affected some $6.3 billion in client assets, making it the largest crypto theft on record.
Experts whom CNBC interviewed said the security incidents on the crypto exchanges aren't surprising, especially in light of recent artificial intelligence hacking incidents .
That's because the hack may have involved a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, Binance said in a post on X .
Two high-profile security breaches this week – including the biggest cryptocurrency theft in history – are raising questions on the safety of storing funds in a wallet on a crypto exchange .
Binance and Polymarket reassured users that they would make affected investors whole.
That's a sign that users should feel confident in crypto exchanges, according to Ido Ben-Natan , CEO of blockchain security company Blockaid.
"I actually think no users will lose any money," he said.
"Binance has said they're going to cover everything… I actually don't think it's a bad idea for users to put money in these exchanges.
As a result, a crypto wallet could ultimately become a safer place to hold funds compared to other options, since the industry will have the experience of how to handle these attacks, Ben-Natan said.
However, crypto may be a unique target for hackers in a changing cybersecurity landscape, these experts told CNBC.

Earlier that day, prediction market platform Polymarket temporarily halted trading on its international exchange after a third-party data provider was hacked, resulting in at least $2.7 million being drained from users' wallets.
The same was true of Polymarket's domestic exchange.
U.S. regulated platforms Coinbase and Robinhood were also unaffected by the security breach on Binance, though shares of both fell on Friday in the aftermath.
In another social media post, BInance later said its investigation uncovered additional points of breach , though the company didn't specify what they were.

extraction.body: Two high-profile security breaches this week – including the biggest cryptocurrency theft in history – are raising questions on the safety of storing funds in a wallet on a crypto exchange . A security incident at digital asset exchange Binance on Thursday affected some $6.3 billion in client assets, making it the largest crypto theft on record. Earlier that day, prediction market platform Polymarket temporarily halted trading on its international exchange after a third-party data provider was hacked, resulting in at least $2.7 million being drained from users' wallets. The company's international platform operates on the Polygon blockchain. Experts whom CNBC interviewed said the security incidents on the crypto exchanges aren't surprising, especially in light of recent artificial intelligence hacking incidents . Most of these experts even said that observers should expect more security incidents, at least in the near term, as that problem worsens. "I think it's extremely dangerous," said Tyler Moore, a cybersecurity professor at the University of Tulsa who has followed the asset class for more than a decade. "I think you should be very wary of leaving any significant amount of funds in an exchange… there are no built-in protections for when these inevitable hacks take place." For instance, banking customers can rely on the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation to insure deposits up to $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, in the event of an institution's failure. There is no similar form of coverage available for funds lost from a cryptocurrency exchange, noted Moore. Binance and Polymarket reassured users that they would make affected investors whole. That's a sign that users should feel confident in crypto exchanges, according to Ido Ben-Natan , CEO of blockchain security company Blockaid. "I actually think no users will lose any money," he said. "Binance has said they're going to cover everything… I actually don't think it's a bad idea for users to put money in these exchanges. These exchanges need to work really hard to make sure they don't take another hit like this." Ben-Natan noted that while he thinks more hacks are likely as the cybersecurity landscape changes due to AI, he said it will only make the crypto industry stronger. As a result, a crypto wallet could ultimately become a safer place to hold funds compared to other options, since the industry will have the experience of how to handle these attacks, Ben-Natan said. A key point is that while Binance experienced a security incident on its offshore platform, its regulated, centralized U.S. exchange did not have a similar issue. The same was true of Polymarket's domestic exchange. U.S. regulated platforms Coinbase and Robinhood were also unaffected by the security breach on Binance, though shares of both fell on Friday in the aftermath. In a Friday appearance on CNBC's " Squawk on the Street ," the Commodity Futures Trading Commission — the federal regulator of derivatives — Chairman Michael Selig said that the offshore nature of these incidents was critical to note. "They don't have the same sorts of safeguards that we have in our financial markets," he said. "We want to offer a federal option to these exchanges to come and register with the CFTC, and they would be subject to the same sorts of cybersecurity safeguards that we have in our markets today." Brett Falk, a professor and director of the Crypto and Society Lab at the University of Pennsylvania, said that U.S. regulations likely wouldn't have stopped an incident like that of Binance on Thursday. That's because the hack may have involved a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, Binance said in a post on X . "Most of the regulation doesn't touch the specific software stack you have to use to authenticate people," Falk said. In another social media post, BInance later said its investigation uncovered additional points of breach , though the company didn't specify what they were. Falk echoed the argument by Ben-Natan that individuals likely won't face losses, and that it's better for traders to leave funds with an exchange where they have the financial backing of a company rather than in a self-custody wallet where no one can refund their losses in the event of a hack. Ben-Natan added that traders should feel secure based on how many incidents companies like his catch that don't become news. That's because the security technology often works and stops them before they become major incidents. However, crypto may be a unique target for hackers in a changing cybersecurity landscape, these experts told CNBC. That's because of how much liquidity individuals can quickly access in the event of a successful breach. It's why Ryan Kirkley, CEO of blockchain infrastructure company Global Settlement Network, thinks traders should be cautious leaving their funds in any wallet that's not backed by insurance until financial companies upgrade their security infrastructure. "I do not think there's anything right now that is a common solution in the marketplace where your assets are truly safe," Kirkley said. "Unless you are dealing with a reputable and firm broker-dealer that provides an asset insurance, you are risking your assets putting them into any ecosystem today just simply because there's so much unknown," he added. sources.title: Binance sees more than $4.6 billion in withdrawals after largest crypto hack in history - Yahoo Finance
passages: Binance has seen $3.64 billion in net outflows since it gradually restored user withdrawals following the largest crypto hack in history, which the FBI linked to North Korea.
The world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange said that it processed $4.649 billion in withdrawals and approximately $1.01 billion in deposits.

"The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) is releasing information advising the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (North Korea) was responsible for the theft of more than $6 billion USD in virtual assets from cryptocurrency exchange Binance, on or about October 29, 2026," a press release said.
Binance was hit late Thursday by a hack that investigators said impacted roughly $6.3 billion in funds, with roughly half of those assets frozen.
Other major crypto assets also tumbled after the hack, with ether ( ETH-USD ) dropping to roughly $2,200.
Binance's native token, BNB ( BND-USD ), also fell.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
"We continue working with industry partners to complete the remaining acquisitions," Binance said in an update on X.
Meanwhile, the total crypto market has lost roughly 3% in value, or $80 billion, over the last seven days, according to CoinMarketCap data.

Binance has seen $3.64 billion in net outflows since it gradually restored user withdrawals following the largest crypto hack in history, which the FBI linked to North Korea. Around $3.24 billion remains in addresses linked to the theft, according to Tom Robinson, chief scientist and co-founder at blockchain analytics company Elliptic. The attack has rattled crypto markets, and bitcoin ( BTC-USD ) traded at around $77,700 on Monday. sources.title: Binance clients pull US$4.7B after hack as crypto world studies fallout
passages: SINGAPORE/PARIS/NEW YORK — Binance’s customers have withdrawn a net $4.72 billion from the world’s biggest cryptocurrency exchange since it reopened, after hackers stole around $6.3 billion of crypto from the platform in what could be the largest-ever financial heist.

Binance, which says it has more than 335 million users worldwide and average daily trading volumes of $95 billion across digital assets and derivatives, said it had also seen $2.7 billion in customer inflows since Sunday and that withdrawal volumes were stabilizing after an “initial spike.” Data from data analytics provider DeFiLlama showed several crypto exchanges received notable inflows to their platforms since Binance opened withdrawals, although it was unclear what share came from users moving funds off Binance.
Binance itself processed net outflows of about $6 billion over 72 hours in 2022 after the collapse of FTX.
Binance said the net outflows amounted to around 3 per cent of the assets on its platform, a relatively modest figure that analysts said suggested customer confidence had largely held up.
“Binance will absorb the financial impact of the stolen funds, not our users,” the company said in a statement on X.
“A hack at a crypto exchange is bank robbery at the speed of the internet, which creates an unstable risk profile for anyone responsible for other people’s capital,” he said.

Analysts and crypto experts said the fallout appeared limited so far, and there was little sign of an impact on broader financial markets despite deepening ties between crypto and mainstream finance in recent years.
NO RUSH TO WITHDRAW Some traders told Reuters they were keeping their accounts on Binance.
Binance started allowing US dollar cash withdrawals again on Monday.

extraction.body: SINGAPORE/PARIS/NEW YORK — Binance’s customers have withdrawn a net $4.72 billion from the world’s biggest cryptocurrency exchange since it reopened, after hackers stole around $6.3 billion of crypto from the platform in what could be the largest-ever financial heist. The exchange froze withdrawals for more than two days after the hack, which the FBI said was carried out by North Korea, then started allowing customers to withdraw again on Sunday morning. The theft has underlined the vulnerability of digital assets to attacks and raised questions about the impact of the hack on Binance, which has vowed to repay customers in full. Binance said the net outflows amounted to around 3 per cent of the assets on its platform, a relatively modest figure that analysts said suggested customer confidence had largely held up. Most withdrawals from the platform were in the form of Tether’s USDT stablecoin, Binance added. The outflow compares with about $7 billion withdrawn from Circle’s USDC stablecoin over a week after the collapse of Silicon Valley Bank in 2023. Binance itself processed net outflows of about $6 billion over 72 hours in 2022 after the collapse of FTX. The attack marks a step-up in North Korea’s crypto thefts. Blockchain analytics firm TRM Labs said North Korea-linked hackers have stolen $7.4 billion so far in 2026. Analysts and crypto experts said the fallout appeared limited so far, and there was little sign of an impact on broader financial markets despite deepening ties between crypto and mainstream finance in recent years. “Binance will absorb the financial impact of the stolen funds, not our users,” the company said in a statement on X. Binance said it was covering the losses with company funds and had already raised $6 billion from its corporate treasury, an insurance fund and reserves set aside for security breaches. “It has not yet triggered widespread panic or a massive, concentrated withdrawal,” said Tim Sun, a senior researcher at HashKey Group 3887.HK, a digital asset financial service company in Hong Kong. Binance, which says it has more than 335 million users worldwide and average daily trading volumes of $95 billion across digital assets and derivatives, said it had also seen $2.7 billion in customer inflows since Sunday and that withdrawal volumes were stabilizing after an “initial spike.” Data from data analytics provider DeFiLlama showed several crypto exchanges received notable inflows to their platforms since Binance opened withdrawals, although it was unclear what share came from users moving funds off Binance. OKX recorded $284.87 million in inflows in the last 24 hours, followed by Gate with $93.22 million in inflows and Bybit, which saw $29.25 million in inflows. NO RUSH TO WITHDRAW Some traders told Reuters they were keeping their accounts on Binance. Ryan Tan, a Binance user, said he was in no hurry to withdraw his funds from the platform, as he had already kept his account fairly light since the collapse of FTX four years ago. “After the FTX collapse, I decided to hold everything on my wallet instead of leaving them on exchanges,” said the 39-year-old. After hitting a six-week low on Friday, bitcoin BTC= prices recovered through the weekend to trade above $77,000 on Monday, while ether ETH= also rebounded from a two-month low. Stablecoin market capitalizations, often viewed as a gauge of money moving into and out of crypto markets, have fallen since Friday, suggesting some investors have shifted funds into cash or traditional assets. Binance started allowing US dollar cash withdrawals again on Monday. “HIGHLY COMPLEX” MONEY LAUNDERING The FBI said on Saturday that the North Korean state-sponsored group TraderTraitor was responsible for the attack. Analysts said the attack’s scale could curb institutional appetite for cryptocurrencies. Spot bitcoin ETFs recorded outflows of $643 million on Friday, the largest daily withdrawal in October, while more than $1.3 billion in leveraged positions were liquidated, according to Ari Redbord, global head of policy at TRM Labs. “A hack at a crypto exchange is bank robbery at the speed of the internet, which creates an unstable risk profile for anyone responsible for other people’s capital,” he said. About half of the stolen funds were held in stablecoins and have been frozen by issuers including Circle, which said on Monday it had frozen more than $1.1 billion in USDC USDC=. According to blockchain analytics firm Elliptic, the hackers still control around $3.28 billion, mostly in bitcoin and ether, and only a negligible amount has been cashed out of crypto and into fiat currency. Elliptic described the laundering process as “highly complex and clearly automated.” Jonathan Benton, founder and chief executive at crypto asset recovery firm iSanctuary, said blockchain technology exists to trace stolen funds, but the challenge is turning that intelligence into rapid, coordinated action before those assets disappear. “The future of crypto won’t be decided by how much money enters the market, but by how safe that money is once it’s there,” said Benton, former head of the international corruption unit of the UK’s National Crime Agency. (Reporting by Rae Wee and Ankur Banerjee in Singapore, Elizabeth Howcroft in Paris and Hannah Lang in New York; Writing by Scott Murdoch and Tom Westbrook; Editing by Sonali Paul, Xevi Fontdegloria, Mark Potter, Rod Nickel)

sources.title: Binance’s $6.3 billion hack raises questions about crypto wallet safety - CNBC
passages: A security incident at digital asset exchange Binance on Thursday affected some $6.3 billion in client assets, making it the largest crypto theft on record.
Experts whom CNBC interviewed said the security incidents on the crypto exchanges aren't surprising, especially in light of recent artificial intelligence hacking incidents .
That's because the hack may have involved a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, Binance said in a post on X .
Two high-profile security breaches this week – including the biggest cryptocurrency theft in history – are raising questions on the safety of storing funds in a wallet on a crypto exchange .
Binance and Polymarket reassured users that they would make affected investors whole.
That's a sign that users should feel confident in crypto exchanges, according to Ido Ben-Natan , CEO of blockchain security company Blockaid.
"I actually think no users will lose any money," he said.
"Binance has said they're going to cover everything… I actually don't think it's a bad idea for users to put money in these exchanges.
As a result, a crypto wallet could ultimately become a safer place to hold funds compared to other options, since the industry will have the experience of how to handle these attacks, Ben-Natan said.
However, crypto may be a unique target for hackers in a changing cybersecurity landscape, these experts told CNBC.

Earlier that day, prediction market platform Polymarket temporarily halted trading on its international exchange after a third-party data provider was hacked, resulting in at least $2.7 million being drained from users' wallets.
The same was true of Polymarket's domestic exchange.
U.S. regulated platforms Coinbase and Robinhood were also unaffected by the security breach on Binance, though shares of both fell on Friday in the aftermath.
In another social media post, BInance later said its investigation uncovered additional points of breach , though the company didn't specify what they were.

extraction.body: Two high-profile security breaches this week – including the biggest cryptocurrency theft in history – are raising questions on the safety of storing funds in a wallet on a crypto exchange . A security incident at digital asset exchange Binance on Thursday affected some $6.3 billion in client assets, making it the largest crypto theft on record. Earlier that day, prediction market platform Polymarket temporarily halted trading on its international exchange after a third-party data provider was hacked, resulting in at least $2.7 million being drained from users' wallets. The company's international platform operates on the Polygon blockchain. Experts whom CNBC interviewed said the security incidents on the crypto exchanges aren't surprising, especially in light of recent artificial intelligence hacking incidents . Most of these experts even said that observers should expect more security incidents, at least in the near term, as that problem worsens. "I think it's extremely dangerous," said Tyler Moore, a cybersecurity professor at the University of Tulsa who has followed the asset class for more than a decade. "I think you should be very wary of leaving any significant amount of funds in an exchange… there are no built-in protections for when these inevitable hacks take place." For instance, banking customers can rely on the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation to insure deposits up to $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, in the event of an institution's failure. There is no similar form of coverage available for funds lost from a cryptocurrency exchange, noted Moore. Binance and Polymarket reassured users that they would make affected investors whole. That's a sign that users should feel confident in crypto exchanges, according to Ido Ben-Natan , CEO of blockchain security company Blockaid. "I actually think no users will lose any money," he said. "Binance has said they're going to cover everything… I actually don't think it's a bad idea for users to put money in these exchanges. These exchanges need to work really hard to make sure they don't take another hit like this." Ben-Natan noted that while he thinks more hacks are likely as the cybersecurity landscape changes due to AI, he said it will only make the crypto industry stronger. As a result, a crypto wallet could ultimately become a safer place to hold funds compared to other options, since the industry will have the experience of how to handle these attacks, Ben-Natan said. A key point is that while Binance experienced a security incident on its offshore platform, its regulated, centralized U.S. exchange did not have a similar issue. The same was true of Polymarket's domestic exchange. U.S. regulated platforms Coinbase and Robinhood were also unaffected by the security breach on Binance, though shares of both fell on Friday in the aftermath. In a Friday appearance on CNBC's " Squawk on the Street ," the Commodity Futures Trading Commission — the federal regulator of derivatives — Chairman Michael Selig said that the offshore nature of these incidents was critical to note. "They don't have the same sorts of safeguards that we have in our financial markets," he said. "We want to offer a federal option to these exchanges to come and register with the CFTC, and they would be subject to the same sorts of cybersecurity safeguards that we have in our markets today." Brett Falk, a professor and director of the Crypto and Society Lab at the University of Pennsylvania, said that U.S. regulations likely wouldn't have stopped an incident like that of Binance on Thursday. That's because the hack may have involved a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, Binance said in a post on X . "Most of the regulation doesn't touch the specific software stack you have to use to authenticate people," Falk said. In another social media post, BInance later said its investigation uncovered additional points of breach , though the company didn't specify what they were. Falk echoed the argument by Ben-Natan that individuals likely won't face losses, and that it's better for traders to leave funds with an exchange where they have the financial backing of a company rather than in a self-custody wallet where no one can refund their losses in the event of a hack. Ben-Natan added that traders should feel secure based on how many incidents companies like his catch that don't become news. That's because the security technology often works and stops them before they become major incidents. However, crypto may be a unique target for hackers in a changing cybersecurity landscape, these experts told CNBC. That's because of how much liquidity individuals can quickly access in the event of a successful breach. It's why Ryan Kirkley, CEO of blockchain infrastructure company Global Settlement Network, thinks traders should be cautious leaving their funds in any wallet that's not backed by insurance until financial companies upgrade their security infrastructure. "I do not think there's anything right now that is a common solution in the marketplace where your assets are truly safe," Kirkley said. "Unless you are dealing with a reputable and firm broker-dealer that provides an asset insurance, you are risking your assets putting them into any ecosystem today just simply because there's so much unknown," he added. sources.title: Binance sees more than $4.6 billion in withdrawals after largest crypto hack in history - Yahoo Finance
passages: Binance has seen $3.64 billion in net outflows since it gradually restored user withdrawals following the largest crypto hack in history, which the FBI linked to North Korea.
The world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange said that it processed $4.649 billion in withdrawals and approximately $1.01 billion in deposits.

"The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) is releasing information advising the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (North Korea) was responsible for the theft of more than $6 billion USD in virtual assets from cryptocurrency exchange Binance, on or about October 29, 2026," a press release said.
Binance was hit late Thursday by a hack that investigators said impacted roughly $6.3 billion in funds, with roughly half of those assets frozen.
Other major crypto assets also tumbled after the hack, with ether ( ETH-USD ) dropping to roughly $2,200.
Binance's native token, BNB ( BND-USD ), also fell.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
"We continue working with industry partners to complete the remaining acquisitions," Binance said in an update on X.
Meanwhile, the total crypto market has lost roughly 3% in value, or $80 billion, over the last seven days, according to CoinMarketCap data.

extraction.body: SINGAPORE/PARIS/NEW YORK — Binance’s customers have withdrawn a net $4.72 billion from the world’s biggest cryptocurrency exchange since it reopened, after hackers stole around $6.3 billion of crypto from the platform in what could be the largest-ever financial heist. The exchange froze withdrawals for more than two days after the hack, which the FBI said was carried out by North Korea, then started allowing customers to withdraw again on Sunday morning. The theft has underlined the vulnerability of digital assets to attacks and raised questions about the impact of the hack on Binance, which has vowed to repay customers in full. Binance said the net outflows amounted to around 3 per cent of the assets on its platform, a relatively modest figure that analysts said suggested customer confidence had largely held up. Most withdrawals from the platform were in the form of Tether’s USDT stablecoin, Binance added. The outflow compares with about $7 billion withdrawn from Circle’s USDC stablecoin over a week after the collapse of Silicon Valley Bank in 2023. Binance itself processed net outflows of about $6 billion over 72 hours in 2022 after the collapse of FTX. The attack marks a step-up in North Korea’s crypto thefts. Blockchain analytics firm TRM Labs said North Korea-linked hackers have stolen $7.4 billion so far in 2026. Analysts and crypto experts said the fallout appeared limited so far, and there was little sign of an impact on broader financial markets despite deepening ties between crypto and mainstream finance in recent years. “Binance will absorb the financial impact of the stolen funds, not our users,” the company said in a statement on X. Binance said it was covering the losses with company funds and had already raised $6 billion from its corporate treasury, an insurance fund and reserves set aside for security breaches. “It has not yet triggered widespread panic or a massive, concentrated withdrawal,” said Tim Sun, a senior researcher at HashKey Group 3887.HK, a digital asset financial service company in Hong Kong. Binance, which says it has more than 335 million users worldwide and average daily trading volumes of $95 billion across digital assets and derivatives, said it had also seen $2.7 billion in customer inflows since Sunday and that withdrawal volumes were stabilizing after an “initial spike.” Data from data analytics provider DeFiLlama showed several crypto exchanges received notable inflows to their platforms since Binance opened withdrawals, although it was unclear what share came from users moving funds off Binance. OKX recorded $284.87 million in inflows in the last 24 hours, followed by Gate with $93.22 million in inflows and Bybit, which saw $29.25 million in inflows. NO RUSH TO WITHDRAW Some traders told Reuters they were keeping their accounts on Binance. Ryan Tan, a Binance user, said he was in no hurry to withdraw his funds from the platform, as he had already kept his account fairly light since the collapse of FTX four years ago. “After the FTX collapse, I decided to hold everything on my wallet instead of leaving them on exchanges,” said the 39-year-old. After hitting a six-week low on Friday, bitcoin BTC= prices recovered through the weekend to trade above $77,000 on Monday, while ether ETH= also rebounded from a two-month low. Stablecoin market capitalizations, often viewed as a gauge of money moving into and out of crypto markets, have fallen since Friday, suggesting some investors have shifted funds into cash or traditional assets. Binance started allowing US dollar cash withdrawals again on Monday. “HIGHLY COMPLEX” MONEY LAUNDERING The FBI said on Saturday that the North Korean state-sponsored group TraderTraitor was responsible for the attack. Analysts said the attack’s scale could curb institutional appetite for cryptocurrencies. Spot bitcoin ETFs recorded outflows of $643 million on Friday, the largest daily withdrawal in October, while more than $1.3 billion in leveraged positions were liquidated, according to Ari Redbord, global head of policy at TRM Labs. “A hack at a crypto exchange is bank robbery at the speed of the internet, which creates an unstable risk profile for anyone responsible for other people’s capital,” he said. About half of the stolen funds were held in stablecoins and have been frozen by issuers including Circle, which said on Monday it had frozen more than $1.1 billion in USDC USDC=. According to blockchain analytics firm Elliptic, the hackers still control around $3.28 billion, mostly in bitcoin and ether, and only a negligible amount has been cashed out of crypto and into fiat currency. Elliptic described the laundering process as “highly complex and clearly automated.” Jonathan Benton, founder and chief executive at crypto asset recovery firm iSanctuary, said blockchain technology exists to trace stolen funds, but the challenge is turning that intelligence into rapid, coordinated action before those assets disappear. “The future of crypto won’t be decided by how much money enters the market, but by how safe that money is once it’s there,” said Benton, former head of the international corruption unit of the UK’s National Crime Agency. (Reporting by Rae Wee and Ankur Banerjee in Singapore, Elizabeth Howcroft in Paris and Hannah Lang in New York; Writing by Scott Murdoch and Tom Westbrook; Editing by Sonali Paul, Xevi Fontdegloria, Mark Potter, Rod Nickel)

facts.text: Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, says it has covered 90% of the $6.3bn (£4.7bn) assets stolen in a hack on Thursday.

Richard Teng, Binance's co-chief executive officer, said the hack was carried out by more than one person, and the hackers used sophisticated methods to hide their tracks, such as a "self-destruct mechanism".
In an update on Sunday, Binance said withdrawals had been restored on several of its networks, after they were suspended following the hack.
"Binance will absorb the financial impact of these stolen funds, not our users," the company said in a statement on Saturday.

Binance's initial investigation suggested an engineer's laptop was compromised, which allowed access to unauthorised withdrawals, but a later update said they had uncovered "additional points of breach".
The US Secret Service said on Friday it is "working around the clock" with private sector partners "to identify, freeze, trace, and recover funds" stolen from Binance.

Two analytics firms previously told the BBC they had robust intelligence pointing to North Korean state-backed hacking unit the Lazarus Group, also known as TraderTraitor - which was specifically named by the FBI - as the likely culprits.
Binance said it had replenished the stolen assets using various funds and its own corporate treasury.
Binance, founded in China in 2017, lets users buy, sell and trade digital assets - it is estimated to have hundreds of millions of users worldwide.
The hack is believed to be the largest in history, eclipsing the record of a $1.5bn heist on the Bybit exchange in 2025 - for which the FBI also said North Korea was responsible.
Crypto is a digital asset, which doesn't exist physically and is instead accessed via digital wallets or computers.
A security incident at digital asset exchange Binance on Thursday affected some $6.3 billion in client assets, making it the largest crypto theft on record.
Experts whom CNBC interviewed said the security incidents on the crypto exchanges aren't surprising, especially in light of recent artificial intelligence hacking incidents .
That's because the hack may have involved a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, Binance said in a post on X .
Two high-profile security breaches this week – including the biggest cryptocurrency theft in history – are raising questions on the safety of storing funds in a wallet on a crypto exchange .
Binance and Polymarket reassured users that they would make affected investors whole.
That's a sign that users should feel confident in crypto exchanges, according to Ido Ben-Natan , CEO of blockchain security company Blockaid.
"I actually think no users will lose any money," he said.
"Binance has said they're going to cover everything… I actually don't think it's a bad idea for users to put money in these exchanges.
As a result, a crypto wallet could ultimately become a safer place to hold funds compared to other options, since the industry will have the experience of how to handle these attacks, Ben-Natan said.
However, crypto may be a unique target for hackers in a changing cybersecurity landscape, these experts told CNBC.

Earlier that day, prediction market platform Polymarket temporarily halted trading on its international exchange after a third-party data provider was hacked, resulting in at least $2.7 million being drained from users' wallets.
The same was true of Polymarket's domestic exchange.
U.S. regulated platforms Coinbase and Robinhood were also unaffected by the security breach on Binance, though shares of both fell on Friday in the aftermath.
In another social media post, BInance later said its investigation uncovered additional points of breach , though the company didn't specify what they were.
Binance has seen $3.64 billion in net outflows since it gradually restored user withdrawals following the largest crypto hack in history, which the FBI linked to North Korea.
The world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange said that it processed $4.649 billion in withdrawals and approximately $1.01 billion in deposits.

"The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) is releasing information advising the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (North Korea) was responsible for the theft of more than $6 billion USD in virtual assets from cryptocurrency exchange Binance, on or about October 29, 2026," a press release said.
Binance was hit late Thursday by a hack that investigators said impacted roughly $6.3 billion in funds, with roughly half of those assets frozen.
Other major crypto assets also tumbled after the hack, with ether ( ETH-USD ) dropping to roughly $2,200.
Binance's native token, BNB ( BND-USD ), also fell.

"We continue working with industry partners to complete the remaining acquisitions," Binance said in an update on X.
Meanwhile, the total crypto market has lost roughly 3% in value, or $80 billion, over the last seven days, according to CoinMarketCap data.

extraction.body: Ford vowed to never sell customer driving data to third-party data brokers as part of a new privacy promise aimed at setting the automaker apart from competitors that have faced legal and regulatory blowback for sharing telematics with data brokers without authorization. As part of its new promise, Ford says it will strive to protect customer data by using aggregating and anonymizing techniques. It will also “provide clear and easy-to-understand information about how we use your personal information.” And while Ford says it will still use data to improve safety, it will allow customers to adjust how much or how little data they would prefer to share. In making an explicit pledge not to sell customer data to outside firms, Ford is trying to position itself as one of the better actors in an industry rife with shady practices. “We know that trust is earned,” Kristin Jones, chief privacy officer at Ford, writes in a blog post. “Protecting your personal information is one way we intend to earn it every day.” "“We know that trust is earned.”" - Kristin Jones, Ford’s chief privacy officer The promise comes in the wake of General Motors agreeing to pay $220 million to settle claims that it illegally sold driver and location information to data brokers. The agreement requires GM to limit the driving data it collects and obtain “express consent” from drivers before collecting their information. Other automakers have been caught with their hands in the customer data cookie jar. A recent examination of 21 vehicle brands found that every single one transmitted data to at least one third-party domain over Wi-Fi. Over half contacted domains that specialize in advertising, tracking, or analytics (ATA), like Adobe, LexisNexis, and Amplitude, which gather details about your vehicle or driving behavior to sell to insurance companies or target you with ads. In a recent report, Mozilla crowned modern connected cars “the worst category of products for privacy” ever reviewed. The global nonprofit found that 92 percent of the reviewed automakers provide drivers with little (if any) control over their personal data, with 84 percent sharing user data with outside parties. Ford said it surveyed over 1,000 US customers, both Ford and non-Ford owners, who agreed that privacy is a top concern while over half of the respondents said they understand that some data sharing is okay. If Ford publicly promises something like, “We never sell your driving data to brokers” but breaks that promise, the FTC and state attorneys general can step in. They can sue Ford, force the company to sign legally binding agreements to correct the issue, and impose substantial financial fines. It should be noted that a company’s blog post or public promise is not a legal contract. Those legal agreements contain standard exceptions that allow Ford to share your data, such as complying with police requests or working with outside service providers. extraction.body: Just days after General Motors agreed to settle a lawsuit over selling customers' data without their consent, Ford announced a new "Privacy Promise" policy . In a statement shared on a new website from the manufacturer, Ford promised owners that they are in the driver's seat when it comes to their data. The site offers guidance on data sharing and collection and how to deactivate and opt out of sharing various types of data, whether on the automaker's webpages, in its app or within the car itself. "We design and build our products with privacy in mind — from collection of data to its use and storage and even disposal. This can include privacy-enhancing technologies like anonymizing or aggregating data to further protect your privacy," the statement began. "We strive to provide clear and easy-to-understand information about how we use your personal information. This empowers you to navigate your privacy choices with confidence. Once you make those choices, we respect your decision," the statement continued. Calling the move the "right thing to do," Ford shared that its updated vehicle privacy settings will allow users "to control what data you want to share, subject to the features and services you wish to enjoy." "We also never sell data about how you drive your vehicle to data brokers," Ford maintained, a sticking point following General Motors' lawsuit , which saw the Ford rival agree to pay $200 million in a settlement with 36 states following the incident, after it illegally sold drivers' personal information to third parties without their consent, per a Washington State release regarding the suit. As much as Ford said it acknowledged user privacy, it noted that after surveying just over 1,000 Ford customers, it found customers also "understand the value of data sharing" and want to be the ones making the ultimate decision when it comes to what they want to share. "A value our survey respondents kept returning to was control: the ability to adjust their settings on demand and in detail," Ford added. But, as automotive outlet The Drive notes, there is no one place to turn everything off, forcing Ford owners to do lots of reading and searching to fully opt out of data sharing and customize their Ford experience. While some found the timing of Ford's new website launch uncoincidental amid its longtime feud with GM, in a statement to TechCrunch , Ford's chief privacy officer Kristin Jones said she wouldn't be commenting "on what our competitors are doing, or anything that's sort of been in the news." She did say, however, that as more and more consumers grow wary of whether companies will "take care with their data," Ford wants to make sure it's "building that trust relationship with them." extraction.body: Ford vowed to never sell customer driving data to third-party data brokers as part of a new privacy promise aimed at setting the automaker apart from competitors that have faced legal and regulatory blowback for sharing telematics with data brokers without authorization. As part of its new promise, Ford says it will strive to protect customer data by using aggregating and anonymizing techniques. It will also “provide clear and easy-to-understand information about how we use your personal information.” And while Ford says it will still use data to improve safety, it will allow customers to adjust how much or how little data they would prefer to share. In making an explicit pledge not to sell customer data to outside firms, Ford is trying to position itself as one of the better actors in an industry rife with shady practices. “We know that trust is earned,” Kristin Jones, chief privacy officer at Ford, writes in a blog post. “Protecting your personal information is one way we intend to earn it every day.” "“We know that trust is earned.”" - Kristin Jones, Ford’s chief privacy officer The promise comes in the wake of General Motors agreeing to pay $220 million to settle claims that it illegally sold driver and location information to data brokers. The agreement requires GM to limit the driving data it collects and obtain “express consent” from drivers before collecting their information. Other automakers have been caught with their hands in the customer data cookie jar. A recent examination of 21 vehicle brands found that every single one transmitted data to at least one third-party domain over Wi-Fi. Over half contacted domains that specialize in advertising, tracking, or analytics (ATA), like Adobe, LexisNexis, and Amplitude, which gather details about your vehicle or driving behavior to sell to insurance companies or target you with ads. In a recent report, Mozilla crowned modern connected cars “the worst category of products for privacy” ever reviewed. The global nonprofit found that 92 percent of the reviewed automakers provide drivers with little (if any) control over their personal data, with 84 percent sharing user data with outside parties. Ford said it surveyed over 1,000 US customers, both Ford and non-Ford owners, who agreed that privacy is a top concern while over half of the respondents said they understand that some data sharing is okay. If Ford publicly promises something like, “We never sell your driving data to brokers” but breaks that promise, the FTC and state attorneys general can step in. They can sue Ford, force the company to sign legally binding agreements to correct the issue, and impose substantial financial fines. It should be noted that a company’s blog post or public promise is not a legal contract. Those legal agreements contain standard exceptions that allow Ford to share your data, such as complying with police requests or working with outside service providers. Also, opting out of data sharing does come with tradeoffs. While Ford states that data collection depends on the features you want to use, turning off vehicle tracking or location sharing often disables key features like built-in navigation, remote start, and wireless software updates.

passages: Apple’s new CEO, John Ternus, is apparently pushing the tech company’s development of household robots—and the first to debut may be a home robot designed to autonomously roam around while supporting FaceTime calls and switching lights on whenever a person enters the room.

A family that has a tablet on the kitchen counter and a speaker in the living room will ask what the robot does that those two cannot. Apple’s answer, based on the reports, is awareness and hands-free calls, and that case has to feel obvious in a store demo.

Retail strategy will matter as much as hardware. Apple stores let shoppers try a device in a staged room, which suits a product built around reacting to people. A boxed robot on a shelf sells poorly, while a live demo of lights switching on as a visitor walks in sells itself. Expect Apple to lean on that kind of showing if the project reaches launch.

A device that watches a room to decide when to act raises obvious privacy questions. Apple has built a brand on privacy, and it will have to explain where camera data is processed, what is stored, and who can see it. None of the reports address these points, so they remain open.

The bar here is higher than for a phone. A phone camera points where the owner points it. A home device with autonomous awareness can capture guests, children and routines without anyone choosing to record. Buyers and regulators will want clear indicators, easy off switches and plain disclosures.

This is also where the hardware category meets policy. Home cameras have already drawn scrutiny from lawmakers and security researchers, and a $1,000 Apple device would draw more. How Apple answers will shape trust in the whole premium home segment.

Support and repair raise a final question. Our coverage of the foldable line already shows how repair costs shape perception of a new Apple category. A robot with moving or sensing parts would add service complexity, and buyers at this price expect strong support. Apple has not said anything about warranty or service for the device, so that stays an open item.

A device with a camera-and-sensor system and a screen creates a new surface for software. If Apple opens it to third parties, developers could build call, reminder and household-routine experiences for a display that reacts to people. If Apple keeps it closed, the robot stays a showcase for first-party features.

The reports do not say which path Apple will take, so we treat both as open. Apple’s pattern with new hardware is to launch with a tight first-party feature set and widen access later. The Apple Watch and the home speaker line both followed that arc, and a robot at $1,000 would likely start the same way.

For accessory makers and smart-home brands, the question is compatibility. Anyone selling lights, locks or sensors will want to know whether the robot can control their devices. The light-control capability in the reports suggests Apple plans some home-control support, but the scope is unconfirmed. Vendors should watch Apple’s developer documentation for clues, since new hardware often shows up there before it ships.

Also track how the reported price evolves. If outlets converge on a different figure, that is a stronger signal than any single report. And watch whether Apple comments at all, because silence is the default until the company is ready to sell.

A roughly $1,000 device with FaceTime and light control, aimed at 2027 and possibly slipping to 2028, is the version in circulation. sources.title: Apple's Robot Ambitions: $1,000 HomeView Ultra Could Land in 2027 - BigGo Finance
passages: Apple is preparing to enter the home robotics market, with a robotic smart-home device code-named J595 that could carry a price tag of roughly $1,000 or more and reach customers as early as 2027, according to reporting from The Information.

The product, which people familiar with the effort expect to be branded HomeView Ultra, would sit alongside Apple's new HomeView stationary smart display, a device that arrives in users' homes within days.
For Apple investors, the project represents a long-horizon bet on a category the company has never sold into, and one whose revenue would not materialize before the end of the decade.
The timing also matters because Apple has been selective about extending its "Ultra" branding to new products.
Component prices could push the final retail figure above the $1,000 target, and the launch could slip to 2028 if software work falls behind.
Rivals in home automation and consumer robotics would have time to respond, and any delay would leave Apple's smart-home lineup anchored by the HomeView display shipping this month.

Beyond the HomeView Ultra, he is backing a separate effort aimed at machines that can handle household chores such as folding laundry, a project that would presumably require robotic arms and manipulators.
It is unclear whether that work points toward a general-purpose humanoid robot of the kind being developed by startups 1X and Figure AI.

The report describes a core group of only about 10 "true roboticists," with many members of the original engineering team having left over the years, while the software organization counts roughly 300 people.
Apple has not publicly confirmed the project, the name, or the price.
Much of the physical hardware has been ready for about two years, but software remains the bottleneck.

The delay stems from Apple's decision to pursue a more ambitious set of AI-powered capabilities than it originally planned, when the device was conceived mostly as a way to make FaceTime calls more engaging by following a person from room to room.
The project's origins trace back to 2018 prototypes, and former Apple chief executive Tim Cook approved continued work on it.
Equipped with cameras and sensors, the robot is meant to understand its surroundings and act on its own, such as turning on lights when someone walks in or shooing a cat off a table.

The open question is commercial rather than technical: whether buyers will pay four figures for a moving screen whose demonstrated functions overlap with far cheaper smart-home gear and robot vacuums.

sources.title: Apple's Robot Ambitions: $1,000 HomeView Ultra Could Land in 2027 - BigGo Finance
passages: Apple is preparing to enter the home robotics market, with a robotic smart-home device code-named J595 that could carry a price tag of roughly $1,000 or more and reach customers as early as 2027, according to reporting from The Information.

The product, which people familiar with the effort expect to be branded HomeView Ultra, would sit alongside Apple's new HomeView stationary smart display, a device that arrives in users' homes within days.
For Apple investors, the project represents a long-horizon bet on a category the company has never sold into, and one whose revenue would not materialize before the end of the decade.
The timing also matters because Apple has been selective about extending its "Ultra" branding to new products.
Component prices could push the final retail figure above the $1,000 target, and the launch could slip to 2028 if software work falls behind.
Rivals in home automation and consumer robotics would have time to respond, and any delay would leave Apple's smart-home lineup anchored by the HomeView display shipping this month.

Beyond the HomeView Ultra, he is backing a separate effort aimed at machines that can handle household chores such as folding laundry, a project that would presumably require robotic arms and manipulators.
It is unclear whether that work points toward a general-purpose humanoid robot of the kind being developed by startups 1X and Figure AI.

The report describes a core group of only about 10 "true roboticists," with many members of the original engineering team having left over the years, while the software organization counts roughly 300 people.
Apple has not publicly confirmed the project, the name, or the price.
Much of the physical hardware has been ready for about two years, but software remains the bottleneck.

The delay stems from Apple's decision to pursue a more ambitious set of AI-powered capabilities than it originally planned, when the device was conceived mostly as a way to make FaceTime calls more engaging by following a person from room to room.
The project's origins trace back to 2018 prototypes, and former Apple chief executive Tim Cook approved continued work on it.
Equipped with cameras and sensors, the robot is meant to understand its surroundings and act on its own, such as turning on lights when someone walks in or shooing a cat off a table.

The open question is commercial rather than technical: whether buyers will pay four figures for a moving screen whose demonstrated functions overlap with far cheaper smart-home gear and robot vacuums.

extraction.body: OpenAI has hired former U.S. Army Secretary Dan Driscoll as senior counselor for national security modernization, a newly created role at the company . Driscoll will focus on how artificial intelligence can be used to strengthen U.S. national security and cybersecurity, OpenAI said, while his updated LinkedIn profile also lists his new position. He will work with OpenAI's senior leadership and external partners, with a particular focus on helping U.S. allies adopt advanced AI responsibly. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said the U.S. has "an extraordinary opportunity to work with other countries to spread the adoption of democratic AI," and that Driscoll's appointment would help strengthen American leadership in the technology. "National security requirements are changing faster than at any time in the past fifty years," Driscoll said. He added that AI could help reduce paperwork, process information and deliver answers more quickly to those working in national security. The appointment comes after Driscoll stepped down as Army secretary earlier this year after months of reported tensions with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. An Iraq war veteran, Driscoll pushed efforts to modernize the U.S. military, including expanding access to drone and counter-drone technologies among U.S. allies, according to a previous U.S. Army announcement. Driscoll also met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Kyiv in November 2025 to discuss a U.S.-proposed peace plan aimed at ending the war with Russia, according to a statement from the Presidential Office of Ukraine. At OpenAI, Driscoll will work with government officials, industry leaders, academic institutions and allied organizations to advance what the company calls "democratic AI." He will also help internal teams understand the operational needs of national security institutions, building on OpenAI's efforts to strengthen cyber resilience and protect essential services through its Daybreak program . The fall out between Driscoll and Hegseth was largely over Army leadership and modernization priorities.

Driscoll will focus on how artificial intelligence can be used to strengthen U.S. national security and cybersecurity, OpenAI said, while his updated LinkedIn profile also lists his new position. He will work with OpenAI's senior leadership and external partners, with a particular focus on helping U.S. allies adopt advanced AI responsibly. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said the U.S. has "an extraordinary opportunity to work with other countries to spread the adoption of democratic AI," and that Driscoll's appointment would help strengthen American leadership in the technology. "National security requirements are changing faster than at any time in the past fifty years," Driscoll said. He added that AI could help reduce paperwork, process information and deliver answers more quickly to those working in national security. The appointment comes after Driscoll stepped down as Army secretary earlier this year after months of reported tensions with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. An Iraq war veteran, Driscoll pushed efforts to modernize the U.S. military, including expanding access to drone and counter-drone technologies among U.S. allies, according to a previous U.S. Army announcement. Driscoll also met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Kyiv in November 2025 to discuss a U.S.-proposed peace plan aimed at ending the war with Russia, according to a statement from the Presidential Office of Ukraine. At OpenAI, Driscoll will work with government officials, industry leaders, academic institutions and allied organizations to advance what the company calls "democratic AI." He will also help internal teams understand the operational needs of national security institutions, building on OpenAI's efforts to strengthen cyber resilience and protect essential services through its Daybreak program . facts.text: Army Secretary Dan Driscoll as senior counselor for national security modernization, a newly created role at the company .
Driscoll will focus on how artificial intelligence can be used to strengthen U.S. national security and cybersecurity, OpenAI said, while his updated LinkedIn profile also lists his new position.
"National security requirements are changing faster than at any time in the past fifty years," Driscoll said.
He added that AI could help reduce paperwork, process information and deliver answers more quickly to those working in national security.
The appointment comes after Driscoll stepped down as Army secretary earlier this year after months of reported tensions with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
An Iraq war veteran, Driscoll pushed efforts to modernize the U.S. military, including expanding access to drone and counter-drone technologies among U.S. allies, according to a previous U.S.
Dan Driscoll, a former US Secretary of the Army has been appointed by OpenAI as its senior counselor for national security modernisation.
The company created a new position for Driscoll for advancing the responsible use of artificial intelligence in national security, cybersecurity and defense.
Driscoll, whose appointment was announced on Monday will work with OpenAI's senior leadership, government officials, industry executives to strengthen national security capabilities.
The announcement by OpenAI comes after Driscoll stepped down as the 26th Army secretary earlier this year over his reported differences with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
Driscoll described his appointment as an opportunity to help military personnel and national security institutions benefit from technology that is advancing rapidly.
"I’m joining OpenAI to help the United States and our allies put this technology to work responsibly, for the people who keep us safe," he said.
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman welcomed the appointment of Driscoll and spoke about the importance of international cooperation in strengthening artificial intelligence further.

OpenAI said it has appointed Dan Driscoll as Senior Counselor for National Security Modernization, a role focused on responsible AI use in national security, cyber resilience and cooperation with U.S. allies.
The company said the post is intended to support policy and strategy modernization, operational needs and responsible adoption, with an emphasis on democratic principles.

The significance of the hire lies in OpenAI's effort to formalize a national-security advisory function at a time when AI developers are increasingly being asked to address defense, cybersecurity and allied cooperation use cases.
Public filings or the company announcement did not specify any compensation, duration or operational authority tied to the role.
OpenAI also linked the appointment to its Daybreak cyber-resilience program.

sources.title: Apple set an iPhone sales record even without a new standard iPhone
passages: Apple had a record-breaking quarter for iPhone sales — despite not releasing a standard model during its latest refresh.
In its fourth-quarter earnings report released on Monday, Apple says it earned $57.58 billion in iPhone revenue, a 17 percent jump from the same time last year.

Its Mac business grew 24 percent to $10.79 billion, while Apple’s services division, which includes App Store commissions along with subscriptions to services like Apple TV and Apple Music, grew to $31.57 billion. iPad revenue declined 10 percent year over year, with $6.23 billion in sales.
The increase in revenue follows the launch of Apple’s iPhone 18 lineup in September, which included a pricier iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max model.
Apple also took the wraps off its first folding phone, the iPhone Duo, but its preorder sales aren’t included in this earnings report.
Meanwhile, Apple only had a “limited” number of iPhone Duos available in store at launch, with some estimated shipment dates extending into 2027.
Apple shook up other areas of its product lineup with some other major launches over the past several weeks.
Like other device-makers, Apple has been dealing with supply chain constraints and rising memory costs, leading it to raise prices across its products.
Last week, Apple also revealed a MacBook Pro with a touchscreen — a design choice that its executives famously resisted.

Notably, the company reported US$57.58 billion (about C$80.5 billion) in iPhone revenue, a 17 per cent jump from the same time last year. The Mac and services businesses grew during Q4, the latter of which actually reaching an all-time high of US$31.57 billion (about C$44.1 billion), although iPad revenue declined 10 per cent year-over-year. Looking ahead to the next quarter, Apple has the aforementioned Duo and a new touchscreen MacBook . It will also be John Ternus’ first full quarter as CEO, as he took over from Apple veteran Tim Cook on Sept. 1 . extraction.body: Apple is rewriting its playbook for the iPhone lineup, and the iPhone 17 is the unexpected beneficiary. With the standard iPhone 18 delayed until spring 2027, the iPhone 17 is set to become the longest-lived standard model in the company’s history. The move comes alongside Apple’s best-ever March quarter revenue, driven by what CEO Tim Cook described as “extraordinary demand” for the iPhone 17 series. For years, Apple has followed a predictable rhythm: new iPhones every September. That rhythm is about to change. According to multiple reports, Apple will launch only the iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, and the much-anticipated iPhone Ultra foldable at its September 2026 event. The standard iPhone 18 will not appear until the following spring. This delay means the iPhone 17, which debuted in September 2025, will remain on sale for roughly 18 months—an unusually long lifecycle for a non-Pro model. Apple has already ramped up production capacity for the iPhone 17, signaling its intention to keep the device in the spotlight through the 2026 holiday season and beyond. The extended production run is expected to allow the phone to participate in major sales events like China’s Double 11 shopping festival later this year. The iPhone 17’s staying power is not just about timing—it is also about hardware. For the first time, a standard iPhone model includes ProMotion technology, giving it a 120Hz variable refresh rate display that matches the Pro lineup. This upgrade addresses one of the most persistent criticisms of Apple’s base models. Apple also eliminated the 128GB entry-level storage tier, starting the iPhone 17 at 256GB. Despite the upgrade, the starting price remains at $876 USD (converted from CNY 5,999 at the reference rate of 0.146). In China, government subsidies of up to $73 USD (CNY 500) can bring the effective price down to about $803 USD. This pricing strategy positions the iPhone 17 as a value-driven option in the premium segment. The strategy is working. According to Counterpoint Research, iPhone sales surged 22% in the first month after the iPhone 17’s launch, even as the overall smartphone market contracted by 2.7%. This growth helped Apple report its best March quarter ever, with total revenue of $111.2 billion—a 17% year-over-year increase. iPhone-specific revenue reached $56.99 billion, slightly above analyst expectations. Tim Cook attributed the results to double-digit growth across every geographic segment and strong demand for the entire iPhone 17 lineup, including the iPhone 17e, which launched during the quarter. Apple also set new March quarter records for operating cash flow (over $28 billion) and earnings per share. Not everything is smooth sailing. Cook warned that memory costs are expected to rise significantly in the coming quarter, driven by an ongoing memory shortage that has already impacted other tech companies. Rising component prices could pressure Apple’s margins, especially as it continues to offer competitive pricing on the iPhone 17. Additionally, Cook is set to step down as CEO later this year, marking the end of an era. His departure adds an element of uncertainty to Apple’s future product and pricing strategies, though the company’s current momentum remains strong. The iPhone 17’s extended lifecycle is a clear sign that Apple is willing to break its own traditions to maximize returns on a winning product. For consumers, it means a well-equipped phone at a stable price—and a longer wait before the next standard model arrives. coreStoryFacts.text: Apple had a record-breaking quarter for iPhone sales — despite not releasing a standard model during its latest refresh.
In its fourth-quarter earnings report released on Monday, Apple says it earned $57.58 billion in iPhone revenue, a 17 percent jump from the same time last year.

Its Mac business grew 24 percent to $10.79 billion, while Apple’s services division, which includes App Store commissions along with subscriptions to services like Apple TV and Apple Music, grew to $31.57 billion. iPad revenue declined 10 percent year over year, with $6.23 billion in sales.
The increase in revenue follows the launch of Apple’s iPhone 18 lineup in September, which included a pricier iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max model.
Apple also took the wraps off its first folding phone, the iPhone Duo, but its preorder sales aren’t included in this earnings report.
Meanwhile, Apple only had a “limited” number of iPhone Duos available in store at launch, with some estimated shipment dates extending into 2027.
Apple shook up other areas of its product lineup with some other major launches over the past several weeks.
Like other device-makers, Apple has been dealing with supply chain constraints and rising memory costs, leading it to raise prices across its products.
Last week, Apple also revealed a MacBook Pro with a touchscreen — a design choice that its executives famously resisted.

Traditionally, Apple has launched the standard and premium versions of its phones in the same September window, but for this year’s iPhone 18 family, it only debuted the 18 Pro and Pro Max , as well as its first-ever foldable, the Duo .
The base iPhone 18 has yet to be released, with reports suggesting it will come in early 2027 alongside the lower-cost 18e and Air 2.
In other words, Apple still managed to have a record iPhone quarter on the back of its more expensive phones.
Looking ahead to the next quarter, Apple has the aforementioned Duo and a new touchscreen MacBook .
It will also be John Ternus’ first full quarter as CEO, as he took over from Apple veteran Tim Cook on Sept.
Apple just had released its fourth-quarter earnings report, and it was a particularly big one.
Overall, Apple reported US$114.5 billion (about C$160 billion) in revenue, marking a 12 percent increase.

facts.text: Apple had a record-breaking quarter for iPhone sales — despite not releasing a standard model during its latest refresh.
In its fourth-quarter earnings report released on Monday, Apple says it earned $57.58 billion in iPhone revenue, a 17 percent jump from the same time last year.

Its Mac business grew 24 percent to $10.79 billion, while Apple’s services division, which includes App Store commissions along with subscriptions to services like Apple TV and Apple Music, grew to $31.57 billion. iPad revenue declined 10 percent year over year, with $6.23 billion in sales.
