extraction.body: OpenAI has hired former U.S. Army Secretary Dan Driscoll as senior counselor for national security modernization, a newly created role at the company . Driscoll will focus on how artificial intelligence can be used to strengthen U.S. national security and cybersecurity, OpenAI said, while his updated LinkedIn profile also lists his new position. He will work with OpenAI's senior leadership and external partners, with a particular focus on helping U.S. allies adopt advanced AI responsibly. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said the U.S. has "an extraordinary opportunity to work with other countries to spread the adoption of democratic AI," and that Driscoll's appointment would help strengthen American leadership in the technology. "National security requirements are changing faster than at any time in the past fifty years," Driscoll said. He added that AI could help reduce paperwork, process information and deliver answers more quickly to those working in national security. The appointment comes after Driscoll stepped down as Army secretary earlier this year after months of reported tensions with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. An Iraq war veteran, Driscoll pushed efforts to modernize the U.S. military, including expanding access to drone and counter-drone technologies among U.S. allies, according to a previous U.S. Army announcement. Driscoll also met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Kyiv in November 2025 to discuss a U.S.-proposed peace plan aimed at ending the war with Russia, according to a statement from the Presidential Office of Ukraine. At OpenAI, Driscoll will work with government officials, industry leaders, academic institutions and allied organizations to advance what the company calls "democratic AI." He will also help internal teams understand the operational needs of national security institutions, building on OpenAI's efforts to strengthen cyber resilience and protect essential services through its Daybreak program . extraction.body: OpenAI just made its most aggressive move yet into the defense sector, hiring former U.S. Army Secretary Dan Driscoll for a newly created national security modernization role. The appointment signals the ChatGPT maker's determination to compete with Palantir and Microsoft for lucrative government AI contracts, coming just days after CEO Sam Altman returned from courting Middle Eastern allies and Asian chipmakers. The company announced it's bringing former U.S. Army Secretary Dan Driscoll on board for a brand-new role focused on national security modernization, marking its most explicit push yet into the defense and intelligence markets that have long been dominated by contractors like Palantir and tech giants like Microsoft. Just last week, CEO Sam Altman was in Abu Dhabi signing four separate deals with the crown prince covering energy, government services, and investment. The pattern is clear: OpenAI is racing to build the infrastructure and relationships needed to compete at nation-state scale. Driscoll's appointment creates a direct channel into Pentagon procurement and classified AI development. His tenure leading the Army gives him exactly the kind of clearance levels and institutional knowledge that OpenAI needs to navigate the labyrinthine world of defense contracting. It's a world where Palantir has been cleaning up lately, though interestingly the data analytics firm just reported that commercial revenue overtook government sales for the first time, suggesting the market dynamics are shifting fast. The national security modernization mandate is deliberately broad. These aren't the kind of flashy consumer features that made ChatGPT a household name, but they're potentially far more lucrative on a per-contract basis. OpenAI's move also reflects growing pressure to diversify revenue beyond its core consumer and API businesses. The company recently slashed its fundraising targets as investor enthusiasm for sky-high AI valuations cooled. Government contracts offer something the consumer market doesn't: multi-year commitments worth hundreds of millions, with built-in switching costs that make them stickier than any subscription service. extraction.body: OpenAI just made its most aggressive move yet into the defense sector, hiring former U.S. Army Secretary Dan Driscoll for a newly created national security modernization role. The appointment signals the ChatGPT maker's determination to compete with Palantir and Microsoft for lucrative government AI contracts, coming just days after CEO Sam Altman returned from courting Middle Eastern allies and Asian chipmakers. The company announced it's bringing former U.S. Army Secretary Dan Driscoll on board for a brand-new role focused on national security modernization, marking its most explicit push yet into the defense and intelligence markets that have long been dominated by contractors like Palantir and tech giants like Microsoft. Just last week, CEO Sam Altman was in Abu Dhabi signing four separate deals with the crown prince covering energy, government services, and investment. The pattern is clear: OpenAI is racing to build the infrastructure and relationships needed to compete at nation-state scale. Driscoll's appointment creates a direct channel into Pentagon procurement and classified AI development. His tenure leading the Army gives him exactly the kind of clearance levels and institutional knowledge that OpenAI needs to navigate the labyrinthine world of defense contracting. It's a world where Palantir has been cleaning up lately, though interestingly the data analytics firm just reported that commercial revenue overtook government sales for the first time, suggesting the market dynamics are shifting fast. The national security modernization mandate is deliberately broad. These aren't the kind of flashy consumer features that made ChatGPT a household name, but they're potentially far more lucrative on a per-contract basis. OpenAI's move also reflects growing pressure to diversify revenue beyond its core consumer and API businesses. The company recently slashed its fundraising targets as investor enthusiasm for sky-high AI valuations cooled. Government contracts offer something the consumer market doesn't: multi-year commitments worth hundreds of millions, with built-in switching costs that make them stickier than any subscription service. Microsoft already has massive defense contracts through Azure Government Cloud and its longstanding relationships with intelligence agencies. Google famously backed away from defense AI work after employee protests over Project Maven, then quietly reversed course. And Palantir has spent two decades building exactly the kind of trust with defense and intelligence communities that OpenAI is now trying to establish overnight. Its models are widely considered state-of-the-art for language understanding and generation, capabilities that map directly onto intelligence analysis, strategic planning, and cybersecurity defense. The company's recent Shepherd model for AI research validation and its Dots personal assistant show it's pushing beyond basic chatbots into more sophisticated reasoning systems. OpenAI has faced criticism over safety practices, with its own monitoring systems failing a third-party audit just last month. Defense contracts will bring even more scrutiny, both from government overseers who demand ironclad security and from employees and researchers who may object to military applications of AI technology. Driscoll will also inherit thorny questions about how OpenAI's technology should and shouldn't be used in national security contexts. Does the company allow its models to help plan military operations? These aren't hypothetical questions but real decisions that will define OpenAI's role in the defense ecosystem and its broader reputation. For the past two years, companies competed mainly on model capabilities and consumer traction. Now they're competing on geopolitical relationships, infrastructure deals, and government access. Altman's globe-trotting diplomacy, the Abu Dhabi energy partnerships, the Seoul chip talks, and now the Driscoll hire all point to the same conclusion: OpenAI believes the next trillion dollars in AI value will come from nations, not individuals. What makes this particularly interesting is how it inverts the usual tech industry playbook. Normally companies build consumer traction first, then gradually move upmarket into enterprise and eventually government. OpenAI is trying to do both simultaneously, maintaining its ChatGPT consumer brand while also positioning itself as a trusted partner for the most sensitive national security applications. Driscoll's appointment marks OpenAI's clearest signal yet that it sees government AI as a strategic imperative, not just an opportunistic revenue stream. As the company navigates funding pressures and competitive threats, defense contracts offer stability that consumer markets can't match. But success will require more than just hiring the right people—it'll demand navigating security clearances, building trust with skeptical agencies, and resolving internal debates about AI's role in national security. The real test isn't whether OpenAI can land its first Pentagon contract, but whether it can do so without fracturing the research culture that made its technology valuable in the first place.

sources.title: Binance customers withdraw more than $4.6 billion after crypto heist
passages: Binance customers withdrew more than $4.6 billion from the cryptocurrency exchange after it suffered what security experts said was the largest digital coin theft ever.In a post on social media, Binance said customers also deposited just over $1 billion after the company allowed people to resume transactions on Sunday for Bitcoin, Ethereum and other cryptocurrencies, resulting in a net outflow of $3.64 billion.

Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange with more than 300 million users, said the value of crypto holdings being withdrawn represents just 2.1% of its $171 billion in total assets."Our top priority right now is to ensure the environment is secure, after which users can withdraw their funds, and Binance can resume operations," Binance cofounder Yi He said in an X post early Monday.Binance did not immediately respond to a request for comment.The fund withdrawals came after cybercriminals, whom the FBI linked to North Korea, stole $6.3 billion in digital currency from Binance.

TraderTraitor was also responsible for a February 2025 attack on another crypto exchange, Bybit, that resulted in a $1.5 billion loss, according to the FBI.Following the Binance attack, the FBI encouraged private-sector entities "to block transactions with or derived from addresses TraderTraitor actors are using to launder these stolen assets."Binance has promised to cover the full losses using company funds.

passages: Binance customers withdrew more than $4.6 billion from the cryptocurrency exchange after it suffered what security experts said was the largest digital coin theft ever.In a post on social media, Binance said customers also deposited just over $1 billion after the company allowed people to resume transactions on Sunday for Bitcoin, Ethereum and other cryptocurrencies, resulting in a net outflow of $3.64 billion.

Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange with more than 300 million users, said the value of crypto holdings being withdrawn represents just 2.1% of its $171 billion in total assets."Our top priority right now is to ensure the environment is secure, after which users can withdraw their funds, and Binance can resume operations," Binance cofounder Yi He said in an X post early Monday.Binance did not immediately respond to a request for comment.The fund withdrawals came after cybercriminals, whom the FBI linked to North Korea, stole $6.3 billion in digital currency from Binance.

TraderTraitor was also responsible for a February 2025 attack on another crypto exchange, Bybit, that resulted in a $1.5 billion loss, according to the FBI.Following the Binance attack, the FBI encouraged private-sector entities "to block transactions with or derived from addresses TraderTraitor actors are using to launder these stolen assets."Binance has promised to cover the full losses using company funds.

BTCPay Server has urged merchants to rebuild outdated payment servers and replace wallets after attackers stole Bitcoin and Litecoin . In a Nov. 2 security advisory , the open-source Bitcoin payment software provider warned that installing the latest update may not protect funds if hackers have already gained access to a server. The warning follows a series of attacks targeting installations running version 2.4.1 or earlier, using a different method to exploit a vulnerability that BTCPay patched on Aug. 7. Blockchain analytics firm Bitquery traced approximately $1.63 million in suspected thefts involving 18.38 BTC and 3,405 LTC across 682 wallet sweeps between Oct. 30 and Nov. 2. Its investigation found that 87% of the funds moved during an eight-hour window on Nov. 1, with the busiest hour accounting for approximately $725,000 in transfers. The findings provide an early indication of the attack's financial scale, although BTCPay has not confirmed a total loss figure or established how many merchants were compromised. BTCPay said it regretted not doing more to reach operators still running outdated installations after its August security advisory. The project has issued several additional security updates since then, including version 2.4.7 on Oct. 29. The suspected thefts continued even after BTCPay publicly warned operators to shut down their servers. According to Bitquery, another 267 wallet sweeps worth approximately $150,000 occurred after BTCPay's Nov. 1 warning at 22:25 UTC. The transfers continued through the night and were still being recorded when the analytics firm stopped counting at 06:00 UTC on Nov. 2. BTCPay said it contacted hosting providers, including LunaNode, to take affected installations offline as a precaution. The project had received its first emailed theft report at 20:56 UTC, although its investigation documented a wallet drain earlier that afternoon. The company said it had seen no impact from these attacks on servers already running version 2.4.2 or later when the November warning was issued. It also confirmed that wallets whose spending keys were stored outside the server, including hardware wallets, were unaffected by the reported thefts. However, BTCPay is urging operators who previously ran vulnerable versions to migrate to entirely new server installations, even if they have since updated their software or have not noticed any missing funds. The concern is that attackers who previously gained administrative access may have obtained credentials or wallet secrets that remain usable after the underlying vulnerability is patched. Consequently, the project recommends generating a new wallet with a fresh seed phrase on a trusted device and transferring any remaining funds from the old hot wallet. Operators must also retire their existing servers, preserve transaction records and relevant logs, and install the latest supported software on a fresh virtual machine without restoring the old system. Potentially exposed hosting passwords, SSH credentials, application access keys, API keys and Lightning credentials should also be replaced from a trusted device. Meanwhile, Bitquery's tracking showed that more than 99% of the suspected stolen funds remained at addresses first used during the thefts as of early Nov. 2, with no identified transfers to known exchanges. The analytics firm cautioned that its 682 recorded sweeps do not represent an equivalent number of affected merchants, as individual wallets could have been drained through multiple transactions. BTCPay has also warned that some activity involving the identified addresses appears to predate the reported incidents. It has yet to establish the complete attack timeline or determine which transactions can be conclusively attributed to the thefts. sources.title: BTCPay Server Hack: Bitcoin Hot Wallets Drained, Shut Your Server Down Now
passages: Every crypto hack since the Binance hack, with status and safety tips, is in Crypto hack news.What happened to BTCPay Server?Late on Saturday, 1 November, the BTCPay Server team posted an emergency alert: it was receiving reports of hot wallets connected to BTCPay instances being emptied by unauthorized attackers.

BTCPay Server, the most widely used self-hosted Bitcoin payment processor, has confirmed that attackers are sweeping hot wallets on older installations and has asked every operator to take their instance offline until the investigation is complete.
Shut your server down with the ./btcpay-down.sh script and wait.By Sunday, the incident response team had narrowed the attack vector.

The message from three separate incidents in three months is the same: Bitcoin payment infrastructure that is not updated is being actively scanned and attacked.What should BTCPay Server operators do right now?Shut the instance down until BTCPay Server gives the all clear, even if you are on a recent version.
In August, BTCPay Server warned of an actively exploited flaw that let attackers lift LND administrator credentials and reach connected Lightning wallets.
That bug was patched in 2.4.2, and the project put up a recovery bounty of 10 percent of recovered funds, capped at 3 BTC.The August flaw explicitly did not touch on-chain hot wallets.
There are no credible reports of drained wallets on the current 2.4.7 release.
LunaNode and others began shutting down older instances automatically, so if your BTCPay dashboard suddenly went dark over the weekend, that may be why.
BTCPay has long recommended keeping only operating float in a hot wallet.Preserve your logs.

relevantPassages.text: Every crypto hack since the Binance hack, with status and safety tips, is in Crypto hack news.What happened to BTCPay Server?Late on Saturday, 1 November, the BTCPay Server team posted an emergency alert: it was receiving reports of hot wallets connected to BTCPay instances being emptied by unauthorized attackers.

BTCPay Server, the most widely used self-hosted Bitcoin payment processor, has confirmed that attackers are sweeping hot wallets on older installations and has asked every operator to take their instance offline until the investigation is complete.
Shut your server down with the ./btcpay-down.sh script and wait.By Sunday, the incident response team had narrowed the attack vector.

The message from three separate incidents in three months is the same: Bitcoin payment infrastructure that is not updated is being actively scanned and attacked.What should BTCPay Server operators do right now?Shut the instance down until BTCPay Server gives the all clear, even if you are on a recent version.
In August, BTCPay Server warned of an actively exploited flaw that let attackers lift LND administrator credentials and reach connected Lightning wallets.
That bug was patched in 2.4.2, and the project put up a recovery bounty of 10 percent of recovered funds, capped at 3 BTC.The August flaw explicitly did not touch on-chain hot wallets.
There are no credible reports of drained wallets on the current 2.4.7 release.
LunaNode and others began shutting down older instances automatically, so if your BTCPay dashboard suddenly went dark over the weekend, that may be why.
BTCPay has long recommended keeping only operating float in a hot wallet.Preserve your logs.

In August, attackers exploited a separate flaw to steal Lightning Network credentials and drain nodes running behind BTCPay, including one operated by hardware wallet maker Foundation.
At that time, BTCPay said its standard on-chain wallets, including hot wallets created inside the software, were not affected.
The key questions are whether BTCPay ties the attacks to a specific software version, and whether servers running the October 29 update were affected.
Until the project gives an all-clear, operators holding funds in a BTCPay hot wallet should follow its shutdown advice.
BTCPay has not yet disclosed the cause of the attack, how many servers were affected or how much was taken.
A hot wallet is one whose private keys sit on an internet-connected server, so it can send funds automatically, for example to pay out refunds.
That makes the latest reports notable, because they point to the type of wallet that was outside the scope of the August flaw.

extraction.body: BTCPay Server, the open-source software many merchants use to accept Bitcoin payments without a third-party processor, has told operators to shut down their instances after receiving reports that hot wallets on multiple servers were being drained by unauthorized attackers. In a post on X, the project asked anyone running an instance to take it offline with its shutdown command until the investigation is complete. BTCPay has not yet disclosed the cause of the attack, how many servers were affected or how much was taken. A hot wallet is one whose private keys sit on an internet-connected server, so it can send funds automatically, for example to pay out refunds. That convenience makes it a bigger target than offline storage. The incident involves software built around Bitcoin, not the Bitcoin network itself. The warning follows two recent security events at the project. On October 29, BTCPay released emergency version 2.4.7 to fix one critical and several medium-risk vulnerabilities. In August, attackers exploited a separate flaw to steal Lightning Network credentials and drain nodes running behind BTCPay, including one operated by hardware wallet maker Foundation. At that time, BTCPay said its standard on-chain wallets, including hot wallets created inside the software, were not affected. That makes the latest reports notable, because they point to the type of wallet that was outside the scope of the August flaw. BTCPay has not said whether the new attacks are linked to the vulnerabilities fixed last week. The key questions are whether BTCPay ties the attacks to a specific software version, and whether servers running the October 29 update were affected. Loss figures and reports from named merchants will show the scale of the problem. In August, BTCPay narrowed the scope considerably after its first alert, so the initial warning may not reflect the final picture. Until the project gives an all-clear, operators holding funds in a BTCPay hot wallet should follow its shutdown advice. There's always something new to learn about the markets. coreStoryFacts.text: In August, hackers emptied Lightning nodes of hardware wallet manufacturer Foundation and Bitcoin publication Citadel21 through a critical vulnerability in BTCPay Server.
Developers of the payment service BTCPay Server have warned about unauthorized withdrawals from users’ hot wallets.
🚨 We are receiving reports of hot wallets on BTCPay Servers being swept by unauthorized attackers.
— BTCPay Server (@BtcpayServer) November 1, 2026
BTCPay supports hot wallets: the seed phrase is stored on an internet-connected server and used for automatically signing outgoing transactions.
BTCPay Server is a free, open-source payment system that allows online stores and other organizations to accept the leading cryptocurrency independently, without intermediaries.
Hackers Target JavaScript Ecosystem to Hijack Crypto Wallets
BTCPay Server has urged merchants to rebuild outdated payment servers and replace wallets after attackers stole Bitcoin and Litecoin .
According to Bitquery, another 267 wallet sweeps worth approximately $150,000 occurred after BTCPay's Nov.
The transfers continued through the night and were still being recorded when the analytics firm stopped counting at 06:00 UTC on Nov.
BTCPay said it contacted hosting providers, including LunaNode, to take affected installations offline as a precaution.
The project had received its first emailed theft report at 20:56 UTC, although its investigation documented a wallet drain earlier that afternoon.
2 security advisory , the open-source Bitcoin payment software provider warned that installing the latest update may not protect funds if hackers have already gained access to a server.
The findings provide an early indication of the attack's financial scale, although BTCPay has not confirmed a total loss figure or established how many merchants were compromised.
The project has issued several additional security updates since then, including version 2.4.7 on Oct.
Blockchain analytics firm Bitquery traced approximately $1.63 million in suspected thefts involving 18.38 BTC and 3,405 LTC across 682 wallet sweeps between Oct.
BTCPay has also warned that some activity involving the identified addresses appears to predate the reported incidents.
It has yet to establish the complete attack timeline or determine which transactions can be conclusively attributed to the thefts.

— BTCPay Server (@BtcpayServer) November 1, 2026
BTCPay supports hot wallets: the seed phrase is stored on an internet-connected server and used for automatically signing outgoing transactions.
BTCPay Server is a free, open-source payment system that allows online stores and other organizations to accept the leading cryptocurrency independently, without intermediaries.

BTCPay Server has urged merchants to rebuild outdated payment servers and replace wallets after attackers stole Bitcoin and Litecoin .

The transfers continued through the night and were still being recorded when the analytics firm stopped counting at 06:00 UTC on Nov.
BTCPay said it contacted hosting providers, including LunaNode, to take affected installations offline as a precaution.
The project had received its first emailed theft report at 20:56 UTC, although its investigation documented a wallet drain earlier that afternoon.
2 security advisory , the open-source Bitcoin payment software provider warned that installing the latest update may not protect funds if hackers have already gained access to a server.

BTCPay has also warned that some activity involving the identified addresses appears to predate the reported incidents.
It has yet to establish the complete attack timeline or determine which transactions can be conclusively attributed to the thefts.

extraction.body: The Apple Watch Ultra 4 is the company’s most capable smartwatch. Of note, those include Sound Recognition, which alerts you to noises like alarms and doorbells, and the Live Rewind feature that lets you revisit the last 15 seconds of an in-person conversation. This model has broader health and fitness capabilities than previous models, too. Its sensors promise more accurate EKG measurements, while the watch can track your heart rate as often as every five seconds. The new Readiness feature (not available on the Ultra 3 and earlier models) also analyzes your recent activity, sleep quality, and other health metrics to generate a score from zero to 10, helping you determine whether to push yourself or take it easy. On the hardware front, battery life is perhaps the biggest highlight, with Apple promising up to 50 hours on a charge — twice as long as the Series 12. Like its predecessor, this model features Apple’s brightest watch display and a rugged design that’s water-resistant up to 100 meters and IP6X-rated for dust resistance. It also retains conveniences like the second-generation Ultra Wideband chip for Precision Finding, and helpful gesture controls so you can you can perform actions with a double tap or flick of your wrist. Read our hands-on impressions of the Apple Watch Ultra 4. Three more ways to save * Ugreen’s FineTrack2 Bluetooth tracker is on sale for $13.99 at Amazon, just a few cents shy of its best price to date. The soccer ball-shaped tracker stands out with its playful design, but it also offers some useful features including a non-rechargeable battery can last up to seven years. It works with Apple’s expansive Find My network to help you locate misplaced belongings, while its lanyard makes it easy to attach to your keys, bag, or other items. * If you’re looking to spruce up your Apple Watch Ultra or Series smartwatch, a variety of Apple’s official bands are on sale for up to 69 percent off at Woot. The silicone Sport Band is down to $14.99 ($35 off), while the soft, breathable Sport Loop is available for $19.99 ($29 off). You can also grab the rugged Trail Loop for $34.99 ($64 off). * Hoto’s new Pulse 4-in-1 Cordless Staple Gun is on sale for $69.99 ($10 off) at Amazon. It works with four types of staples and nails, letting you switch between them depending on the task, while offering two firing modes. It also features a built-in display that shows battery life and alerts you when you can safely fire the stapler and when it’s time to reload it.

extraction.body: The Apple Watch Ultra 4 is the company’s most capable smartwatch. Of note, those include Sound Recognition, which alerts you to noises like alarms and doorbells, and the Live Rewind feature that lets you revisit the last 15 seconds of an in-person conversation. This model has broader health and fitness capabilities than previous models, too. Its sensors promise more accurate EKG measurements, while the watch can track your heart rate as often as every five seconds. The new Readiness feature (not available on the Ultra 3 and earlier models) also analyzes your recent activity, sleep quality, and other health metrics to generate a score from zero to 10, helping you determine whether to push yourself or take it easy. On the hardware front, battery life is perhaps the biggest highlight, with Apple promising up to 50 hours on a charge — twice as long as the Series 12. Like its predecessor, this model features Apple’s brightest watch display and a rugged design that’s water-resistant up to 100 meters and IP6X-rated for dust resistance. It also retains conveniences like the second-generation Ultra Wideband chip for Precision Finding, and helpful gesture controls so you can you can perform actions with a double tap or flick of your wrist. Read our hands-on impressions of the Apple Watch Ultra 4. Three more ways to save * Ugreen’s FineTrack2 Bluetooth tracker is on sale for $13.99 at Amazon, just a few cents shy of its best price to date. The soccer ball-shaped tracker stands out with its playful design, but it also offers some useful features including a non-rechargeable battery can last up to seven years. It works with Apple’s expansive Find My network to help you locate misplaced belongings, while its lanyard makes it easy to attach to your keys, bag, or other items. * If you’re looking to spruce up your Apple Watch Ultra or Series smartwatch, a variety of Apple’s official bands are on sale for up to 69 percent off at Woot. The silicone Sport Band is down to $14.99 ($35 off), while the soft, breathable Sport Loop is available for $19.99 ($29 off). You can also grab the rugged Trail Loop for $34.99 ($64 off). * Hoto’s new Pulse 4-in-1 Cordless Staple Gun is on sale for $69.99 ($10 off) at Amazon. It works with four types of staples and nails, letting you switch between them depending on the task, while offering two firing modes. It also features a built-in display that shows battery life and alerts you when you can safely fire the stapler and when it’s time to reload it.

passages: Ford has introduced a new Privacy Promise, publicly committing to protect customer vehicle data and give owners greater control over the information they share.

Jones reiterated that Ford's objective is to offer products and services that provide value to customers, not to monetize their personal information..Privacy Resources to Expand Beyond US.Ford said the Privacy Promise website will provide information about its privacy practices and available controls.

extraction.body: Ford has introduced a new Privacy Promise, publicly committing to protect customer vehicle data and give owners greater control over the information they share. The initiative comes as connected vehicles collect more personal information, including driving behavior, vehicle diagnostics, and location data.Announced on November 2, the initiative includes a new website that explains Ford's data collection practices and shows customers how to manage their privacy settings through their vehicles or the Ford App..Ford Aims to Build Trust Around Connected Car Data.The automaker said the Privacy Promise is designed to make its data practices easier to understand. Customers can learn what information Ford collects, how it is used, and how they can opt in or out of data sharing.Kristin Jones, Ford's Chief Privacy Officer, said the company wants to communicate its data practices more clearly and help customers understand their privacy choices.The announcement comes as automakers introduce increasingly connected vehicles with features such as remote start, navigation, and driver-assistance technology. A survey cited in the report found that only 14% of US consumers fully understand what data their vehicles collect.Also Read: Ford Fathom vs Slate Truck: Price, Range, Features, Key Differences.Survey Finds Data Privacy is a Major Consumer Concern.Ford surveyed 1,000 consumers to understand their views on vehicle data and privacy. According to Jones, 91% of respondents said data privacy was an important consideration.The survey also found that customers value the benefits of connected technology but want greater control over their information. Respondents identified the ability to adjust privacy settings whenever required as an important factor.Jones said the company wanted to build trust by ensuring customers have access to clear information about their data choices. She also noted that automakers were viewed as more trusted custodians of privacy than several other large organizations handling personal information..Turning Off Data Sharing Could Affect Connected Features.Ford said customers can manage their data-sharing preferences through their vehicle's center display. However, opting out of certain services could affect features that depend on connected vehicle data.For instance, disabling connected services would make real-time navigation and built-in roadside assistance unavailable. Vehicle health information can also help owners receive maintenance updates while supporting research and development for future technologies.The company said it does not sell information about customers' driving behavior to data brokers. It learned that while privacy is important to them, customers understand the value of data sharing.

“Even for a tech-savvy consumer, it can be hard to understand the relationship between your vehicle, the data it generates, and your privacy and rights,” says Kristin Jones, chief privacy officer and deputy general counsel for data and privacy at Ford.
“With our connected vehicle and app user communities growing every day, Ford takes its responsibility in safeguarding customer data seriously.”
Ford says it designs and builds its products with privacy in mind — from collection of data to its use, storage, and disposal.
This can include privacy-enhancing technologies like anonymizing or aggregating data to further protect a customer’s privacy.
As a result, Ford offers vehicle privacy settings that allow customers to control what data they want to share, subject to the features and services they wish to enjoy.
Ford stresses that it never sells data about how customers drive their vehicle to data brokers.

sources.title: Ford Makes a Privacy Promise as GM Pays $220 Million Over Driver Data - MotorBiscuit
passages: Data privacy has become an uncomfortable subject for America’s automakers.
Within days of General Motors agreeing to a $220 million settlement over how it handled driver information, Ford announced a new customer-facing commitment on the same issue.
GM must now restrict the driving data it collects and obtain a driver’s explicit consent before gathering or sharing it.
According to a report by MotorBiscuit , an outside party will also audit its privacy programs.
Earlier, in January 2025, it agreed with the Federal Trade Commission to stop sharing geolocation and driving-behavior data with consumer reporting agencies for five years.
It is not yet clear whether affected owners will receive any of the $220 million.
Against that backdrop, Ford has introduced the Ford Privacy Promise, which is meant to assure owners that their information is protected and that they decide what to share.
The data came from Smart Driver, a program that enrolled millions of motorists from 2016 until GM discontinued it in 2024.
To support the effort, Ford surveyed more than 1,000 U.S. customers about their understanding of data privacy.
Respondents overwhelmingly said they want the ability to control and adjust their privacy settings whenever they choose.
Ford says it develops its products with privacy in mind and tries to make clear how personal details are used.

extraction.body: Data privacy has become an uncomfortable subject for America’s automakers. Within days of General Motors agreeing to a $220 million settlement over how it handled driver information, Ford announced a new customer-facing commitment on the same issue. The contrast is hard to miss. GM stood accused of letting driving data reach insurance companies, while Ford is now telling owners that they decide what their vehicles share. Here is what led to the settlement, and what Ford is promising in response. The data came from Smart Driver, a program that enrolled millions of motorists from 2016 until GM discontinued it in 2024. Many participants also subscribed to OnStar. GM must now restrict the driving data it collects and obtain a driver’s explicit consent before gathering or sharing it. According to a report by MotorBiscuit , an outside party will also audit its privacy programs. GM said the agreement reinforces steps it has already taken. This is not the company’s first penalty on the subject. It paid $12.75 million to settle a California investigation in May. Earlier, in January 2025, it agreed with the Federal Trade Commission to stop sharing geolocation and driving-behavior data with consumer reporting agencies for five years. It is not yet clear whether affected owners will receive any of the $220 million. According to Ford Authority , Ford maintains that it does not sell driving data to third parties, although a recent study found that it shares some personal vehicle data with outside companies. Against that backdrop, Ford has introduced the Ford Privacy Promise, which is meant to assure owners that their information is protected and that they decide what to share. The company has built a dedicated website explaining how to change data settings, either inside the vehicle or through the Ford App. Ford says it develops its products with privacy in mind and tries to make clear how personal details are used. The pledge also states that Ford never sells data on how customers drive to data brokers. That is the practice at the center of GM’s legal trouble. To support the effort, Ford surveyed more than 1,000 U.S. customers about their understanding of data privacy. Respondents overwhelmingly said they want the ability to control and adjust their privacy settings whenever they choose. Control comes with a catch. Owners can decline to share certain categories of data, but some features reportedly stop working properly without it. BlueCruise, internet connectivity, and vehicle location services in the Ford App are among the features that may not function as intended without data sharing. Anyone adjusting their privacy settings should weigh what they are giving up. Your email address will not be published. passages: Data privacy has become an uncomfortable subject for America’s automakers. Within days of General Motors agreeing to a $220 million settlement over how it handled driver information, Ford announced a new customer-facing commitment on the same issue.

The contrast is hard to miss. GM stood accused of letting driving data reach insurance companies, while Ford is now telling owners that they decide what their vehicles share. Here is what led to the settlement, and what Ford is promising in response.
The data came from Smart Driver, a program that enrolled millions of motorists from 2016 until GM discontinued it in 2024. Many participants also subscribed to OnStar.

GM must now restrict the driving data it collects and obtain a driver’s explicit consent before gathering or sharing it. According to a report by MotorBiscuit , an outside party will also audit its privacy programs.
GM said the agreement reinforces steps it has already taken. This is not the company’s first penalty on the subject. It paid $12.75 million to settle a California investigation in May.

Earlier, in January 2025, it agreed with the Federal Trade Commission to stop sharing geolocation and driving-behavior data with consumer reporting agencies for five years. It is not yet clear whether affected owners will receive any of the $220 million.

According to Ford Authority , Ford maintains that it does not sell driving data to third parties, although a recent study found that it shares some personal vehicle data with outside companies. Against that backdrop, Ford has introduced the Ford Privacy Promise, which is meant to assure owners that their information is protected and that they decide what to share.

The company has built a dedicated website explaining how to change data settings, either inside the vehicle or through the Ford App. Ford says it develops its products with privacy in mind and tries to make clear how personal details are used.
The pledge also states that Ford never sells data on how customers drive to data brokers. That is the practice at the center of GM’s legal trouble.

To support the effort, Ford surveyed more than 1,000 U.S. customers about their understanding of data privacy. Respondents overwhelmingly said they want the ability to control and adjust their privacy settings whenever they choose.

Control comes with a catch. Owners can decline to share certain categories of data, but some features reportedly stop working properly without it. BlueCruise, internet connectivity, and vehicle location services in the Ford App are among the features that may not function as intended without data sharing. Anyone adjusting their privacy settings should weigh what they are giving up.

coreStoryFacts.text: Ford has introduced a new Privacy Promise, publicly committing to protect customer vehicle data and give owners greater control over the information they share.

Jones reiterated that Ford's objective is to offer products and services that provide value to customers, not to monetize their personal information..Privacy Resources to Expand Beyond US.Ford said the Privacy Promise website will provide information about its privacy practices and available controls.

Customers can learn what information Ford collects, how it is used, and how they can opt in or out of data sharing.Kristin Jones, Ford's Chief Privacy Officer, said the company wants to communicate its data practices more clearly and help customers understand their privacy choices.The announcement comes as automakers introduce increasingly connected vehicles with features such as remote start, navigation, and driver-assistance technology.

She also noted that automakers were viewed as more trusted custodians of privacy than several other large organizations handling personal information..Turning Off Data Sharing Could Affect Connected Features.Ford said customers can manage their data-sharing preferences through their vehicle's center display.

The company also plans to introduce privacy resources for Lincoln customers and users in Mexico and Canada in the coming weeks, with additional markets to follow.The initiative comes as connected vehicle technology becomes more widespread, making transparency around data collection and customer consent increasingly important..Join our WhatsApp Channel to get the latest news, exclusives and videos on WhatsApp
Ford Motor Co. in Dearborn is launching the Ford Privacy Promise to make an “explicit commitment to customers that their vehicle data is safe” and they’re in control of what they share.
As Ford created the Privacy Promise, it surveyed more than 1,000 U.S. consumers — both Ford and non-Ford owners.
It learned that while privacy is important to them, customers understand the value of data sharing.

“Even for a tech-savvy consumer, it can be hard to understand the relationship between your vehicle, the data it generates, and your privacy and rights,” says Kristin Jones, chief privacy officer and deputy general counsel for data and privacy at Ford.
“With our connected vehicle and app user communities growing every day, Ford takes its responsibility in safeguarding customer data seriously.”
Ford says it designs and builds its products with privacy in mind — from collection of data to its use, storage, and disposal.
This can include privacy-enhancing technologies like anonymizing or aggregating data to further protect a customer’s privacy.
As a result, Ford offers vehicle privacy settings that allow customers to control what data they want to share, subject to the features and services they wish to enjoy.
Ford stresses that it never sells data about how customers drive their vehicle to data brokers.
Data privacy has become an uncomfortable subject for America’s automakers.
Within days of General Motors agreeing to a $220 million settlement over how it handled driver information, Ford announced a new customer-facing commitment on the same issue.
GM must now restrict the driving data it collects and obtain a driver’s explicit consent before gathering or sharing it.
According to a report by MotorBiscuit , an outside party will also audit its privacy programs.
Earlier, in January 2025, it agreed with the Federal Trade Commission to stop sharing geolocation and driving-behavior data with consumer reporting agencies for five years.
It is not yet clear whether affected owners will receive any of the $220 million.
Against that backdrop, Ford has introduced the Ford Privacy Promise, which is meant to assure owners that their information is protected and that they decide what to share.
The data came from Smart Driver, a program that enrolled millions of motorists from 2016 until GM discontinued it in 2024.
To support the effort, Ford surveyed more than 1,000 U.S. customers about their understanding of data privacy.
Respondents overwhelmingly said they want the ability to control and adjust their privacy settings whenever they choose.

Equipment vendors should remove barriers to isolation and recovery, CISA said, while managed service providers and integrators should help operators with engineering and planning work. In addition to the guidance, which CISA will periodically update, the agency will also perform “targeted assessments” of participating critical infrastructure operators’ resilience measures, including their ability to operate in isolation, Andersen told reporters during a briefing on Tuesday. “We've already started to kick off the first couple of assessments under a pilot phase of this initiative,” he said. As concerns mount about potential cyber sabotage by the Chinese government, the U.S. is warning operators to practice maintaining services in a degraded state.
The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) wants to help critical infrastructure operators keep their systems running during a major cyberattack or other serious incident.

CISA on Tuesday released guidance as part of an international “CI Fortify” initiative focused on activities that infrastructure operators can take to isolate the effects of a cyber intrusion and recover from them.

“In a geopolitical crisis, the critical infrastructure organizations Americans rely on must be able to continue delivering—at a minimum—crucial services,” acting CISA Director Nick Andersen said in a statement. “They must be able to isolate vital systems from harm, continue operating in that isolated state, and quickly recover any systems that an adversary may successfully compromise.”

The new guidance, modeled on advice that the Australian government published in 2025, comes as intelligence agencies warn that China might sabotage Western critical infrastructure to keep the U.S. and its allies from interfering with Beijing’s long-rumored invasion of Taiwan. China’s Volt Typhoon hacking campaign indicated that Beijing had already begun laying the groundwork for such disruption, prompting U.S. officials to step up warnings about the dangers of interdependencies in operational technology.

“Operators should assume that in a conflict scenario third-party connections — such as telecommunications, internet, vendors, service providers, and upstream dependencies — will be unreliable and that threat actors will have some access to the OT network,” CISA said on its CI Fortify page. “Isolation and Recovery are emergency planning objectives that can mitigate this threat within the next few years.”

The isolation advice includes identifying “critical customers,” such as nearby military bases, establishing service delivery expectations for them, identifying the OT assets necessary to provide that service and maintaining up-to-date “business continuity plans and engineering processes” to facilitate safe isolated operations “for weeks to months.”

The recovery advice covers documenting how systems operate, backing up important files and “practicing the replacement of systems or the transition to manual in case isolation fails and components are rendered inoperable.”
Critical infrastructure operators should discuss CISA’s advice with their vendors, the agency said, “to help understand their communications dependencies and potential workarounds.”

CI Fortify also includes recommendations for how other companies in the critical infrastructure ecosystem can support operators. Equipment vendors should remove barriers to isolation and recovery, CISA said, while managed service providers and integrators should help operators with engineering and planning work.

In addition to the guidance, which CISA will periodically update, the agency will also perform “targeted assessments” of participating critical infrastructure operators’ resilience measures, including their ability to operate in isolation, Andersen told reporters during a briefing on Tuesday.
“We've already started to kick off the first couple of assessments under a pilot phase of this initiative,” he said.

CISA’s regional offices will play a key role in supporting this assessment work, but they have been hit hard by layoffs, retirements and forced relocations as part of the Trump administration’s efforts to downsize CISA. The administration has approved CISA’s request to hire 329 new employees to fill critical vacancies, and Andersen told reporters that the regional teams “are high on that priority [list]” for the hiring plan.

Each infrastructure facility assessment will prioritize different outcomes depending on the sector and operator in question, Andersen said. Energy utilities and transportation systems can choose to supply or transport one customer versus another in the event of degraded capacity, he noted, while the water sector isn’t designed to work that way.

As concerns mount about potential cyber sabotage by the Chinese government, the U.S. is warning operators to practice maintaining services in a degraded state. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) wants to help critical infrastructure operators keep their systems running during a major cyberattack or other serious incident. CISA on Tuesday released guidance as part of an international “CI Fortify” initiative focused on activities that infrastructure operators can take to isolate the effects of a cyber intrusion and recover from them. “In a geopolitical crisis, the critical infrastructure organizations Americans rely on must be able to continue delivering—at a minimum—crucial services,” acting CISA Director Nick Andersen said in a statement. “They must be able to isolate vital systems from harm, continue operating in that isolated state, and quickly recover any systems that an adversary may successfully compromise.” The new guidance, modeled on advice that the Australian government published in 2025, comes as intelligence agencies warn that China might sabotage Western critical infrastructure to keep the U.S. and its allies from interfering with Beijing’s long-rumored invasion of Taiwan. China’s Volt Typhoon hacking campaign indicated that Beijing had already begun laying the groundwork for such disruption, prompting U.S. officials to step up warnings about the dangers of interdependencies in operational technology. “Operators should assume that in a conflict scenario third-party connections — such as telecommunications, internet, vendors, service providers, and upstream dependencies — will be unreliable and that threat actors will have some access to the OT network,” CISA said on its CI Fortify page. “Isolation and Recovery are emergency planning objectives that can mitigate this threat within the next few years.” The isolation advice includes identifying “critical customers,” such as nearby military bases, establishing service delivery expectations for them, identifying the OT assets necessary to provide that service and maintaining up-to-date “business continuity plans and engineering processes” to facilitate safe isolated operations “for weeks to months.” The recovery advice covers documenting how systems operate, backing up important files and “practicing the replacement of systems or the transition to manual in case isolation fails and components are rendered inoperable.” Critical infrastructure operators should discuss CISA’s advice with their vendors, the agency said, “to help understand their communications dependencies and potential workarounds.” CI Fortify also includes recommendations for how other companies in the critical infrastructure ecosystem can support operators. Equipment vendors should remove barriers to isolation and recovery, CISA said, while managed service providers and integrators should help operators with engineering and planning work. In addition to the guidance, which CISA will periodically update, the agency will also perform “targeted assessments” of participating critical infrastructure operators’ resilience measures, including their ability to operate in isolation, Andersen told reporters during a briefing on Tuesday. “We've already started to kick off the first couple of assessments under a pilot phase of this initiative,” he said. CISA’s regional offices will play a key role in supporting this assessment work, but they have been hit hard by layoffs, retirements and forced relocations as part of the Trump administration’s efforts to downsize CISA. The administration has approved CISA’s request to hire 329 new employees to fill critical vacancies, and Andersen told reporters that the regional teams “are high on that priority [list]” for the hiring plan. Each infrastructure facility assessment will prioritize different outcomes depending on the sector and operator in question, Andersen said. Energy utilities and transportation systems can choose to supply or transport one customer versus another in the event of degraded capacity, he noted, while the water sector isn’t designed to work that way. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) wants to help critical infrastructure operators keep their systems running during a major cyberattack or other serious incident.

CISA on Tuesday released guidance as part of an international “CI Fortify” initiative focused on activities that infrastructure operators can take to isolate the effects of a cyber intrusion and recover from them.

“In a geopolitical crisis, the critical infrastructure organizations Americans rely on must be able to continue delivering—at a minimum—crucial services,” acting CISA Director Nick Andersen said in a statement. “They must be able to isolate vital systems from harm, continue operating in that isolated state, and quickly recover any systems that an adversary may successfully compromise.”

The new guidance, modeled on advice that the Australian government published in 2025, comes as intelligence agencies warn that China might sabotage Western critical infrastructure to keep the U.S. and its allies from interfering with Beijing’s long-rumored invasion of Taiwan. China’s Volt Typhoon hacking campaign indicated that Beijing had already begun laying the groundwork for such disruption, prompting U.S. officials to step up warnings about the dangers of interdependencies in operational technology.

“Operators should assume that in a conflict scenario third-party connections — such as telecommunications, internet, vendors, service providers, and upstream dependencies — will be unreliable and that threat actors will have some access to the OT network,” CISA said on its CI Fortify page. “Isolation and Recovery are emergency planning objectives that can mitigate this threat within the next few years.”

The isolation advice includes identifying “critical customers,” such as nearby military bases, establishing service delivery expectations for them, identifying the OT assets necessary to provide that service and maintaining up-to-date “business continuity plans and engineering processes” to facilitate safe isolated operations “for weeks to months.”

The recovery advice covers documenting how systems operate, backing up important files and “practicing the replacement of systems or the transition to manual in case isolation fails and components are rendered inoperable.”
Critical infrastructure operators should discuss CISA’s advice with their vendors, the agency said, “to help understand their communications dependencies and potential workarounds.”

CI Fortify also includes recommendations for how other companies in the critical infrastructure ecosystem can support operators. Equipment vendors should remove barriers to isolation and recovery, CISA said, while managed service providers and integrators should help operators with engineering and planning work.

In addition to the guidance, which CISA will periodically update, the agency will also perform “targeted assessments” of participating critical infrastructure operators’ resilience measures, including their ability to operate in isolation, Andersen told reporters during a briefing on Tuesday.
“We've already started to kick off the first couple of assessments under a pilot phase of this initiative,” he said.

CISA’s regional offices will play a key role in supporting this assessment work, but they have been hit hard by layoffs, retirements and forced relocations as part of the Trump administration’s efforts to downsize CISA. The administration has approved CISA’s request to hire 329 new employees to fill critical vacancies, and Andersen told reporters that the regional teams “are high on that priority [list]” for the hiring plan.

Each infrastructure facility assessment will prioritize different outcomes depending on the sector and operator in question, Andersen said. Energy utilities and transportation systems can choose to supply or transport one customer versus another in the event of degraded capacity, he noted, while the water sector isn’t designed to work that way.

Bitcoin's four-hour chart offers a somewhat more encouraging picture, with the moving average convergence divergence indicator showing early signs of improving buying momentum. Source: crypto.news The MACD line stood at negative 356, above its signal line at negative 553, while the histogram had turned positive at 197. The bullish crossover suggests selling momentum has weakened and buyers are attempting to regain control. The Fibonacci retracement drawn between the recent $84,843 swing high and $76,173 low places immediate resistance at $78,219, corresponding to the 23.6% retracement level. extraction.body: Bitcoin traded at $77,749.01 at 10:24 a.m. ET on Monday, November 2, down $165.70 or 0.21% over 24 hours, with $8.81 billion in spot volume across major venues. Coinbase printed $77,791.26. Binance’s BTC-USDT pair traded at $77,928, a premium of under $140 to the dollar benchmark, which says the exchange at the center of last week’s hack is trading normally again. The network’s market value stands at $1.56 trillion on a circulating supply of 20,105,365 coins, and Bitcoin’s share of the total $2.69 trillion crypto market sits at 58.5%. The price action is the problem. U.S. equities ripped higher at the open, with the Nasdaq Composite up 0.82% and the Dow up 510 points as crude oil collapsed 6% on Iran-Qatar peace talks. Bitcoin did not join the move. It traded in a $77,000 to $78,700 band all weekend, touched $78,727 in early Asian hours and gave it back. When a risk asset fails to rally on a morning when oil, yields and the VIX all fall, the market is telling you the marginal buyer is missing, not that the seller has disappeared. That distinction drives this forecast. The supply side of Bitcoin’s problem has been absorbed. A record $6.4 billion exchange theft, $4.7 billion in exchange withdrawals and a $643.3 million single-day exit from spot ETFs all hit within 72 hours, and the price never broke October’s $76,141 low. The demand side has not recovered. Spot ETFs logged a losing week, the Fear and Greed Index sits at 37 after dropping to 30 on Friday, and Bitcoin remains 5.3% below its 50-day moving average. The weekend showed resilience rather than strength. Bitcoin moved between $77,600 and $78,500 on Sunday as Binance restored withdrawals network by network, with Bitcoin the first chain reopened. There was no capitulation wick, no liquidation cascade and no break of the 200-day exponential moving average at $76,459. That is the best news in the tape. The largest theft in crypto history hit Binance on the evening of Thursday, October 29. Attackers drained $6.4 billion in tokens from the exchange’s hot wallets in under 20 minutes. The company’s initial investigation traced the breach to a compromised engineer’s laptop that gave the attacker access to a service container and let them submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions. The FBI attributed the theft to North Korean state hackers in a Saturday statement, naming the group known as TraderTraitor. The previous record was a $1.5 billion exploit of Bybit in February 2025, also tied to North Korea, which makes last week’s attack more than four times larger. The first-hour damage was sharp. Bitcoin fell 5% on the news, Ether dropped 6% and BNB, Binance’s native token, tumbled 10%. Binance suspended deposits and withdrawals for 30 hours to secure its systems and coordinate recovery. The response is why the market held. Binance said it set aside more than $6.34 billion in company funds to cover losses in full, so customer balances were never impaired. Stablecoin issuers froze $3 billion of the stolen funds within 70 minutes, and Binance said it had locked almost half of the total within the first day and secured 95% of the coverage needed by Sunday. Withdrawals reopened Sunday, starting with the Bitcoin network, then Ethereum and BNB Smart Chain. The withdrawal test came in better than feared. Net outflows from Binance reached $4.7 billion by Monday morning in London, under 3% of the $166 billion in assets the exchange holds. The company said withdrawals were in line with expectations and that deposits were steadily increasing. Binance’s co-chief executive added that part of the outflow reflected transfers between Binance’s own wallets, not customers leaving. A bank-run scenario, the real tail risk after an exchange hack, never materialized. The price of Bitcoin across the whole episode tells the same story. Bitcoin fell to $76,300 at the worst point, recovered to $78,000 by the weekend and is trading at $77,749 on Monday. Compare that to the market’s reaction to past exchange crises, when Bitcoin dropped 20% or more in days. A $6.4 billion theft, absorbed with a 2% net move from Thursday’s pre-hack level, shows the market structure is deeper and more institutional than in prior cycles. The trade-off is that the hack removed a near-term catalyst without adding one. Traders who spent Friday and the weekend braced for contagion now have nothing to sell into and nothing compelling to buy. That explains the flat Monday tape: the fear premium has bled out, and no fresh demand has taken its place. The next leg depends on whether institutions treat the episode as a resolved event or a reason to stay underweight into year-end. Not all of the stolen funds carry the same risk for Bitcoin’s price. The $3 billion frozen by stablecoin issuers within 70 minutes is dead money for the attackers, locked at the contract level and unrecoverable for them. The problem sits in the remaining $2.4 billion in Bitcoin and Ether, which no issuer can freeze. That portion of the haul is native crypto, held in wallets the attackers control, and it represents a supply overhang that will hang over the market for months. The scale needs context. At $77,749, $2.4 billion split between Bitcoin and Ether amounts to less than 0.2% of Bitcoin’s $1.56 trillion market value. Spot Bitcoin trading volume runs $8.81 billion per day on the benchmark venues alone, and futures volume runs $46.10 billion per day. Even if the entire stolen balance hit the market at once, it would be absorbed within a single session’s turnover. The overhang is a sentiment problem first and a supply problem second. How the attackers cash out matters for timing. Previous North Korean thefts followed a pattern: move funds through mixers and cross-chain bridges over weeks and months, convert in small tranches through over-the-counter desks and decentralized exchanges, and avoid the large, visible sales that would trigger exchange blacklists. The Bybit funds from February 2025 took months to launder. A similar timeline here means steady, low-level selling pressure through the first quarter of 2027 rather than a single dump. That slow bleed has a specific market effect. It does not crash the price, but it caps rallies. Every time Bitcoin approaches resistance, traders will watch blockchain tracking firms for movement in the flagged wallets, and any large transfer becomes a reason to take profit early. Expect headline-driven intraday drops of 1% to 2% whenever the stolen coins move, with the dips bought as long as the broader structure holds. The recovery side could also move price. Blockchain intelligence firms are tracing the funds, and exchanges have blocked deposits from addresses linked to the hack. Every additional freeze or seizure announcement shrinks the overhang and removes a reason to sell. If law enforcement recovers a meaningful slice of the Bitcoin portion, that becomes a positive catalyst the market has not priced. For the forecast, the overhang argues against a straight-line recovery. It reinforces the base case that Bitcoin trades a range rather than trending in either direction through November. A clean break above $80,000 would need demand strong enough to absorb both the normal flow of profit-taking and a persistent seller with $2.4 billion to unload. Until spot ETF flows turn decisively positive, that demand does not exist on the scale required. The spot ETF tape gives the clearest read on institutional demand, and Friday’s print was ugly. U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded $643.3 million in net outflows on October 30, ending a four-day inflow streak and posting the largest single-day withdrawal since June 25. Every fund that moved posted a loss: BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust led with $233.7 million out, Fidelity’s Wise Origin Bitcoin Fund lost $201.0 million, ARK 21Shares Bitcoin ETF lost $129.5 million, Grayscale Bitcoin Trust shed $53.3 million and Bitwise Bitcoin ETF gave up $25.7 million. Trading volume across the funds hit $6.35 billion, with IBIT alone accounting for $5.21 billion. IBIT closed the day at $43.36, down 5.1%. The outflow erased the month’s gains in two sessions. From October 1 through October 28, spot Bitcoin ETFs had collected $111.2 million in net inflows. The last two sessions alone took out $626.3 million, flipping October to a net outflow of $515.9 million. The week of October 26 to 30 ended with $202.4 million in net outflows, reversing the $304.7 million that came in the week before. The October 22 session had already logged a $635.5 million exit, so October carried two of the largest outflow days since late June. The split inside the numbers is the more constructive detail. IBIT finished October with $932.1 million in net inflows despite its $233.7 million Friday outflow, while the rest of the ETF complex lost money. Long-term allocators using BlackRock’s fund kept buying through most of the month; the selling concentrated in funds with shorter-term holders and in Grayscale’s legacy vehicle. That gives the bulls a core of sticky demand to build on. The cost basis math sets the key upside level. The average entry price across the spot ETF investor base sits at $84,714. At $77,749, the average ETF holder is underwater by 8.2%. That creates a natural ceiling: as Bitcoin approaches $84,714, holders who bought the summer rally have a chance to exit at breakeven, and that supply will slow any recovery. The first full week of November flows decides the next leg. A weekly total above the $202.4 million lost last week turns Friday into a one-day risk reduction tied to the hack. Continued IBIT outflows alongside the Ether ETF losing streak would confirm institutions are cutting crypto exposure into year-end. Today’s flow data lands after the U.S. close. The largest corporate holder kept buying through the hack. Strategy disclosed in an 8-K filed Monday that it bought 811 Bitcoin for $65.5 million between October 26 and November 1, an average purchase price of $80,764 per coin. The company funded the buy by selling 1,178,552 shares of its common stock under its at-the-market program for net proceeds of $164.0 million. It directed $65.5 million to Bitcoin and $98.5 million to its USD Cash liquidity account, and it repurchased $208.2 million of its STRC preferred stock during the same week. Holdings now stand at 849,327 Bitcoin, acquired for an aggregate $64.08 billion at an average cost of $75,451 per coin. That is the first reported purchase since the week of October 12 to 18, when the company added 267 Bitcoin; the October 19 to 25 week showed no purchases or sales. Strategy holds 4.2% of the circulating Bitcoin supply. The cost line is the number to watch. At $77,749, Bitcoin trades just 3% above Strategy’s $75,451 average purchase price. The company’s unrealized gain on its holdings stands at $1.95 billion, a thin cushion on a $66 billion position. A move below $75,451 would put the largest corporate Bitcoin treasury underwater on its full stack, a headline the market has used as a selling trigger before, even though the company’s structure does not force it to sell. The capital allocation choices say more than the buy itself. Strategy put more money into buying back its own preferred stock, $208.2 million, than into Bitcoin, $65.5 million. Sending $98.5 million to cash reserves rather than coins signals a company prioritizing liquidity and dividend coverage over aggressive accumulation at these prices. When the most committed buyer in the market slows its pace, the marginal bid gets thinner. The second is the 200-day exponential moving average at $76,459. This is the technical level the market has watched most closely since the hack. Holding it on a daily close keeps the long-term trend intact; losing it shifts the trend signal to bearish for the first time since the June-to-October rally began. The third is $76,141, the October 30 low printed on the same day as the $643.3 million ETF outflow. That low marks the point where the hack, the ETF exit and the Nasdaq’s 2.86% collapse all hit at once. If Bitcoin breaks below a low set under maximum stress, the market has found new sellers beyond the event-driven ones, and that changes the forecast. A break of $76,141 is 2.1% below the current price. Below that, the gap widens. Strategy’s average cost at $75,451 offers a psychological level 3% below spot. The long liquidation cluster below $76,000 means a break of the October low could accelerate quickly to the next major support: the 200-day simple moving average at $73,059, 6% below the current price. The $73,000 zone also aligns with the level that historical midterm-year pattern analysis has flagged as the critical floor if post-election selling materializes. Inflation data has kept the Fed cautious. The consumer price index rose 3.4% from a year earlier in August. The October ISM Manufacturing report, released Monday, showed prices paid easing to 75.2 from 77.9, the first meaningful decline in input-cost pressure in months, while the headline index rose to 55.5. Stronger growth with softer inflation is the combination that supports risk assets, and it is the best macro print Bitcoin has had in weeks. Friday’s jobs report is the next test. The October payrolls report lands at 8:30 a.m. ET on November 6, with consensus calling for a gain of 65,000 jobs after September’s 29,000. Unemployment stood at 4.2%. A print near consensus keeps the Fed on hold. A weak number below 30,000 would revive rate-cut hopes and likely lift Bitcoin. A strong number above 120,000 would strengthen the hawkish case and push yields higher, a headwind for Bitcoin at a moment when it lacks fresh demand. Gold offers a useful comparison. Gold futures rebounded 1.43% to $3,954.60 on Monday after breaking below $4,000 last week on forced liquidations. Both gold and Bitcoin sold off in late October as leveraged positions unwound across asset classes. Gold has started to recover; Bitcoin has not. That gap reflects the Binance hack’s specific weight on crypto sentiment, and it should narrow if the hack fades from headlines. The cross-asset picture favors Bitcoin more than its price shows. Falling oil, easing inflation pressure, a stable bond market and a recovering equity tape are a constructive backdrop. Bitcoin’s lag reflects crypto-specific sentiment damage, which is the kind of discount that closes quickly once the next catalyst lands. The forecast rests on one thesis: Bitcoin has absorbed the supply shock and now needs demand to return. The $6.4 billion Binance hack, the $4.7 billion in exchange withdrawals and the $643.3 million spot ETF outflow all landed within 72 hours, and Bitcoin held above its October low of $76,141 through all of it. What it has not done is rally. Flat price action on a day when the Nasdaq rose 0.82% and oil fell 6% shows the marginal buyer is still absent. The base case, with the highest probability through mid-November, is a range between $76,000 and $82,000. The floor is defended by the 200-day exponential moving average at $76,459, the October low at $76,141 and Strategy’s $75,451 average cost. The ceiling is set by the moving average cluster at $81,022 to $81,906 and the stolen-coin overhang that will cap rallies. Inside that range, the crowded short book between $79,200 and $80,900 gives the upside a squeeze mechanism that the downside lacks. The asymmetry favors patience over chasing. Bitcoin sits 2.1% above the bear trigger and 9% below the bull target, while the macro backdrop of falling oil, easing input costs and a recovering equity market leans constructive. The midterm-year pattern says the bottom either formed in June at $57,800 or arrives soon, and either way the six months after past midterms have averaged gains of 86.5%. The verdict is neutral with a bullish tilt: Bitcoin holds the range between $76,000 and $82,000 into Friday’s jobs report, with a break above $80,000 opening the path to $84,714 in November, and a daily close below $76,141 invalidating that view and shifting the target to $73,059.
