The department’s projected total investment for the new system’s design, development, training and implementation is approximately $65 million.

An early review of cases supported by PATH NC and the new SDM tools shows promising results – county intake decisions are consistently aligned with state policies and best practice in child protective services. “We’ve built PATH NC from the ground up in collaboration with county leaders to ensure it meets the current, real-world needs of North Carolina’s child welfare social workers,” said NCDHHS Deputy Secretary for Opportunity and Well-Being Michael Leighs. “It’s designed to improve the everyday experience of staff while making it easier to track, report and respond to what’s happening in real time.

PATH NC is a critical part of our work to transform the child welfare system and improve the lives of children and families in North Carolina.” The new system aligns with NCDHHS’ broader efforts to strengthen system oversight and modernize service delivery.

Key features of PATH NC include: Mobile-Friendly Design – The system supports documentation from the field, including some offline functionality, so that staff can update case records while conducting assessments, facilitating family visits, attending court and more.
Decision-Making Tools – PATH NC’s new certified SDM tools provide built-in risk and safety assessments, dashboards and real-time alerts for county staff and supervisors.
The platform also has the capability to add automated policy support functions and dedicated portals for providers and families in the future.

Comprehensive Case Management – Fully implemented, PATH NC will include modules for intake, assessment, in-home services, foster care, adoption, financials, licensing and eligibility all together in one system.

Data Accessibility – Once all counties have transitioned to PATH NC, staff will be able to access statewide data, including a family’s full history with child welfare services, regardless of whether they move or transfer to a different county.

Integrated Systems – PATH NC is designed to interface with other child-serving systems such as NC Medicaid, the NC Department of Public Instruction and other partner agencies in the future, which will streamline information sharing and reduce administrative burden across the system.
The statewide rollout of PATH NC began June 2, 2025, with an initial cohort of 15 counties using the system to support child welfare intakes and assessments.
Over the next eight months, all remaining counties will transition to PATH NC for intake and assessment.
This phased rollout allows NCDHHS to provide targeted training and individualized support as each cohort of counties prepares to transition to PATH NC.

The department will continue to update and improve the system based on user feedback throughout the implementation process. “PATH NC is going to be a game changer for the state, and we’re excited to be among the first counties leading the way,” said Christa Smith, Director of Forsyth County DSS. “The system gives our staff the right tools to make timely, informed decisions, and it gives our supervisors the data they need to identify trends and improve practice.

We look forward to seeing everything PATH NC will do for us and our DSS partners across the state.” PATH NC is a critical step forward in NCDHHS’ ongoing effort to transform child welfare in North Carolina through systemic change, increased access to services, better data and stronger alignment among state and county systems.

By streamlining documentation processes and providing real-time access to child welfare data for users across the system, PATH NC offers more opportunity for state and county staff to pinpoint trends or challenges in child welfare practice and address them sooner – ultimately leading to a stronger system and better outcomes for children and families.

extraction.body: For decades, child welfare workers have struggled to follow the lives and progress of children in the state’s child welfare system. Families in financial and emotional crisis can have chaotic lives, and case workers often end up a step behind. Sometimes that time lag can have tragic results. Child advocates have long wished for a better way to consistently assess, follow and manage the progress of children caught up in the system, and track what’s happening with their families. In 2025 — after a decade of failed attempts — the state’s Department of Health and Human Services started rolling out a software package to do just that . Now all of the state’s counties have the Partnership and Technology Hub, or PATH NC, to track the intake and assessment portion of each child’s case. More than two-thirds of North Carolina’s county departments of social services are also now using the case management portion of the information system, state health officials said during an Oct. 20 North Carolina Child Fatality Task Force meeting. And by early 2027, all counties are expected to be using the full software suite, including case management. Last year, state officials said they hoped to have the system fully operational by this past summer. But adding the ongoing case management — tracking foster care, in-home services, adoption, and the like — was complicated for county social services departments, said Donna Fayko, deputy director for child welfare with NC DHHS. “It’s just a more complex system to train and implement than intake and assessment,” she told Child Fatality Task Force members. “So we’re seeing more challenges with implementation with this phase at the county level.” The expansion of PATH NC is one of many efforts North Carolina has made as it overhauls its child welfare system, said Lisa Tucker Cauley, a division director for human services with NC DHHS. That work has included redesigning worker training and expanding prevention services to “strengthen statewide infrastructure and support counties in their daily work,” Cauley said. “These initiatives have laid a stronger foundation for child welfare services across the state,” she said. “But at the same time, this infrastructure alone can’t meet the needs of children and families without enough qualified workers, supervisors, funding and services to support its use.” The improvements can’t come soon enough. In the first five months that the entire state has been on the system for intake and assessment, 22 children have died of maltreatment. The goal is that better tracking of cases could help prevent these tragedies. North Carolina is one of only nine states in the U.S. where the child welfare system is supervised by the state but county workers do the actual work. That’s led to a patchwork of independent data systems in county departments of social services, who administer child welfare services. Tracking a child or a family who moved across county lines, for instance, could easily become a bureaucratic nightmare. Before PATH NC, more than half of North Carolina counties relied on manual processes and paper records, DHHS officials said. Coupled with high staff turnover keeping track of everything was often difficult. Now, social workers have easier access to up-to-date information on any child in the system. They can access PATH NC on their phones, tablets or computers while out in the field working with families. “This is a big deal for child welfare because families … they move across county lines frequently,” she said. “Tracking them, being able to see their history, really adds to the safety decision making and assessment.” Before PATH NC, one of the state’s biggest challenges had been inconsistent screening decisions, she said. Now, as social workers enter information into PATH NC, they are prompted by the system through structured decision-making tools to improve how they identify, assess and respond to safety concerns, she said. Trishana Jones, a task force member from the North Carolina Coalition Against Domestic Violence , asked if there is county-by-county data on the number of children involved in the child welfare system with domestic violence as a contributing factor in their referral. “That really helps whenever I’m doing trainings talking about childhood exposure to domestic violence for people to understand prevalence,” she said. Morrell said that is a data point that can be tracked and shared with her. During the five months that all of North Carolina’s counties have been using the PATH NC system: Data show that 8,163 children were involved in child welfare cases where maltreatment allegations were substantiated. In that group, there were 22 cases where a child died of suspected maltreatment. State health officials said counties are struggling with high turnover among social workers and supervisors. They often leave over low pay and high workloads, Cauley said. Very few counties are fully staffed to meet the state’s caseload standards of no more than 10 for Child Protective Services or 15 for foster care, she said. “They report that they can’t recruit and find enough … people to fill positions,” Cauley said. She noted that caseworkers frequently leave lower paying counties in search of higher pay in neighboring counties. Other reasons for leaving include secondary trauma, stress and personal safety concerns, Cauley said. That turnover contributes to longer stays in foster care, a lower likelihood of timely reunification and a lack of stability for children and families, Cauley said. “New workers need time and supervision to build judgment in assessing safety, engaging families, documenting decisions and working with courts,” she said. “When supervisors are stretched thin or frequently turned over, they have less capacity to provide the coaching and consultation necessary for effective practice.” To strengthen the workforce pipeline, the department has reintroduced a stipend for students at some schools within the Child Welfare Education Collaborative , a long-held goal for the department to restore a program that was terminated in 2016. Out of 21 social work programs in universities and colleges statewide, the stipend — which covers tuition and fees — is now offered at three universities — Appalachian State, East Carolina and N.C. A&T. Fayko said it will be expanded to more sites. Students receive pre-service training and get hands-on experience in county child welfare agencies. When they finish the program, they’re ready to start work immediately, she said. In the most recent school year, the program graduated 45 child welfare professionals. “These students are entering the workforce equipped to support children and families with skill, empathy, and professionalism,” said Kayla Warren, a social work professor at Appalachian, in a news release about the program . “Investing in programs like [the Child Welfare Education Collaborative] is critical to building and sustaining a strong child welfare workforce in North Carolina.” This work is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution-NoDerivatives 4.0 International License . extraction.body: On Wednesday, June 18, the North Carolina Department of Health and Human Services announced the start of PATH NC, the Partnership and Technology Hub for North Carolina, a new statewide information system designed to modernize the administration of child welfare services. The program works to get child welfare staff with real-time data and decision-making tools in order to protect children better and improve outcomes for children and families across the state. Up until this time, officials say, North Carolina's 100 county departments of social services, which administer child welfare services, operate with a patchwork of independent data systems, with nearly half of counties still largely reliant on manual processes and paper records for child welfare operations. PATH NC aims to bring a unified system to all 100 counties for the first time. PATH NC is more than a technology upgrade – it’s an investment in North Carolina’s children and families,” said NC Health and Human Services Secretary Dev Sangvai. “By providing social services staff with better tools, clearer data and integrated support, we are laying the foundation for a safer, more responsive child welfare system that delivers better, more consistent results – no matter where you live. The NCDHHS says the following in a release: NCDHHS' goal for PATH NC was not merely to create a system that collects information, but also to improve child welfare practice through evidence-based tools and actionable insights for the workforce. While developing the new system, the department worked in close collaboration with county leaders to fully redesign the state’s Structured Decision-Making (SDM) tools. Nationally certified by Evident Change for accuracy and consistent results, the new SDM tools within PATH NC help frontline staff better identify and assess risk and safety concerns when responding to reports of child abuse or neglect. Over the last five years, NCDHHS has worked hand-in-hand with North Carolina’s county departments of social services to plan, develop and test both PATH NC and the SDM tools. The department’s projected total investment for the new system’s design, development, training and implementation is approximately $65 million. An early review of cases supported by PATH NC and the new SDM tools shows promising results – county intake decisions are consistently aligned with state policies and best practice in child protective services. “We’ve built PATH NC from the ground up in collaboration with county leaders to ensure it meets the current, real-world needs of North Carolina’s child welfare social workers,” said NCDHHS Deputy Secretary for Opportunity and Well-Being Michael Leighs. “It’s designed to improve the everyday experience of staff while making it easier to track, report and respond to what’s happening in real time. PATH NC is a critical part of our work to transform the child welfare system and improve the lives of children and families in North Carolina.” The new system aligns with NCDHHS’ broader efforts to strengthen system oversight and modernize service delivery. Key features of PATH NC include: Mobile-Friendly Design – The system supports documentation from the field, including some offline functionality, so that staff can update case records while conducting assessments, facilitating family visits, attending court and more. Decision-Making Tools – PATH NC’s new certified SDM tools provide built-in risk and safety assessments, dashboards and real-time alerts for county staff and supervisors. The platform also has the capability to add automated policy support functions and dedicated portals for providers and families in the future. Comprehensive Case Management – Fully implemented, PATH NC will include modules for intake, assessment, in-home services, foster care, adoption, financials, licensing and eligibility all together in one system. Data Accessibility – Once all counties have transitioned to PATH NC, staff will be able to access statewide data, including a family’s full history with child welfare services, regardless of whether they move or transfer to a different county. Integrated Systems – PATH NC is designed to interface with other child-serving systems such as NC Medicaid, the NC Department of Public Instruction and other partner agencies in the future, which will streamline information sharing and reduce administrative burden across the system. The statewide rollout of PATH NC began June 2, 2025, with an initial cohort of 15 counties using the system to support child welfare intakes and assessments. Over the next eight months, all remaining counties will transition to PATH NC for intake and assessment. This phased rollout allows NCDHHS to provide targeted training and individualized support as each cohort of counties prepares to transition to PATH NC. The department will continue to update and improve the system based on user feedback throughout the implementation process. “PATH NC is going to be a game changer for the state, and we’re excited to be among the first counties leading the way,” said Christa Smith, Director of Forsyth County DSS. “The system gives our staff the right tools to make timely, informed decisions, and it gives our supervisors the data they need to identify trends and improve practice. We look forward to seeing everything PATH NC will do for us and our DSS partners across the state.” PATH NC is a critical step forward in NCDHHS’ ongoing effort to transform child welfare in North Carolina through systemic change, increased access to services, better data and stronger alignment among state and county systems. By streamlining documentation processes and providing real-time access to child welfare data for users across the system, PATH NC offers more opportunity for state and county staff to pinpoint trends or challenges in child welfare practice and address them sooner – ultimately leading to a stronger system and better outcomes for children and families.

extraction.body: For decades, child welfare workers have struggled to follow the lives and progress of children in the state’s child welfare system. Families in financial and emotional crisis can have chaotic lives, and case workers often end up a step behind. Sometimes that time lag can have tragic results. Child advocates have long wished for a better way to consistently assess, follow and manage the progress of children caught up in the system, and track what’s happening with their families. In 2025 — after a decade of failed attempts — the state’s Department of Health and Human Services started rolling out a software package to do just that . Now all of the state’s counties have the Partnership and Technology Hub, or PATH NC, to track the intake and assessment portion of each child’s case. More than two-thirds of North Carolina’s county departments of social services are also now using the case management portion of the information system, state health officials said during an Oct. 20 North Carolina Child Fatality Task Force meeting. And by early 2027, all counties are expected to be using the full software suite, including case management. Last year, state officials said they hoped to have the system fully operational by this past summer. But adding the ongoing case management — tracking foster care, in-home services, adoption, and the like — was complicated for county social services departments, said Donna Fayko, deputy director for child welfare with NC DHHS. “It’s just a more complex system to train and implement than intake and assessment,” she told Child Fatality Task Force members. “So we’re seeing more challenges with implementation with this phase at the county level.” The expansion of PATH NC is one of many efforts North Carolina has made as it overhauls its child welfare system, said Lisa Tucker Cauley, a division director for human services with NC DHHS. That work has included redesigning worker training and expanding prevention services to “strengthen statewide infrastructure and support counties in their daily work,” Cauley said. “These initiatives have laid a stronger foundation for child welfare services across the state,” she said. “But at the same time, this infrastructure alone can’t meet the needs of children and families without enough qualified workers, supervisors, funding and services to support its use.” The improvements can’t come soon enough. In the first five months that the entire state has been on the system for intake and assessment, 22 children have died of maltreatment. The goal is that better tracking of cases could help prevent these tragedies. North Carolina is one of only nine states in the U.S. where the child welfare system is supervised by the state but county workers do the actual work. That’s led to a patchwork of independent data systems in county departments of social services, who administer child welfare services. Tracking a child or a family who moved across county lines, for instance, could easily become a bureaucratic nightmare. Before PATH NC, more than half of North Carolina counties relied on manual processes and paper records, DHHS officials said. Coupled with high staff turnover keeping track of everything was often difficult. Now, social workers have easier access to up-to-date information on any child in the system. They can access PATH NC on their phones, tablets or computers while out in the field working with families. “This is a big deal for child welfare because families … they move across county lines frequently,” she said. “Tracking them, being able to see their history, really adds to the safety decision making and assessment.” Before PATH NC, one of the state’s biggest challenges had been inconsistent screening decisions, she said. Now, as social workers enter information into PATH NC, they are prompted by the system through structured decision-making tools to improve how they identify, assess and respond to safety concerns, she said. Trishana Jones, a task force member from the North Carolina Coalition Against Domestic Violence , asked if there is county-by-county data on the number of children involved in the child welfare system with domestic violence as a contributing factor in their referral. “That really helps whenever I’m doing trainings talking about childhood exposure to domestic violence for people to understand prevalence,” she said. Morrell said that is a data point that can be tracked and shared with her. During the five months that all of North Carolina’s counties have been using the PATH NC system: Data show that 8,163 children were involved in child welfare cases where maltreatment allegations were substantiated. In that group, there were 22 cases where a child died of suspected maltreatment. State health officials said counties are struggling with high turnover among social workers and supervisors. They often leave over low pay and high workloads, Cauley said. Very few counties are fully staffed to meet the state’s caseload standards of no more than 10 for Child Protective Services or 15 for foster care, she said. “They report that they can’t recruit and find enough … people to fill positions,” Cauley said. She noted that caseworkers frequently leave lower paying counties in search of higher pay in neighboring counties. Other reasons for leaving include secondary trauma, stress and personal safety concerns, Cauley said. That turnover contributes to longer stays in foster care, a lower likelihood of timely reunification and a lack of stability for children and families, Cauley said. “New workers need time and supervision to build judgment in assessing safety, engaging families, documenting decisions and working with courts,” she said. “When supervisors are stretched thin or frequently turned over, they have less capacity to provide the coaching and consultation necessary for effective practice.” To strengthen the workforce pipeline, the department has reintroduced a stipend for students at some schools within the Child Welfare Education Collaborative , a long-held goal for the department to restore a program that was terminated in 2016. Out of 21 social work programs in universities and colleges statewide, the stipend — which covers tuition and fees — is now offered at three universities — Appalachian State, East Carolina and N.C. A&T. Fayko said it will be expanded to more sites. Students receive pre-service training and get hands-on experience in county child welfare agencies. When they finish the program, they’re ready to start work immediately, she said. In the most recent school year, the program graduated 45 child welfare professionals. “These students are entering the workforce equipped to support children and families with skill, empathy, and professionalism,” said Kayla Warren, a social work professor at Appalachian, in a news release about the program . “Investing in programs like [the Child Welfare Education Collaborative] is critical to building and sustaining a strong child welfare workforce in North Carolina.” This work is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution-NoDerivatives 4.0 International License . North Carolina is one of only nine states in the U.S. where the child welfare system is supervised by the state but county workers do the actual work.
That’s led to a patchwork of independent data systems in county departments of social services, who administer child welfare services.
Tracking a child or a family who moved across county lines, for instance, could easily become a bureaucratic nightmare.
by Jennifer Fernandez, North Carolina Health News November 3, 2026
20 North Carolina Child Fatality Task Force meeting.
In 2025 — after a decade of failed attempts — the state’s Department of Health and Human Services started rolling out a software package to do just that .
Before PATH NC, more than half of North Carolina counties relied on manual processes and paper records, DHHS officials said.
Data show that 8,163 children were involved in child welfare cases where maltreatment allegations were substantiated.
And by early 2027, all counties are expected to be using the full software suite, including case management.
State health officials said counties are struggling with high turnover among social workers and supervisors.
“New workers need time and supervision to build judgment in assessing safety, engaging families, documenting decisions and working with courts,” she said.
“When supervisors are stretched thin or frequently turned over, they have less capacity to provide the coaching and consultation necessary for effective practice.”
Child advocates have long wished for a better way to consistently assess, follow and manage the progress of children caught up in the system, and track what’s happening with their families.

facts.text: On Wednesday, June 18, the North Carolina Department of Health and Human Services announced the start of PATH NC, the Partnership and Technology Hub for North Carolina, a new statewide information system designed to modernize the administration of child welfare services.
PATH NC aims to bring a unified system to all 100 counties for the first time.
Over the next eight months, all remaining counties will transition to PATH NC for intake and assessment.

passages: Connect Media's inaugural 2026 Top Women in Retail Technology Awards puts a spotlight on women who have made their mark in retail technology innovation and who will prove to have a strong impact on the retail technology sector in the years ahead.
Judy Mottl is the editor of RetailCustomerExperience.com and DigitalSignageToday.com at Connect Media.

She is an award-winning editor, reporter and blogger who has worked for top media for nearly four decades, including AOL, InformationWeek and Internet News, as well as for leading technology providers including HP.
Get the latest news and resources from Retail Customer Experience.

The 25 female retail innovators come from a variety of sectors, from brands striving to drive a rewarding customer experience to technology providers innovating solutions to help brands attain that goal.
The award winners also represent a wide range of industries as well, from retail to hospitality to restaurants, healthcare and financial institutions.

sources.title: Ethereum pitches public-sector infrastructure for digital identity - Blockchain News
passages: Ethereum Foundation has framed Ethereum as a potential base layer for digital public infrastructure, arguing that public services can share digital systems without handing control of the underlying network to a single operator.

In a blog post published on 3 November 2026, the foundation said the network’s open-source and publicly verifiable design could help institutions collaborate across organizational and national boundaries while preserving more control over their own policies and systems.

extraction.body: Public services increasingly rely on digital systems that enable institutions to collaborate across organizational and national boundaries. Such cooperation may involve government agencies verifying documents issued by other authorities, or humanitarian organizations coordinating assistance while safeguarding sensitive personal information. Yet technical interoperability alone does not resolve a more fundamental question: who controls the infrastructure on which this cooperation depends? Ethereum offers a different foundation for digital public infrastructure. It is a global network that no single organization controls, and its software is open source for anyone to inspect, use, and build on. When shared infrastructure is operated by a single organization, other participants may depend on that provider for continued access or verification of records. For public services expected to endure beyond individual contracts and political cycles, such dependencies can have significant consequences. Ethereum allows institutions to use shared infrastructure without granting any single organization control over the underlying network. They can independently verify records and choose how they access the network, including through different service providers or their own infrastructure. At the same time, they retain authority over their own policies and systems. For individuals, sovereignty concerns control over personal information and the freedom to decide what to disclose. Applications using Ethereum can be designed so people hold their own digital credentials and choose how to present them. Services can verify the authenticity of these credentials without requiring the underlying personal information to be published on Ethereum. This allows institutions to retain responsibility for the information they certify, while individuals exercise greater control over how that information is held and shared. For communities spread across Bhutan's mountainous terrain, accessing services in person can involve long and costly journeys. Bhutan's National Digital Identity (NDI) system supports remote identity verification using digital credentials issued by authorized organizations. Rather than storing these credentials in a centralized government database, individuals hold them in their own NDI Wallets and decide what information to share when accessing services. A shared registry on Ethereum helps participating services verify the authenticity of these credentials without publishing them on the network. Bhutanese institutions remain responsible for determining which organizations can issue trusted credentials, while individuals retain greater control over their personal information. A different challenge arises in humanitarian assistance, where organizations serving overlapping populations need to coordinate support without unnecessarily sharing sensitive personal records. Drawing on discussions with humanitarian organizations and work with engineers and product leads, the Ethereum Foundation's Technical Foundations team developed a proof of concept exploring how aid coordination could work on Ethereum's public network while protecting sensitive personal information. The approach combines decentralized identity and private payment mechanisms. Participating organizations can coordinate through shared infrastructure without needing to exchange the personal records they hold, or rely on a single agency to operate the underlying network. Each organization retains responsibility for the information it collects and the assistance it provides. The Technical Foundations team has published a series of articles examining the proof of concept in greater depth, including its technical design, key learnings, and directions for future development. The long-term promise of digital public infrastructure is not simply that more services can be connected. It is that institutions can cooperate without surrendering their independence, while individuals can participate in digital systems with greater control over their personal information. Ethereum can support both objectives through open, shared infrastructure that no single organization controls.

The foundation said a new website, publicsector.ethereum.foundation, collects explanations, case studies and practical resources for governments, multilateral organizations, NGOs and other public-interest institutions.

The foundation distinguished between institutional and individual sovereignty. For institutions, it said shared infrastructure can create dependency if one provider operates the system and can affect continued access or verification of records. extraction.body: Public services increasingly rely on digital systems that enable institutions to collaborate across organizational and national boundaries. Such cooperation may involve government agencies verifying documents issued by other authorities, or humanitarian organizations coordinating assistance while safeguarding sensitive personal information. Yet technical interoperability alone does not resolve a more fundamental question: who controls the infrastructure on which this cooperation depends? Ethereum offers a different foundation for digital public infrastructure. It is a global network that no single organization controls, and its software is open source for anyone to inspect, use, and build on. When shared infrastructure is operated by a single organization, other participants may depend on that provider for continued access or verification of records. For public services expected to endure beyond individual contracts and political cycles, such dependencies can have significant consequences. Ethereum allows institutions to use shared infrastructure without granting any single organization control over the underlying network. They can independently verify records and choose how they access the network, including through different service providers or their own infrastructure. At the same time, they retain authority over their own policies and systems. For individuals, sovereignty concerns control over personal information and the freedom to decide what to disclose. Applications using Ethereum can be designed so people hold their own digital credentials and choose how to present them. Services can verify the authenticity of these credentials without requiring the underlying personal information to be published on Ethereum. This allows institutions to retain responsibility for the information they certify, while individuals exercise greater control over how that information is held and shared. For communities spread across Bhutan's mountainous terrain, accessing services in person can involve long and costly journeys. Bhutan's National Digital Identity (NDI) system supports remote identity verification using digital credentials issued by authorized organizations. Rather than storing these credentials in a centralized government database, individuals hold them in their own NDI Wallets and decide what information to share when accessing services. A shared registry on Ethereum helps participating services verify the authenticity of these credentials without publishing them on the network. Bhutanese institutions remain responsible for determining which organizations can issue trusted credentials, while individuals retain greater control over their personal information. A different challenge arises in humanitarian assistance, where organizations serving overlapping populations need to coordinate support without unnecessarily sharing sensitive personal records. Drawing on discussions with humanitarian organizations and work with engineers and product leads, the Ethereum Foundation's Technical Foundations team developed a proof of concept exploring how aid coordination could work on Ethereum's public network while protecting sensitive personal information. The approach combines decentralized identity and private payment mechanisms. Participating organizations can coordinate through shared infrastructure without needing to exchange the personal records they hold, or rely on a single agency to operate the underlying network. Each organization retains responsibility for the information it collects and the assistance it provides. The Technical Foundations team has published a series of articles examining the proof of concept in greater depth, including its technical design, key learnings, and directions for future development. The long-term promise of digital public infrastructure is not simply that more services can be connected. It is that institutions can cooperate without surrendering their independence, while individuals can participate in digital systems with greater control over their personal information. Ethereum can support both objectives through open, shared infrastructure that no single organization controls.

extraction.body: While AI and memory stocks get hammered on bubble fears, these three companies just posted sold-out demand, record revenue, and raised guidance. Artificial intelligence (AI) stocks have been getting hammered for weeks now, and the headlines all sound the same: bubble fears, AI financing anxiety, investors suddenly nervous that the hundreds of billions pouring into data centers won't pay off. Vertiv's third-quarter results beat estimates, and management raised full-year net sales guidance to $13.5 billion to $14 billion, yet the stock still sits well below its earlier high this year, dragged down by the same hyperscaler spending worries hitting everything AI-adjacent.

The company has also been buying its way into adjacent capabilities, picking up a microgrid developer and two liquid-cooling specialists this year, building out a fuller stack of what a next-generation data center actually needs. A business raising guidance while its stock gets punished for sectorwide anxiety is the definition of a gap between price and reality.

I'm not going to pretend none of this carries risk. AI capital spending could genuinely slow , and all three of these stocks would feel it if that happens. But that's a different risk than the one the market is currently pricing in, which is closer to panic than analysis. Each of these companies backed up its business with real numbers this earnings season: record demand, raised guidance, sold-out production, while the stock price moved in the opposite direction. That gap doesn't last forever. Buying into fear only works when the fear turns out to be bigger than the problem, and based on what these three companies just reported, that's exactly where we are right now.

passages: Binance announced Monday it had secured assets covering approximately 95% of the $6.3 billion in digital currencies stolen last Thursday in the largest cryptocurrency breach on record.

He purchased various cryptocurrencies on the open market and published evidence based on cryptographically verified internal records and blockchain transactions to substantiate the recovery efforts.The Federal Bureau of Investigation and independent analysts have attributed the attack to TraderTraitor, a North Korean state-linked hacking group previously associated with several major cryptocurrency thefts.

The incident has renewed criticism of the cryptocurrency sector's lack of government-backed deposit insurance available to traditional banking customers — protections absent from an industry that remains largely unregulated compared with conventional financial institutions.Cryptocurrency exchanges have frequently been targeted by North Korean hackers, with some platforms unable to fully compensate users for their losses.

Indian exchange WazirX, for example, lost approximately $234 million — nearly half of its assets — in a 2024 hack and subsequently underwent restructuring, unlike Binance which maintains sufficient reserves to absorb the current breach.The hack has also raised questions about whether artificial intelligence could be used to identify and exploit vulnerabilities in financial systems, although there is currently no clear evidence that AI was used in the Binance attack.

The exchange said it would fully cover user losses through a combination of corporate assets, an insurance fund, and a $1 billion strategic bitcoin reserve.Changpeng Zhao, the company's former chief executive who remains its largest shareholder, sought to reassure customers as the platform resumed withdrawals following a temporary suspension.

extraction.body: Here’s a question straight out of sci-fi: What if AI could predict what you were going to do before you decided to, even in a completely new situation? Israeli startup 42AI says it is developing a “behavioral world model” that can do just that, and it has just come out of stealth with $62.5 million in seed funding. The company is initially running its predictive system at a handful of financial brokerages, where it says the model can help predict how individual traders will respond to volatile conditions. “Behavior is not deterministic; it’s constantly probabilistic,” 42AI’s CEO and co-founder Amit Gal-Or told TechCrunch when I asked him to justify his company’s tall claim. He argues that people have underlying psychological tendencies that influence their decisions even when their circumstances change, and that’s what the startup is trying to measure and convert into data that the model can understand. “A week from now, you might be a different person, but your tendencies will always play out in certain areas to a probability or distribution,” his co-founder and CTO Ehud Ezra added. And that, the company argues, is what the model does: show the probability of a person making a certain decision. 42AI says the model tries to figure out people’s internal motivations instead of extrapolating patterns based on their previous actions. To do that, 42AI examines how people react to seemingly unrelated events. For an investor or trader, for example, such events might include completing KYC processes, onboarding, support calls, money transfers, or trading stocks. “When the person is talking to support or sales in the initial process […] we’re looking at the sentiment, we’re looking at the voice, we’re looking at a lot of interactions that they’re doing, how many times do they call, and so forth,” added Ezra. “And all of those data points are going into the model. Later on, you have the interactions: how you buy and sell, and when, and we’re looking at the market at that stage.” “So we’re trying to look at how they’re looking at the world. In a world model, every individual is the world,” he added. The company then converts those observations into mathematical representations of traits, which are then fed into a transformer-based world model that lays out probabilities for possible decisions under different circumstances. (The company uses a separate language model to generate explanations for its predictions.) Ezra said the model is trained to preserve a person’s underlying tendencies during simulations. So if someone is usually risk-averse, but the model suddenly treats them as a risk-taker, “the target is off,” he said, explaining how the model’s training rewards are structured. 42AI spent three years developing this approach, combining psychological research with neuroscience and genetics, as well as advice from experts in psychology and PTSD, and Dan Shechtman, who was awarded the 2011 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Gal-Or said the team first studied thousands of people via psych assessments and behavioral scenarios, before adding government and biobank datasets covering more than 2 million people. Its customer datasets have since expanded to cover almost 30 million people, he said. In live deployments, the model analyzes customers’ existing records, including transactions and support calls. Gal-Or pointed out the system doesn’t need personally identifiable information, arguing that “the model never knows who the person is.” However, it seems the company still creates individual behavioral profiles from linked customer activity. He also said the model consistently achieves an F1 score of 0.8 to 0.85 for predicting trading direction and volume. (F1 score is a metric in machine learning that measures how well a classification model can balance correct predictions against false alarms and missed events.)

And it’s not like the model can work everywhere, given it’s still a machine in a box. “There’s a natural ceiling because you really don’t have access to everything that a person experiences,” Gal-Or said. Ezra explained that the system’s accuracy also suffers when it misses important situational context, like if someone chooses to change their trading choices based on advice from a friend or a colleague.

Gal-Or said 42AI is working with 10 large brokerages, who are using it to manage liquidity, margin requirements, and hedging exposure. The company is onboarding more customers, he said, and is generating more than “seven figures” in revenue, though he wouldn’t specify a number.

Customers pay the startup a flat fee, or a percentage of the value the platform helps them gain. He claimed one brokerage generated approximately $30 million in additional value through dynamic hedging.

The $62.5 million seed funding came from the founders and Infinity Group over three years, and wasn’t entirely raised from external investors, Gal-Or said. Infinity was founded by his father, Amir Gal-Or, who is also 42AI’s chairman and a co-founder. 42AI now plans to raise more money.

Beyond finance, 42AI is now exploring applications for its model in gaming, fraud prevention, and cybersecurity, and one day wants to use it to help robots and AI agents understand people. But that may be a ways off yet: Ezra acknowledged that the model needs to be trained on rules and context for each new domain.

And like with all AI tools, there’s a potentially troubling side to 42AI’s technology: If a brokerage can anticipate what its customers may do, what’s to stop someone from using that knowledge to their own benefit? Ezra admitted that this was “a valid concern” when I raised it, and the founders pointed to regulations, monitoring, and an internal ethics committee, though they didn’t explain what, if anything, would stop their customers from using the technology to gain an advantage over the very people it’s profiling.
Amit Gal-Or, however, was confident that the technology could help address such risks. “We are very proud that actually we are part of the solution; we are the solution to this problem,” he said.
